NAMES.name: fast_electron_energy_due_to_electron_cyclotron_heating
NAMES.short: Population-integrated kinetic energy stored in the suprathermal electron population generated by electron cyclotron resonance heating.
NAMES.long: The fast electron energy quantifies the total kinetic energy $E_{\text{fast, e}} = \sum_i (\gamma_i - 1) m_e c^2$ of the suprathermal electron population produced by electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH) and current drive (ECCD). This stored energy represents a fraction of the injected EC wave power that is transferred to the non-thermal tail of the electron distribution rather than to the bulk Maxwellian. Typical values for ITER baseline scenarios are 0.1–1 MJ, depending on the ECRH power level and plasma parameters. The energy is inferred from electron cyclotron emission (ECE) measurements or from Fokker–Planck simulations that model the wave-particle interaction. This quantity is the electron counterpart of [fast_ion_energy_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating](name:fast_ion_energy_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating) and complements the global [diamagnetic stored energy](name:diamagnetic_stored_energy) diagnostic.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_absorbed_power_due_to_wave_particle_interaction
NAMES.short: Total power transferred from a coherent wave to the fast-ion population through resonant wave-particle interactions.
NAMES.long: The fast ion absorbed wave power quantifies the total energy per second deposited on suprathermal ions by a coherent electromagnetic wave, typically in the ion cyclotron range of frequencies (ICRF). This power transfer occurs through resonant Landau damping or cyclotron damping, where the wave's electric field component resonates with the fast ion gyromotion, governed by the resonant condition $\omega = n\Omega_{ci} + k_\parallel v_\parallel$, where $\omega$ is the wave frequency, $\Omega_{ci}$ is the ion cyclotron frequency, $k_\parallel$ is the parallel wave number, and $v_\parallel$ is the parallel velocity. Typical values range from 1 MW to 20 MW in present-day tokamaks for ICRF heating of fast ions from neutral beam injection or fusion-born alpha particles. This quantity is the spatial integral of the [fast_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density](name:fast_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density) over the plasma volume. The analogous quantity for thermal ions is the [thermal_ion_absorbed_power_due_to_wave_particle_interaction](name:thermal_ion_absorbed_power_due_to_wave_particle_interaction). Knowledge of this power deposition is essential for predicting fast ion confinement, energetic particle-driven instabilities, and fusion reactivity in burning plasmas.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_fast_electron_power_density
NAMES.short: Volumetric power density deposited onto the fast electron population, averaged over a magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long: The flux-surface-averaged power density quantifies the volumetric power transferred to the fast electron population by resonant wave-particle interactions, auxiliary heating, or other processes. It is defined as $\langle p_{\rm fast} \rangle = \frac{1}{V'(\psi)} \oint p_{\rm fast}(\psi, \theta) \frac{dS}{|\nabla \psi|}$, where $\psi$ is the poloidal flux label and $V'(\psi) = dV/d\psi$ is the flux-surface volume derivative. The fast electron population, with energies well above the thermal bulk, is commonly generated by electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH) or lower hybrid current drive. The typical range in fusion-grade plasmas spans from $10^5$ to $10^7\;{\rm W\,m^{-3}}$ near the resonance layers, depending on the injected power and damping profile. This quantity provides the radial source term for fast electron kinetic models and is related to the per-toroidal-mode decomposition [`per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_wave_power_density`](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_wave_power_density) via summation over toroidal mode number $n_\phi$.

NAMES.name: launched_power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna
NAMES.short: Net radio-frequency power delivered by an ion cyclotron heating antenna to the plasma, equal to the forward power minus the reflected power at the antenna input.
NAMES.long: The ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) launched power $P_{\mathrm{launched,IC}}$ is the net RF power coupled from the antenna into the vacuum vessel, representing the forward minus reflected power measured at the antenna transmission line. This quantity determines the maximum power available for absorption by the plasma and is a key input to ICRH system design and plant energy balance calculations. Typical launched power values for individual antennas range from 1–6 MW per antenna in present-day large tokamaks (e.g., JET, DIII-D, AUG) and are planned at up to 20 MW per antenna for ITER. The launched power is distinct from the power actually coupled into the plasma, which depends on the antenna–plasma coupling resistance, and is related to the [power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna](name:power_of_ion_cyclotron_heating_antenna) as the coupled power. This quantity is measured by directional couplers and power meters in the antenna transmission lines and is used as a boundary condition for wave propagation and heating codes.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_launching_position
NAMES.short: Major radius (R) coordinate of the point from which a diagnostic or heating system launches its beam or line of sight into the plasma.
NAMES.long: The launching position is the spatial origin of a beam-based plasma system, such as a microwave launcher for electron cyclotron heating or the entry point of a Thomson scattering laser. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, this coordinate specifies the major radius $R$ of that starting point. Typical values range from 2.0 to 3.0 m in medium-size tokamaks and up to 6.5 m in ITER. The launching position is directly related to the beam path geometry and is used together with the beam direction to define the trajectory. See also [major_radius_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:major_radius_of_beam_tracing_beam) for the propagating beam coordinate along the trajectory.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R$ increases outward from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: minimum_of_ion_state_charge
NAMES.short: Minimum ionization charge state Z of the ion charge-state bundle in wave deposition profiles.
NAMES.long: This quantity defines the lower ionization charge state $Z_{\mathrm{min}}$ of a bundled group of charge states for a given ion species, as used in wave deposition profile calculations. When multiple charge states are combined into a single bundle for computational efficiency (e.g., in ICRF modeling), $Z_{\mathrm{min}}$ specifies the lowest charge state in that bundle; for a single-state bundle it equals $Z_{\mathrm{max}}$. The value is an integer dimensionless charge number $Z$. The parent quantity [ion_state_charge](name:ion_state_charge) represents each individual charge state in the bundle, while the sibling [maximum_of_ion_state_charge](name:maximum_of_ion_state_charge) gives the upper bound of the same bundle. This quantity is used together with [ion_state_atomic_number](name:ion_state_atomic_number) to fully describe the ionization state of the ion species in wave heating models.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the charge state $Z_{\mathrm{min}}$ corresponds to a higher degree of ionization (more electrons removed).

NAMES.name: parallel_refractive_index
NAMES.short: Component of the wave refractive index along the local magnetic field direction, evaluated along a beam-tracing ray path.
NAMES.long:
The parallel refractive index $N_{\parallel} = \mathbf{N} \cdot \hat{b}$ is the projection of the wave refractive index vector $\mathbf{N} = c \mathbf{k} / \omega$ onto the local magnetic field direction $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B} / |\mathbf{B}|$, where $c$ is the speed of light, $\mathbf{k}$ is the wave vector (in m$^{-1}$), and $\omega$ is the angular frequency (in rad/s). It determines the parallel phase velocity $v_{\phi,\parallel} = c / N_{\parallel}$ and sets the resonance condition for electron cyclotron (EC) and ion cyclotron (IC) heating, where $\omega - k_{\parallel} v_{\parallel} = n \Omega_c$, with $n$ an integer harmonic and $\Omega_c$ the cyclotron frequency. Along an ECE or beam-tracing ray path, $N_{\parallel}$ evolves through the plasma according to the cold-plasma or warm-plasma dispersion relation and is a key parameter in accessibility calculations and absorption modeling.

See the parent vector quantity [refractive_index](name:refractive_index) for the full two-component description. The perpendicular complement is [perpendicular_refractive_index](name:perpendicular_refractive_index), and the related normalized components [normalized_parallel_wave_vector](name:normalized_parallel_wave_vector) and [normalized_perpendicular_wave_vector](name:normalized_perpendicular_wave_vector) provide an alternative decomposition. In fusion plasmas, typical values of $N_{\parallel}$ range from near unity for electron cyclotron waves to order 10 for ion cyclotron waves, depending on launch conditions and plasma parameters.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wave vector component $k_{\parallel}$ points in the direction of the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: particle_flux_due_to_neutral_beam_shinethrough
NAMES.short: Particle flux lost from the plasma due to neutral beam injection particles that traverse the plasma without ionizing.
NAMES.long: The shinethrough particle flux quantifies the rate at which neutral beam particles exit the plasma without undergoing ionization inside the confined region. These neutrals are lost through the last closed flux surface and deposit their energy and particles onto plasma-facing components, primarily the first wall. The flux is computed from the beam attenuation along its path through the plasma, integrating the neutral density lost via shinethrough for each beamlet. Shinethrough losses are most significant at low plasma density, high beam energy, or in the plasma edge, where the ionization mean free path exceeds the plasma chord length. Typical values for neutral beam injection in present-day tokamaks range from $10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ s$^{-1}$ depending on the beam energy and target density, decreasing at higher densities where beam collisional ionization becomes more effective. This quantity complements the associated power loss described by [power_due_to_neutral_beam_shinethrough](name:power_due_to_neutral_beam_shinethrough). The particle flux compares with the incident beam particle flux and the fraction of ions that are thermalized in the core, which are not part of the shinethrough process.
NAMES.sign: Positive when particles are lost from the plasma due to shinethrough.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_fast_electron_absorbed_wave_power_density
NAMES.short: Volumetric power density deposited onto the fast electron population by auxiliary wave heating, resolved per toroidal mode number.
NAMES.long: This quantity represents the local power density $P_{n_\phi}(R,Z)$ absorbed by the fast (suprathermal) electron population from a coherent auxiliary wave, decomposed by toroidal mode number $n_\phi$. It is obtained from full-wave or ray-tracing codes that compute the spatial distribution of wave power absorption on the fast electron distribution function, typically via quasi-linear diffusion models. In tokamaks, fast electrons are generated by electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH) and lower hybrid current drive, with absorbed power densities ranging from $10^3$ to $10^6~\mathrm{W/m^3}$ in the core depending on the heating system and plasma parameters. The sum over all toroidal mode numbers of this quantity recovers the total absorbed power density on fast electrons: $P_{\mathrm{fast}}(R,Z) = \sum_{n_\phi} P_{n_\phi}(R,Z)$. For the corresponding quantity on thermal electrons, see [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_absorbed_wave_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_absorbed_wave_power_density); for the fast-ion analog, see [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density).

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density
NAMES.short: Absorbed wave power density deposited on fast ions by auxiliary heating, resolved per toroidal mode number.
NAMES.long: The per-toroidal-mode absorbed wave power density on fast ions quantifies the volumetric power transferred from a coherent wave (e.g., ICRF or lower hybrid) to the fast-ion population through resonant wave-particle interactions, decomposed by toroidal mode number $n_\phi$. This quantity is essential for modeling the spatial distribution of heating in the poloidal cross-section and for understanding the radial deposition profile of auxiliary power onto fast ions. The power density is typically computed from full-wave or ray-tracing codes (e.g., TORIC, AORSA, GENRAY) that solve the wave equation in toroidal geometry, yielding the local absorption rate $P_\mathrm{abs}(\psi, n_\phi) = \langle \mathbf{J}_\mathrm{fast} \cdot \mathbf{E} \rangle$, where $\mathbf{J}_\mathrm{fast}$ is the fast-ion current density driven by the wave electric field $\mathbf{E}$ and $\langle \cdot \rangle$ denotes a flux-surface average. Typical values in the plasma core range from $10^5$ to $10^7$ W/m$^3$ for dominant mode numbers, with the total power integrated over $n_\phi$ matching the species-specific absorbed power. Integrating over toroidal mode number $n_\phi$ recovers the total fast-ion absorbed wave power density (e.g., [fast_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density](name:fast_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density)), while the same decomposition for thermal ions is given by [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density). This quantity is sign-invariant as absorbed power is a positive-definite energy transfer.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_absorbed_wave_power_density
NAMES.short: Volumetric power density deposited onto the thermal electron population by auxiliary wave heating, resolved per toroidal mode number.
NAMES.long: This quantity describes the absorbed wave power per unit volume transferred from an auxiliary heating wave to the thermal electron population, separated by toroidal mode number $n$. It is defined locally in space and captures the spatial distribution of power deposition for each toroidal harmonic of the wave field. The total absorbed power density on thermal electrons is obtained by summing over all toroidal mode numbers. Typical values range from kW/m$^3$ in low-power scenarios to tens of MW/m$^3$ in high-power auxiliary heating, depending on wave frequency, plasma conditions, and resonance location.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the power flows from the wave field into the thermal electron population.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged absorbed RF power density on thermal ions resolved by toroidal mode number.
NAMES.long: The absorbed wave power density per unit volume on the thermal ion population, Fourier-decomposed in the toroidal direction. This quantity represents the volumetric power deposition $P_{\mathrm{th},i}(n_\phi)$ per toroidal mode number $n_\phi$, where $n_\phi$ is the toroidal mode number of the coherent wave. The total absorbed power density on thermal ions is obtained by summing over toroidal modes: $P_{\mathrm{th},i}^{\mathrm{total}} = \sum_{n_\phi} P_{\mathrm{th},i}(n_\phi)$. Typical values in ICRF-heated tokamak plasmas range from $0.1\, \mathrm{MW\, m^{-3}}$ in the core to $<0.01\, \mathrm{MW\, m^{-3}}$ at the edge, depending on the wave spectrum and plasma parameters. This quantity is commonly computed by full-wave or ray-tracing codes (e.g., TORIC, AORSA, GENRAY) that model RF wave propagation and damping in toroidal geometry. See also [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_absorbed_wave_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_electron_absorbed_wave_power_density) for the electron counterpart, and [fast_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density](name:fast_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density) for the fast-ion contribution without toroidal mode resolution.

NAMES.name: per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_due_to_wave_particle_interaction
NAMES.short: Wave power absorbed by the thermal ion population, integrated over the plasma volume and resolved per toroidal mode number.
NAMES.long:
This quantity represents the total, volume-integrated power deposited onto the thermal ion population by a coherent electromagnetic wave, decomposed by the toroidal mode number $n_\phi$ of the wave. It is obtained by summing the local absorbed power density over the plasma volume for each toroidal harmonic. The power transferred to thermal ions is a key figure of merit for heating schemes such as ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH).

Typical values for this quantity in high-power ICRH scenarios range from a few MW up to tens of MW, depending on the auxiliary heating power, plasma parameters, and antenna coupling efficiency. The toroidal mode spectrum is determined by the antenna geometry and plasma response. This quantity differs from the volumetric power density resolved per toroidal mode, `[per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density)`, by being an integrated total. It is also related to the total power absorbed by all thermal species, `[thermal_ion_absorbed_power_due_to_wave_particle_interaction](name:thermal_ion_absorbed_power_due_to_wave_particle_interaction)`, which sums over all toroidal mode numbers.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net power flows from the wave field to the thermal ion population.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_refractive_index
NAMES.short: Component of the wave refractive index perpendicular to the local magnetic field direction.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular refractive index $n_{\perp} = \mathbf{n} \cdot \hat{e}_{\perp}$ is the projection of the refractive index vector $\mathbf{n} = c\mathbf{k}/\omega$ onto the direction perpendicular to the local magnetic field, where $c$ is the speed of light, $\mathbf{k}$ is the wave vector, and $\omega$ is the wave angular frequency. Together with the [parallel refractive index](name:parallel_refractive_index), this component determines the propagation and polarization of electromagnetic waves in the magnetized plasma, governing the accessibility conditions for electron cyclotron resonance heating. In beam-tracing codes for ECRH, $n_{\perp}$ is evaluated along the ray path using the cold-plasma or warm-plasma dispersion relation; typical values range from 0.5 to 2.0 in the plasma core for O-mode and X-mode waves at 100–200 GHz.

See [refractive_index](name:refractive_index) for the full vector description.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $n_{\perp}$ points in the direction of increasing $\mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{e}_{\perp}$.

NAMES.name: power_due_to_neutral_beam_injection
NAMES.short: Net thermal power deposited onto plasma-facing wall components by incident neutral particles.
NAMES.long: The power due to neutral beam injection represents the thermal energy flux carried by neutral particles—both beam-injected and charge-exchange-generated—that strike the first wall. In the scrape-off layer, charge-exchange neutrals and beam neutrals that are not fully ionized deposit energy on wall surfaces, contributing to the global wall heat load. This quantity is the surface-integrated power $P_\mathrm{n} = \int_S \Gamma_\mathrm{n} \, E_\mathrm{n} \, dS$, where $\Gamma_\mathrm{n}$ is the neutral particle flux density (m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$) and $E_\mathrm{n}$ is the mean energy per neutral (eV). Positive values indicate net power deposition onto the wall. Typical values in present-day tokamaks range from 1–100 MW for NBI-heated plasmas, depending on beam energy, plasma density, and neutral penetration depth. The related quantity [neutral_count_of_wall](name:neutral_count_of_wall) tracks the cumulative particle inventory, while [ion_particle_flux_at_wall](name:ion_particle_flux_at_wall) gives the corresponding charged-particle energy flux.

NAMES.name: radial_wave_vector
NAMES.short: Radial (major radius R) component of the EC beam wave vector at the launcher launch point.
NAMES.long: The radial component $k_R$ of the wave vector $\mathbf{k}$ for an electron cyclotron (EC) beam, evaluated at the launching aperture in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This component determines the radial spatial oscillation rate of the wave phase and, together with the vertical and toroidal components, defines the beam propagation direction in the plasma. Typical values for EC launchers range from $-10$ to $10\,\text{m}^{-1}$, depending on the launch angle and EC frequency. This quantity is the unnormalized counterpart of the normalized radial wave vector $[k_{R,\text{norm}} = k_R / |\mathbf{k}|]$ (see `[normalized_perpendicular_wave_vector](name:normalized_perpendicular_wave_vector)` for its normalized form). The radial wave vector is an input to beam-tracing codes that model EC wave propagation and absorption. It is also related to the launching geometry via `[major_radius_of_launching_position](name:major_radius_of_launching_position)` and the beam spot size `[size_of_b eam_tracing_beam](name:size_of_beam_tracing_beam)`.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_absorbed_power_density_due_to_wave_particle_interaction
NAMES.short: Volumetric power density absorbed by the thermal ion population through resonant wave-particle interactions, averaged over a magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long: The quantity $P_{abs,i}^{th}$ represents the power per unit volume transferred from a coherent auxiliary wave (e.g., ICRF, LH) to the thermal ion population via resonant wave-particle interactions, evaluated as a flux-surface-averaged radial profile. It is derived from the wave electric field and the ion susceptibility tensor, $P_{abs}^{th} = \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{Re}\left( \mathbf{j}_{abs}^{th} \cdot \mathbf{E}^* \right)$, where $\mathbf{j}_{abs}^{th}$ is the induced current density in the thermal ion population. Deposition profiles are typically computed by ray-tracing or full-wave codes coupled to a quasilinear Fokker–Planck solver; in tokamaks, core values can reach several MW/m$^3$ for high-power ICRF heating. The flux-surface-averaged absorbed power density on thermal ions is distinguished from the total [absorbed_wave_power_density](name:absorbed_wave_power_density) by considering only the thermal ion channel. See also [thermal_ion_power_density_due_to_wave_particle_interaction](name:thermal_ion_power_density_due_to_wave_particle_interaction) and the per-toroidal-mode counterpart [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density).

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_absorbed_power_due_to_wave_particle_interaction
NAMES.short: Total wave power absorbed by the thermal ion population through resonant wave-particle interactions, integrated over the full plasma volume.
NAMES.long: This quantifies the total power $P_{\text{th},i}$ transferred from a launched auxiliary wave (e.g., ion cyclotron or lower hybrid wave) to the thermal ion population via resonant wave-particle interactions. The power is the volume integral of the absorbed power density over the plasma, with the two-dimensional profile captured by [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_absorbed_wave_power_density). For a wave field with multiple toroidal mode numbers $n_\phi$, the total absorbed power for each $n_\phi$ is obtained by summing the contributions from the Fourier components of the wave field, and the total power across all modes is the sum over $n_\phi$: $P_{\text{th},i,\text{total}} = \sum_{n_\phi} P_{\text{th},i}(n_\phi)$. Typical values for ion cyclotron heating in medium-size tokamaks (e.g., JET, DIII-D) range from 1–15 MW for a single antenna. The related quantity [per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_power) captures the power deposited onto the fast (suprathermal) ion population, which is often a critical component of the heating scheme when ion cyclotron resonances generate fast-ion tails.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_power_density_due_to_wave_particle_interaction
NAMES.short: Volumetric wave power density deposited onto the thermal ion population through resonant wave-particle interactions.
NAMES.long: The volumetric power density $P_{\mathrm{th,i}}$ quantifies the rate of energy transfer from an auxiliary radio-frequency wave to thermal ions via resonant wave-particle interactions. In the quasi-linear regime, the local power transfer is $P_{\mathrm{th,i}} = \langle \mathbf{j}_\mathrm{th,i} \cdot \mathbf{E} \rangle$, where $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{th,i}$ is the driven current density on thermal ions and $\mathbf{E}$ is the wave electric field. This quantity is evaluated as a 2D poloidal cross-section profile, resolving the spatial structure of deposition not captured by flux-surface-averaged quantities. Typical values reach $10^5$–$10^7\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$ in the core of ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) scenarios, with the peak located near the ion cyclotron resonance layer. It is modeled by ray-tracing or full-wave codes (e.g., TORIC, AORS), coupled with a quasi-linear Fokker–Planck solver, and is a key input for transport simulations. See also [thermal_ion_absorbed_power_density_due_to_wave_particle_interaction](name:thermal_ion_absorbed_power_density_due_to_wave_particle_interaction) for the flux-surface-averaged counterpart, and [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_density) for the decomposition in toroidal mode number.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_power_due_to_wave_particle_interaction
NAMES.short: Wave power absorbed by the thermal ion population through resonant wave-particle interactions, integrated over the plasma volume.
NAMES.long: This quantity represents the net power transferred from a coherent electromagnetic wave, typically in the ion cyclotron range of frequencies (ICRF), to the thermal ion population. The absorbed power $P_{\rm therm, i} = \int_V p_{\rm abs}(\mathbf{r})\, dV$ is the volume integral of the local absorbed power density $p_{\rm abs}(\mathbf{r})$ over the plasma region. It is a key metric for assessing the efficiency of RF heating schemes, such as ICRH minority heating or mode conversion heating, in raising the bulk ion temperature. Typical absorbed powers from ICRF systems in medium-size tokamaks range from 1 to 10 MW depending on the plasma scenario and antenna coupling. This quantity is distinguished from the power absorbed by fast ions via [fast_ion_absorbed_power_due_to_wave_particle_interaction](name:fast_ion_absorbed_power_due_to_wave_particle_interaction) and from the spectral decomposition in [per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_due_to_wave_particle_interaction](name:per_toroidal_mode_thermal_ion_power_due_to_wave_particle_interaction). The absorbed power is computed by integrating the local power density from RF full-wave or ray-tracing codes (e.g., TORIC, AORSA, GENRAY) over the plasma volume.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_launching_position
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle coordinate of the point from which a heating or diagnostic system launches its beam into the plasma.
NAMES.long: The toroidal launching position angle $\phi_{\rm launch}$ identifies the toroidal location in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where the beam centerline exits the launcher aperture or waveguide. This angle, measured in radians, sets the toroidal injection geometry and influences the wave propagation path, absorption location, and current drive efficiency. The position is defined at the launcher exit aperture or the first wall penetration point, depending on the system design. This coordinate is paired with the major radius and vertical coordinates through `major_radius_of_launching_position` and `vertical_coordinate_of_launching_position` to fully specify the beam origin. The toroidal angle is measured from a reference direction (typically the midplane of a toroidal field coil or the machine equatorial plane), with positive values corresponding to the direction of increasing toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system. For electron cyclotron launchers, typical values range from 0 to $2\pi$ radians, with the specific angle determined by the launcher port location and steering capability. The coordinate is defined irrespective of the launching system type, applying equally to electron cyclotron, ion cyclotron, and neutral beam injection systems.

NAMES.name: toroidal_fast_particle_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the torque density exerted on fast particles by the J×B force due to radial currents.
NAMES.long: This quantity gives the volumetric torque density $\tau_\phi = (\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B})_\phi$ acting on the fast-particle population, resolved in the toroidal direction. It represents the local exchange of toroidal angular momentum between the fast ions and the bulk plasma via the Lorentz force produced by radial currents (e.g., from neutral beam injection or wave-driven transport). Typical values in the core of a beam-heated tokamak range from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-1}\,\text{N}\,\text{m}^{-2}$, depending on beam power and fast-ion pressure gradients. The toroidal component is distinguished from the total vector torque density by its projection onto the $\hat{\phi}$ direction, and integrating it over the plasma volume yields the total [toroidal torque](name:toroidal_torque). For the full vector quantity, see [fast_particle_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force](name:fast_particle_torque_density_due_to_j_cross_b_force).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the torque accelerates the fast particles in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above).

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_beamlet_group
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the beamlet group center within a neutral beam injector unit in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ defines the height of the beamlet group center relative to the tokamak midplane ($Z = 0$). This geometric datum determines the aiming and alignment of the neutral beam with respect to the plasma, affecting the beam deposition profile and shine-through losses. Typical values range from -1 m to +1 m depending on the vertical port allocation of the beamline. The coordinate is measured or designed as part of the beamline geometry and is referenced alongside the major radius coordinate to fully locate the beamlet group. This quantity follows the same spatial-sign convention as all vertical positions in the IMAS cylindrical frame, ensuring consistency across heating and diagnostic systems.

See also the beam orientation given by [angle_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:angle_of_neutral_beam_injector) and the analogous vertical coordinates for other components such as [vertical_coordinate_of_limiter](name:vertical_coordinate_of_limiter).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the beamlet group center lies above the tokamak midplane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_launching_position
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the beam launching position in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long: The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates the height of the point from which an auxiliary heating or diagnostic system launches its beam (e.g., an electron cyclotron heating launcher or a neutral beam injector). This coordinate is used together with the major radius coordinate to define the full launching position in the machine frame. Typical values for tokamak systems range from $-1$ to $+1$ m for mid-plane launchers and $\pm 0.5$ to $\pm 2$ m for off-axis launchers, depending on the port location. The pair of coordinates is [major_radius_of_launching_position](name:major_radius_of_launching_position).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the launching position is above the midplane ($Z = 0$), increasing in the vertical direction of the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_lower_hybrid_antenna_row
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the row reference point in a lower hybrid antenna, measured in the IMAS cylindrical frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z_{\rm LH,row}$ locates the center of a lower hybrid antenna row in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ increases vertically upward from the midplane. This coordinate is essential for modeling the poloidal launch spectrum of lower hybrid waves, which depends on the antenna row position relative to the magnetic flux surfaces. Typically measured in meters from the machine midplane, values in present tokamaks range from $\pm 0.5$ to $\pm 2$ m for multiple row arrays, scaling with the plasma major radius. The vertical coordinate is determined from engineering drawings or laser alignment surveys during installation and is used in ray tracing or full-wave codes to compute the wave coupling and deposition profile. See also [vertical_coordinate_of_launching_position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_launching_position) for the general launching geometry and [major_radius_of_launching_position](name:major_radius_of_launching_position) for the radial counterpart.

The row coordinate pairs with the radial coordinate of the antenna to fully define the launching position in the poloidal plane.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the antenna row is above the machine midplane ($Z>0$).

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the geometric center of the neutral beam injector aperture in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z_{\mathrm{NBI}}$ defines the height of the neutral beam injector aperture center relative to the tokamak midplane ($Z=0$). This geometric parameter determines the beam injection angle and vertical aiming of the neutral beam, which together with the major radius coordinate sets the beam-line geometry. The aperture center is a key reference point for beam alignment and is typically obtained from engineering drawings or laser tracker surveys of the installed system. Common NBI installations have aperture center heights ranging from -2 m to +2 m depending on the port location and machine size.

See also the vertical coordinates of the beam source components such as [vertical_coordinate_of_launching_position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_launching_position) and [vertical_coordinate_of_beamlet_group](name:vertical_coordinate_of_beamlet_group), which define related vertical positions within the same neutral beam injector unit.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the injector aperture center lies above the tokamak midplane ($Z>0$).

NAMES.name: argon_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Number density of argon impurity ions in the plasma layer immediately adjacent to the divertor target surface.
NAMES.long: The argon density at the divertor target quantifies the concentration of ionized argon impurities arriving at the plasma-facing surface. Argon is commonly injected as a radiative impurity to reduce the peak heat flux to the divertor through line radiation; its density near the target is determined by the balance between upstream transport, ionization, and recombination within the divertor volume. The quantity is routinely inferred from spectroscopic line ratios (e.g., Ar XVI to Ar XVIII emission) combined with collisional-radiative modeling, or from Langmuir probe measurements assuming known argon charge-state distribution. Typical values in seeded-divertor operation range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on the seeding rate and divertor detachment state. The argon density is closely coupled to the electron density and electron temperature at the target, and it directly affects the divertor radiation front location and the total ion density at the target.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the number density of argon ions is defined, increasing as the ion density rises in the plasma layer contacting the target.

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Number density of free electrons in the plasma layer immediately adjacent to the divertor target surface.
NAMES.long:
The electron density at the divertor target, $n_{e,\text{target}}$, is a key parameter in the two-point model of the scrape-off layer (SOL). It controls the ion saturation current density, $j_{\text{sat}} = e n_e c_s$, where $e$ is the elementary charge and $c_s$ is the sound speed, and sets the power flux to the target via the sheath heat transmission. Typical values range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ in high-recycling and detached divertor conditions, and are inferred from Langmuir probe measurements or spectroscopic line ratios combined with collisional-radiative modeling.

The electron density is closely coupled to the [electron temperature at the target](name:electron_temperature_at_divertor_target) through pressure balance along the field line and to the [total ion density](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target) via quasi-neutrality.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the number of electrons per unit volume is defined.

NAMES.name: electron_power_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Total thermal power carried by electrons to the inner divertor target surface.
NAMES.long: The electron power at the inner divertor target is the integral of the incident electron heat flux density over the target surface area. It represents the power transported by the electron population along open magnetic field lines to the divertor region, typically dominated by parallel transport and sheath acceleration. The power is positive when electrons deposit energy onto the target (i.e., net power flow into the surface). Typical values in a tokamak range from kilowatts to tens of megawatts, scaling with the input heating power and divertor geometry. This quantity is measured via Langmuir probes or inferred from infrared thermography and spectroscopy.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Electron temperature of the plasma incident on the divertor target surface.
NAMES.long:
The electron temperature at the divertor target, $T_{e,\mathrm{div}}$, quantifies the thermal energy of electrons striking the divertor plate. It is a critical parameter for determining the heat flux deposited on the target, the onset of detachment, and the erosion rate of plasma-facing components. Typical values range from 1–10 eV in detached plasmas to 20–100 eV in attached, high-recycling regimes, measured by Langmuir probes or interpreted from spectrometer line ratios. This quantity is closely related to the [ion_temperature_at_divertor_target](name:ion_temperature_at_divertor_target) and the [scrape_off_layer_heat_length_at_divertor_target](name:scrape_off_layer_heat_length_at_divertor_target), which together characterize the divertor plasma state.

In steady-state conditions, the target electron temperature is governed by parallel power balance along the magnetic field line and the sheath heat transmission factors. For attached plasmas, $T_{e,\mathrm{div}}$ scales approximately with the upstream temperature $T_{e,u}$ as $T_{e,\mathrm{div}} \approx T_{e,u} / 2$ under the two-point model, while strong divertor radiation or detachment reduces it below 5 eV.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron temperature value is greater than zero.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Number density of singly-ionized helium-3 (³He⁺) particles in the plasma layer incident on the divertor target surface.
NAMES.long:
The helium-3 density at the divertor target quantifies the ³He⁺ ion concentration in the plasma scrape-off layer as it reaches the target surface. This density is determined by the balance between core helium-3 transport, edge neutral recycling, and divertor pumping — processes critical for controlling fusion ash accumulation and fuel mixture in reactors. Typical divertor target densities span 10¹⁶–10¹⁹ m⁻³ in tokamaks, depending on heating power, divertor regime, and helium-3 gas injection rate. The density is inferred from spectroscopic line emission measurements (e.g., He II 468.6 nm) combined with collisional-radiative modeling, or from target Langmuir probe data combined with local ion composition analysis. The companion quantity [total_ion_density_at_divertor_target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target) gives the sum over all species, while [helium_3_density_at_separatrix](name:helium_3_density_at_separatrix) provides the upstream reference.

In diverted configurations, the helium-3 density at the target is a key boundary condition for both core impurity transport modeling, via the [helium_3_density_at_pedestal](name:helium_3_density_at_pedestal), and for helium exhaust optimization in steady-state reactor scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the number density of helium-3 ions is defined in the rest frame of the target surface, i.e., positive for any finite particle concentration.

NAMES.name: helium_4_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Number density of singly-ionized helium-4 (⁴He⁺) particles in the plasma layer immediately adjacent to the divertor target surface.
NAMES.long: The helium-4 density at the divertor target quantifies the concentration of singly-ionized ⁴He⁺ ions incident on the target surface. In burning-plasma scenarios, ⁴He is the primary fusion ash, and its accumulation in the divertor region affects tritium retention and core fueling. The local density $n_{⁴He⁺}$ is governed by transport along the scrape-off layer and by volumetric recombination and ionization processes. Typical divertor target densities for helium ash range from $10^{17}$ to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on the core fusion rate and the divertor detachment state. This quantity is inferred from spectroscopic line emission (e.g., He II 468.6 nm) interpreted through collisional-radiative models, or from Langmuir-probe ion-saturation current with mass-resolved correction. It is naturally paired with $[\text{argon\_density\_at\_divertor\_target}](name:argon_density_at_divertor_target)$ and $[\text{electron\_density\_at\_divertor\_target}](name:electron_density_at_divertor_target)$ to characterize impurity and fuel species in the divertor plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the local density of ⁴He⁺ particles is non-zero in the plasma layer immediately adjacent to the target surface.

NAMES.name: ion_temperature_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Thermal energy of the ion population incident on the divertor target, averaged over all ion species.
NAMES.long: The ion temperature at the divertor target is the mean thermal energy per ion, averaged over all ion species present in the incident plasma, expressed as a temperature via $T_i = 2 \langle E_i \rangle / (3 k_B)$. It is a key parameter controlling the plasma heat flux to the target surface, the ion impact energy for sputtering, and the sheath potential drop. Typical values range from 1–50 eV in detached divertor conditions to 50–200 eV in attached regimes. The ion temperature is often inferred from Langmuir probe measurements (assuming $T_i \approx T_e$) or from spectroscopic line broadening. For comparison, the [electron temperature at the divertor target](name:electron_temperature_at_divertor_target) can differ significantly from the ion temperature in detached plasmas due to thermal decoupling.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion thermal motion is directed toward the target surface.

NAMES.name: iron_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Number density of ionized iron impurity in the plasma layer immediately adjacent to the divertor target surface.
NAMES.long:
The iron density $n_{\mathrm{Fe}}$ at the divertor target quantifies the local concentration of sputtered or injected iron impurity ions, which can radiatively cool the divertor plasma and affect erosion rates. In tokamaks, iron impurities typically originate from plasma-facing components (e.g., steel tiles) and are transported along field lines into the divertor region. Typical values range from $10^{14}\,\text{m}^{-3}$ in well-controlled low-Z scenarios to $10^{18}\,\text{m}^{-3}$ during high-recycling or detached regimes with elevated sputtering. This density is routinely derived from spectroscopic line emission or from probe measurements combined with collisional-radiative modeling. The quantity is closely related to [iron_density_at_separatrix](name:iron_density_at_separatrix) and to the total impurity inventory [total_ion_density_at_divertor_target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target).

The local iron density also influences the [ion_temperature_at_divertor_target](name:ion_temperature_at_divertor_target) through radiation losses and charge-exchange energy exchange, and is a key input for erosion modeling alongside the target heat flux.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the iron impurity ion density is measured as a particle number per unit volume.

NAMES.name: krypton_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Number density of krypton impurity ions incident on the plasma-facing surface of the divertor target.
NAMES.long: The krypton density at the divertor target $n_{\mathrm{Kr}}(R_{\mathrm{targ}})$ quantifies the local concentration of injected or intrinsic krypton impurities in the plasma layer immediately adjacent to the target surface. Krypton is commonly introduced as a radiative impurity to reduce peak heat fluxes in the divertor, and its density is inferred from spectroscopic line emission (e.g., Kr VIII at 133.7 nm) combined with collisional-radiative modeling, or from residual gas analyzer signals calibrated against known injection rates. Typical values range from $10^{14}$ to $10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$ in attached divertor conditions and increase in detached or high-density regimes as the impurity accumulates near the target. Understanding $n_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is critical for predicting radiative losses, fuel dilution, and erosion of tungsten plasma-facing components. For comparison across impurity species, see [iron_density_at_divertor_target](name:iron_density_at_divertor_target); the total ion population is captured by [total_ion_density_at_divertor_target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the number density of krypton ions is defined as a non-negative quantity.

NAMES.name: lithium_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Number density of lithium impurity ions in the plasma layer incident on the divertor target surface.
NAMES.long:
Lithium is commonly injected into tokamaks for wall conditioning and plasma-facing surface coating. The lithium density at the divertor target quantifies the local concentration of ionized lithium, which can affect recycling, radiative losses, and plasma dilution in the divertor region. Typical values range from $10^{15}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on the seeding rate, divertor regime, and proximity to the strike point. This quantity is inferred from spectroscopic line emission (e.g., Li II 548.5 nm) combined with collisional-radiative modeling or from local Langmuir probe measurements with mass discrimination. The sister quantity [iron_density_at_divertor_target](name:iron_density_at_divertor_target) captures a similar impurity species, while [total_ion_density_at_divertor_target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target) gives the total ion inventory at the target.

Measurement context includes divertor spectroscopy arrays and retarding-field analyzers, with spatial resolution along the divertor target surface. The density profile is sensitive to the divertor thermal state, with higher values typically observed in detached regimes where volumetric recombination is suppressed. Cross-calibration against [electron_density_at_divertor_target](name:electron_density_at_divertor_target) helps constrain the ionization balance of lithium within the divertor plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when defined.

NAMES.name: neon_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Number density of ionized neon impurity in the plasma layer immediately adjacent to the divertor target surface.
NAMES.long: Neon density at the divertor target quantifies the local concentration of ionized neon (Ne$^{+}$) within the sheath or presheath region adjacent to the target plate. It is a key metric for impurity seeding scenarios in tokamaks, where neon is injected to radiate power and reduce heat flux to the divertor. The density depends on the local ionization source, transport along field lines (often from the core or separatrix), and the recombination sink at the target surface. Typical values range from $10^{15}$ to $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in H-mode plasmas, scaling with the injected neon puff rate and the divertor neutral pressure. Measurement is obtained via spectroscopy (line emission from excited neutral neon near the target) combined with collisional-radiative modeling. This quantity is the natural partner to `electron_temperature_at_divertor_target` in the two-point model, which relates upstream and target conditions along a flux tube. The number density is defined as the total count of Ne$^{+}$ ions per unit volume, and is intrinsically non-negative.
NAMES.sign: Positive when number density is non-negative.

NAMES.name: parallel_heat_flux_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Heat flux density parallel to the magnetic field line at the divertor target surface, mapped to the outboard midplane.
NAMES.long: The parallel heat flux $q_{\parallel}$ at the divertor target quantifies the power per unit area conducted and convected along the magnetic field onto the target surface. It is a key quantity governing divertor heat loads, target erosion, and detachment physics in tokamak scrape-off layer (SOL) plasmas. $q_{\parallel}$ is inferred from infra-red (IR) thermography of target surface temperatures, combined with heat-flux accounting that maps the measured power back along the field line to the outboard midplane. Typical values in high-power H-mode discharges range 10–100 MW/m² at the strike point, falling to 1–10 MW/m² in the far SOL. The total power deposited on the target is given by the integral of $q_{\parallel}$ over the wetted area; see [peak_heat_flux_at_divertor_target](name:peak_heat_flux_at_divertor_target) for the peak value and [scrape_off_layer_heat_length_at_divertor_target](name:scrape_off_layer_heat_length_at_divertor_target) for the radial decay length.

NAMES.name: peak_heat_flux_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Maximum heat flux density deposited on a divertor target surface from plasma interaction.
NAMES.long: The peak heat flux $q_{\text{peak}}$ is the maximum value of the power per unit area incident on a divertor target surface, typically located at or near the strike point where the plasma intercepts the target. It is a critical engineering parameter for assessing thermal loads on plasma-facing components, influencing material erosion and component lifetime. Measured using infrared thermography or Langmuir probes, typical values range from 1–15 MW/m² in H-mode tokamaks, with transient events like edge-localized modes producing much higher instantaneous fluxes. The peak heat flux depends on the scrape-off layer power width $\lambda_q$ as described by [scrape_off_layer_heat_length_at_divertor_target](name:scrape_off_layer_heat_length_at_divertor_target) and the local [electron_temperature_at_divertor_target](name:electron_temperature_at_divertor_target).

NAMES.name: total_ion_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Total ion particle density at the divertor target, summed over all ion species.
NAMES.long:
The total ion density $n_{\text{i,total}}$ at the divertor target surface quantifies the total number of ions (including main fuel and all impurity species) per unit volume incident on the plasma-facing component. This quantity is a key input for determining the particle flux $\Gamma = n_{\text{i,total}} v_{\parallel}$ onto the target and the resulting erosion, deposition, and hydrogenic recycling. Typical values in the divertor region range from $10^{19}\,\text{m}^{-3}$ in low-density attached plasmas to over $10^{21}\,\text{m}^{-3}$ in high-recycling or detached regimes. It is routinely inferred from Langmuir probe measurements (ion saturation current) and collisional-radiative modeling of spectroscopic line emission. See also [ion_temperature_at_divertor_target](name:ion_temperature_at_divertor_target) for the corresponding ion thermal energy, [iron_density_at_divertor_target](name:iron_density_at_divertor_target) for a specific impurity contribution, and [electron_temperature_at_divertor_target](name:electron_temperature_at_divertor_target) for the electron temperature at the same location.

This quantity is a summed total over all ion species — main ions, seeded impurities, and intrinsic impurities alike.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion density is measured in the direction from the plasma toward the target surface.

NAMES.name: total_ion_power_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Total thermal power deposited on the inner divertor target by all ion species, combining convective and conductive heat transport.
NAMES.long: The total ion power at the inner divertor target represents the heat flux carried by all ion species striking the divertor surface. It includes both the convective contribution from the plasma flow and the conductive contribution from the thermal ion motion: $P_{\text{ion,target}} = \sum_s \left( \frac{5}{2} k_B T_s + E_{\text{rec},s} \right) \Gamma_s$, where $T_s$ is the ion temperature at the target, $\Gamma_s$ is the ion flux density, and $E_{\text{rec},s}$ accounts for surface recombination energy release summed over species $s$ (typically deuterium, tritium, and helium). This power drives material erosion and requires active cooling; typical values for ITER-scale inner divertors reach $50-100\,\text{MW}$ steady state, with transient excursions up to $200\,\text{MW}$ during ELMs. The equivalent electron-side quantity is [electron_power_at_divertor_target](name:electron_power_at_divertor_target), and the complementary species density distribution is [total_ion_density_at_divertor_target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target).

NAMES.name: tungsten_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Number density of tungsten impurity ions in the plasma layer immediately adjacent to the divertor target surface. This high-Z ion density governs radiative cooling and erosion in the divertor region. Measured in particles per cubic meter.
NAMES.long: The tungsten density at the divertor target is the local concentration of tungsten impurity ions situated in the plasma layer immediately adjacent to the divertor target surface. It quantifies the tungsten particle number per unit volume and is critical for assessing radiative power losses, impurity erosion rates, and core contamination risks in the divertor. The density is related to the electron density and the fractional tungsten impurity concentration by $n_W \approx f_{W} \, n_e$, where $n_W$ is the tungsten density in m$^{-3}$, $f_W$ is the fractional concentration of tungsten ions, and $n_e$ is the electron density in m$^{-3}$. Typical values range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{20}\,\text{m}^{-3}$, varying with discharge conditions such as divertor plasma temperature and particle flux. The tungsten density originates from sputtering or injection of tungsten from plasma-facing components and is commonly inferred from spectroscopic measurements of tungsten line emission (e.g., WI, WII, WIII) combined with collisional-radiative modeling, or from Langmuir probe data with assumptions on the ionization state.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net flow of tungsten ions is directed toward the target surface.

NAMES.name: xenon_density_at_divertor_target
NAMES.short: Number density of xenon impurity ions in the plasma layer incident on the divertor target surface.
NAMES.long:
Xenon is injected as a radiating impurity to mitigate divertor heat fluxes, and its local density at the target determines the ionization balance and radiative losses in the divertor region. The density is typically inferred from spectroscopic measurements of Xe emission lines combined with collisional-radiative modeling, or from Langmuir probe data with appropriate impurity fractions. Typical values range from $10^{16}$ to $10^{19}\,\text{m}^{-3}$ in detached divertor conditions, depending on the seeding rate and plasma transport. This quantity is linked to the total divertor impurity content via the relation to the electron density, with $n_{\text{Xe}} \ll n_e$ in most operational scenarios. See also [krypton_density_at_divertor_target](name:krypton_density_at_divertor_target) and [tungsten_density_at_divertor_target](name:tungsten_density_at_divertor_target) for comparisons with other impurity species.

$n_{\text{Xe}}$ is a scalar density, always nonnegative; no sign variation applies.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the number density of xenon ions is defined as a non-negative real number (density is a nonnegative scalar field).

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Magnitude of the net current density driven by the diamagnetic drift of the bulk plasma, arising from the pressure gradient perpendicular to the magnetic field.
NAMES.long: The diamagnetic drift current density $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}} = \left( \mathbf{B} \times \nabla p \right) / B^2$ arises from the imbalance between the ion and electron diamagnetic drifts in the presence of a pressure gradient $\nabla p$ across the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, where $p$ is the total plasma pressure in Pa and $B$ is the magnetic field magnitude in T. This scalar quantity gives the magnitude of the diamagnetic current density vector, which contributes to the total current density in magnetized edge and scrape-off layer (SOL) plasmas and plays a key role in the radial force balance. Typical values in the tokamak edge region range from 0.1–10 MA·m$^{-2}$ in H-mode pedestals depending on the steepness of the pressure gradient. The diamagnetic current density is related to the diamagnetic drift velocities of individual species via $j_{\mathrm{dia}} = e (n_i v_{i,\mathrm{dia}} - n_e v_{e,\mathrm{dia}})$, where $n_i$ and $n_e$ are the ion and electron densities. For species-resolved drift velocities, see [ion_diamagnetic_velocity](name:ion_diamagnetic_velocity) and corresponding electron quantities. The directional components are available as [radial_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:radial_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), [poloidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), and [toroidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). This current density is distinct from the parallel viscous and perpendicular viscous current densities [current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) and [current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity), which originate from different momentum transport mechanisms.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic current density vector points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle relative to the right-handed $(R, \phi, Z)$ cylindrical frame, consistent with the sign of the pressure gradient driving the drift.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity
NAMES.short: Current density arising from the parallel component of the viscous force density in the edge plasma. It results from neoclassical parallel force balance and contributes to radial current transport near the separatrix.
NAMES.long: The parallel viscous current density arises from the imbalance of neoclassical parallel forces when the ion pressure tensor becomes anisotropic along the magnetic field. It appears in the parallel component of the generalized Ohm's law and is described by the parallel momentum balance equation $\nabla_\parallel \cdot \boldsymbol{\pi}_\parallel = F_\parallel$, where $\boldsymbol{\pi}_\parallel$ is the parallel component of the ion viscous stress tensor and $F_\parallel$ is the parallel frictional force. In the collisional (Pfirsch-Schlüter) regime, the parallel viscosity is proportional to the ion parallel viscosity coefficient $\eta_0$ and the gradient of the parallel flow velocity $V_\parallel$. The current density is computed from the viscous force density via $\mathbf{j}_{\parallel}^{\text{visc}} = \frac{1}{B} \hat{b} \times (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\pi}_\parallel)$, which is a vector quantity whose radial component contributes to radial current balance. Typical values range from $10^2$ to $10^4\,\text{A}\,\text{m}^{-2}$ in the pedestal region of H-mode tokamaks, depending on collisionality and edge gradients. This current is closely related to flow damping and radial electric field formation near the separatrix.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the parallel viscous current density vector points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.short: Electron number density at the top of the H-mode pedestal, marking the radial location where the steep density gradient begins.
NAMES.long:
The electron density at the pedestal top, $n_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$, quantifies the electron density at the radial location where the steep gradient region of the H-mode pedestal begins. This density is a critical parameter for pedestal stability, as it directly sets the pedestal pressure and the bootstrap current drive through $j_{\mathrm{BS}} \propto \nabla p_e / B_p$. Typical values range from $2 \times 10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in present-day tokamaks to $>10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ for ITER scenarios, and are routinely inferred from edge Thomson scattering or reflectometry profiles. The pedestal top density is closely linked to the profile shape parameters, such as the pedestal width and height, and is used together with [electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top](name:electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top) to compute the pedestal pressure. See also [electron_density_at_pedestal_maximum](name:electron_density_at_pedestal_maximum) for the density at the point of maximum gradient, and [electron_density_at_separatrix](name:electron_density_at_separatrix) for the density at the last closed flux surface.

This quantity is sign-invariant — electron density is always non-negative by definition.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the number density of free electrons is greater than zero.

NAMES.name: electron_pedestal_width
NAMES.short: Width of the electron pressure pedestal in normalized poloidal flux, measured between the pedestal top and foot locations derived from a linear fit of the steep-gradient region.
NAMES.long: The electron pedestal width characterizes the radial extent of the steep-gradient region of the electron pressure profile in the H-mode pedestal. It is defined as the difference in normalized poloidal flux between the pedestal top and pedestal foot, obtained from a linear fit to the pressure gradient profile. This width is a dimensionless quantity because it is expressed in normalized poloidal flux coordinates. The pedestal width, together with the pressure at the pedestal top, determines the edge pressure gradient $\nabla p_e$, which governs the stability of edge-localized modes (ELMs) through the peeling–ballooning model. Typical normalized widths range from $\Delta \psi_N \approx 0.01$–$0.04$ in contemporary tokamaks. The width is derived from profile fits to Thomson scattering or lithium-beam emission spectroscopy data; the linear fit method assumes a constant gradient across the pedestal. Related quantities include the [pedestal position](name:position_at_pedestal_maximum) and the [maximum pressure gradient](name:gradient_of_electron_pressure_at_pedestal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pedestal width is a finite positive interval (the quantity is inherently non-negative).

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_pedestal_maximum
NAMES.short: Electron temperature at the radial location of the maximum gradient of the H-mode pedestal, near the separatrix. This value characterizes the pedestal height and is a key input for pedestal stability and confinement models.
NAMES.long: The electron temperature at the pedestal maximum gradient point, $T_{e,\mathrm{ped, max}}$, is the value of $T_e$ at the radial position $r_{\mathrm{max}|\nabla T_e|}$ where the absolute radial derivative of the electron temperature profile peaks in the edge transport barrier of an H-mode plasma. This point lies between the pedestal top and the separatrix, indicating the steepest temperature drop. Typical values range from 100 eV to 1 keV in current tokamaks, scaling with the pedestal pressure height. The quantity is derived from Thomson scattering or ECE measurements and used in modeling pedestal stability and ELM dynamics. Related pedestal parameters include $T_{e,\mathrm{ped, top}}$ at the top of the pedestal and $\nabla p_{e,\mathrm{ped}}$ at the same gradient location.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_iron_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged density of iron impurity ions, evaluated at the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long: This quantity represents the density of iron (Fe) impurity ions averaged over a flux surface at the last closed flux surface (LCFS). Iron impurities typically originate from plasma-facing components and can significantly affect plasma performance through radiation losses and dilution of the fuel ions. Typical values in tokamaks range from 1e14 m^-3 to 1e18 m^-3 depending on the machine, discharge conditions, and proximity to the LCFS. The flux-surface average is defined as the mean of the iron density over the poloidal and toroidal extent of the flux surface, computed as $\langle n_{\mathrm{Fe}} \rangle = \frac{1}{V'} \oint n_{\mathrm{Fe}} \, \frac{d\ell}{|\nabla \psi|}$, where $V' = \mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}\psi$ is the differential volume per unit poloidal flux. This quantity is a key input for modeling edge impurity transport and assessing divertor heat loads.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_limiter
NAMES.short: Number density of singly-ionized helium-3 ($^3$He$^+$) particles in the plasma region that intersects the limiter surface.
NAMES.long:
The helium-3 ion density at the limiter quantifies the local $^3$He$^+$ concentration in the scrape-off layer zone in contact with the limiter, a critical quantity for fuel ion inventory and neutral-beam-driven fusion reactivity in devices using $^3$He as a minority species. This density is typically inferred from filtered charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or deduced from residual gas analyzer signals combined with edge plasma modeling; values in the limiter shadow range from $10^{15}$ to $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on fueling, pumping, and recycling conditions. The density couples to the neutral $^3$He source via ionization balance and to parallel transport along open field lines, with nearby companion quantities such as [helium_3_density_at_pedestal](name:helium_3_density_at_pedestal) and [helium_3_density_at_separatrix](name:helium_3_density_at_separatrix) characterizing radial variation across the edge.

The quantity is related to the ion temperature through the kinetic pressure and informs the edge fueling balance when compared to [ion_temperature_at_limiter](name:ion_temperature_at_limiter) within the limiter region.
NAMES.sign: Positive for all values; the quantity is a non-negative scalar number density.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-3 ions at the pedestal location in the plasma edge, typically just inside the separatrix.
NAMES.long: The helium-3 density at the pedestal, $n_{^{3}\text{He}}(\psi_{N,\text{ped}})$, quantifies the thermal ion density of helium-3 at the top of the edge transport barrier, typically just inside the separatrix. This species is relevant as a fusion ash product and minority heating fuel, with values typically ranging from $10^{17}$ to $10^{19}\,\text{m}^{-3}$ in H-mode pedestals. The radial coordinate is the normalized poloidal flux $\psi_N$, which maps the pedestal position. The density is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or passive spectroscopy, aided by equilibrium reconstruction to map to $\psi_N$. Measured values combine spectroscopic line intensities with collisional-radiative modeling to separate the $^{3}\text{He}$ signal from background deuterium and impurities.
NAMES.sign: Positive when describing physical particle number density in the volume at the pedestal location.

NAMES.name: ion_diamagnetic_velocity
NAMES.short: Diamagnetic drift velocity for a specific ion charge state, arising from the pressure gradient perpendicular to the magnetic field.
NAMES.long: The ion diamagnetic velocity is the fluid drift of a specific ion charge state due to an equilibrium pressure gradient perpendicular to the magnetic field. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the drift direction is given by $\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p_i$, where $p_i$ is the pressure of that ion species. The magnitude is $v_{\mathrm{dia}} = |\nabla p_i \times \mathbf{B}| / (n_i Z_i e B^2)$, where $n_i$ is the ion density, $Z_i e$ is the ion charge, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field. Typical values range from 1–100 m/s for main ions in the scrape-off layer, increasing with the pressure gradient and charge state for impurity ions. This drift represents the lowest-order fluid motion perpendicular to the magnetic field in a collisional plasma and is independent of particle mass. It is often inferred from measurements of the ion pressure gradient, as from Thomson scattering and charge exchange recombination spectroscopy.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the drift is in the direction of $\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p_i$, consistent with the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis.

NAMES.name: ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Diamagnetic drift velocity of an ion species in a specific charge state, resulting from the pressure gradient perpendicular to the magnetic field direction. This quantity is a scalar magnitude defined per charge state, independent of the storage representation.
NAMES.long: The diamagnetic drift velocity for an ion species in a particular charge state is given by $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia},z} = \frac{\nabla p_{z} \times \mathbf{B}}{n_z q_z B^2}$, where $p_z$ is the pressure of ions in charge state $z$, $n_z$ is their density, $q_z = z e$ is their charge, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field. In a fluid description, this drift arises from the balance of the pressure gradient and the Lorentz force and does not directly transport particles across flux surfaces in the absence of collisions or parallel dynamics. Typical diamagnetic drift speeds in the edge and scrape-off layer range from $10^2$ to $10^5$ m/s, depending on the local pressure gradient and magnetic field strength. The magnitude is measured in the rest frame of the bulk plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the local pressure gradient points radially inward (i.e., $\partial p_z / \partial R > 0$) and the magnetic field is in the $+\phi$ direction, consistent with the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ basis.

NAMES.name: iron_density_at_pedestal
NAMES.short: Number density of iron impurity ions at the pedestal location in the plasma edge.
NAMES.long:
The iron impurity ion density at the pedestal characterizes the concentration of sputtered or injected iron atoms in the steep-gradient edge transport barrier. In tokamak plasmas, iron is a common high-Z impurity originating from plasma-facing components; its accumulation at the pedestal increases radiative losses and can degrade confinement through fuel dilution. The density is measured via spectroscopic line ratios (e.g., from extreme ultraviolet spectroscopy) or inferred from filtered soft X-ray tomography, with typical pedestal values in the range of $10^{15}$–$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$ for medium-size devices. Spatial profiles of this quantity are closely linked to [iron density at the separatrix](name:iron_density_at_separatrix) and the pedestal transport modeled via neoclassical and anomalous impurity fluxes. The pedestal iron density also directly impacts the core impurity dynamics described by [iron density at the magnetic axis](name:iron_density_at_magnetic_axis).

The iron density is a positive-definite scalar quantity and carries no sign reversal under the standard IMAS coordinate conventions; the sign convention is stated for completeness.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the local iron impurity ion concentration exceeds zero, as physically required for a number density.

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_pedestal
NAMES.short: Magnetic shear at the top of the pedestal region, quantifying the local radial variation of the safety factor.
NAMES.long: The magnetic shear $s = (\rho_\mathrm{tor}/q)\,dq/d\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is evaluated at the pedestal top, where $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius and $q$ is the safety factor. This dimensionless parameter governs the local pitch-angle variation of magnetic field lines and is a critical stability parameter for edge-localized modes (ELMs) via the peeling-ballooning model. The pedestal magnetic shear is typically in the range $s \approx 1$–$3$ in H-mode tokamak plasmas, with values inferred from equilibrium reconstruction constrained by profile and magnetic measurements. Positive magnetic shear ($s > 0$) corresponds to the safety factor increasing with radius, which is the usual monotonic $q$-profile case in tokamaks; negative shear ($s < 0$) indicates a non-monotonic $q$-profile with a reversed central region. See also [magnetic_shear](name:magnetic_shear) for the radial profile, [magnetic_shear_at_separatrix](name:magnetic_shear_at_separatrix) for the value at the last closed flux surface, and [magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis](name:magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis) for the core value.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the safety factor increases with increasing radial coordinate (normal monotonic $q$-profile).

NAMES.name: neutral_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Drift velocity of neutral particles in a specific charge state driven by the diamagnetic current arising from the perpendicular pressure gradient.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic drift velocity $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia}} = (\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p) / (q n B^2)$ arises from the pressure gradient perpendicular to the magnetic field when the gyroradius is finite, even for neutral species coupled to the plasma via charge-exchange or ionization collisions. Here $p$ is the neutral partial pressure, $n$ the neutral density, $q$ the effective charge, and $B$ the magnetic field magnitude. This quantity is the magnitude of the diamagnetic drift for neutral particles in a specified charge state, computed on the generalized Gaussian decomposition (GGD) grid in the edge plasma. Typical drift velocities range from 0.1 to 10 km/s in the scrape-off layer and pedestal, depending on the local pressure gradient and magnetic field strength. It is distinct from the [radial_neutral_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:radial_neutral_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) which isolates the radial component, and from the [ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:ion_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) for charged species. The sign convention follows the diamagnetic drift direction relative to the magnetic field gradient.

In the edge plasma, this drift contributes to the radial transport of neutral particles and affects the fueling efficiency, neutral penetration depth, and the overall particle balance. It is typically inferred from kinetic neutral transport codes (e.g., EIRENE) or from fluid models that solve the neutral momentum equation including diamagnetic effects.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the drift velocity points in the direction of $\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p$.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_pedestal
NAMES.short: Normalized poloidal flux coordinate at the top of the pedestal region, marking the radial position of the steep gradient zone onset.
NAMES.long: The normalized poloidal flux coordinate $ho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ at the pedestal top (the radial location where the edge density and temperature gradients steepen into the H-mode pedestal) is defined as $ho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \sqrt{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}} / \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,LCFS}}}$, where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,LCFS}}$ is the flux at the last closed flux surface. This dimensionless radial marker typically falls in the range 0.92–0.98 in conventional H-mode tokamaks and is routinely determined from equilibrium reconstruction codes such as EFIT or LIUQE. The pedestal top position, where $ho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is evaluated, is the outermost region of steep gradient that governs edge transport and core-confinement coupling, and is cross-referenced with [magnetic_shear_at_pedestal](name:magnetic_shear_at_pedestal) to characterize stability limits.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $ho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ increases from the magnetic axis ($\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = 0$) toward the last closed flux surface ($\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = 1$).

NAMES.name: parallel_current_density_due_to_ohmic
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged component of the ohmic current density parallel to the magnetic field, representing the inductive current driven by the toroidal electric field and limited by plasma resistivity.
NAMES.long:
The ohmic parallel current density $j_{\parallel,\mathrm{ohmic}}$ is defined as the flux-surface average $j_{\parallel,\mathrm{ohmic}} = \langle \mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{ohmic}} \cdot \mathbf{B} \rangle / B_0$, where $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{ohmic}}$ is the ohmic current density vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic field, $B_0$ is the flux-surface-averaged magnetic field magnitude, and $\langle \cdot \rangle$ denotes the flux-surface average. This quantity represents the inductive component of the parallel current density, driven by the toroidal electric field via Ohm's law and limited by the plasma resistivity (Spitzer or neoclassical). In tokamak H-mode plasmas, the ohmic current density typically peaks in the core (order 0.1–1 MA/m²) and decreases towards the edge, where it becomes small compared to the bootstrap current. This value range is consistent with typical JET and DIII-D H-mode discharges. It is a critical input for current-drive calculations, resistive MHD stability analysis, and sawtooth modeling.

Measured indirectly from equilibrium reconstruction (e.g., EFIT) combined with resistivity profiles, or from polarimetry and MSE diagnostic data. Typical uncertainties are 10–20% depending on diagnostic constraints. In the scrape-off layer, the ohmic parallel current dominates and determines the divertor heat-flux width.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ohmic current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ aligned with the plasma current.

NAMES.name: parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure
NAMES.short: The component of the fast ion pressure tensor parallel to the local magnetic field for a specific charge state.
NAMES.long:
The parallel fast ion state pressure $p_{ \parallel , f, z}$ is the field-aligned element of the anisotropic pressure tensor for suprathermal ions in a given charge state $z$. It arises from the parallel kinetic energy of the fast-ion population and contributes to the total pressure balance via $p_{f,z} = (p_{\parallel ,f,z} + 2p_{\perp ,f,z})/3$. In the edge plasma, this quantity is typically derived from neutral-beam or ICRH fast-ion distributions, with core values reaching tens of kilopascals.
