Measurement combines neutron spectrometry, fast-ion D-alpha (FIDA) diagnostics, and equilibrium reconstruction. The parent quantity is [fast_ion_state_pressure](name:fast_ion_state_pressure), which is the isotropic (kinetic) pressure for that charge state. The perpendicular counterpart is the parallel pressure contribution from fast electrons [parallel_fast_electron_pressure](name:parallel_fast_electron_pressure). The parallel and perpendicular components quantify the pressure anisotropy of suprathermal populations.

Typical values in H-mode tokamak pedestals range from 1–10 kPa for beam-injected fast ions, diminishing with charge state due to confinement and slowing-down. The parallel component can exceed the perpendicular in strongly anisotropic distributions (e.g., co-injected beam ions).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the field-aligned component of the pressure tensor acts to expand the plasma along the magnetic field direction.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_energy_flux
NAMES.short: Parallel projection of the ion energy flux along the magnetic field direction.
NAMES.long: The parallel ion energy flux $Q_{\parallel,i} = \mathbf{Q}_i \cdot \hat{b}$ represents the component of the total ion energy flux vector (thermal plus kinetic) projected onto the magnetic field unit vector $\hat{b}$. This quantity governs energy transport along field lines in the edge plasma, where parallel transport dominates due to high magnetic field-aligned conductivity. In the scrape-off layer, $Q_{\parallel,i}$ determines the heat flux deposited on divertor targets, with typical values ranging from 1$\,\mathrm{MW\,m^{-2}}$ to 10$\,\mathrm{MW\,m^{-2}}$ in high-power tokamaks. It is routinely inferred from upstream profile measurements combined with two-point SOL models, or directly from Langmuir probe and infrared camera data. The total parallel energy transport is described by [parallel_total_ion_energy_flux](name:parallel_total_ion_energy_flux), which sums over all charge states, while the full energy flux vector is given by [ion_energy_flux](name:ion_energy_flux). For neutral species, the analogous quantity is [parallel_neutral_energy_flux](name:parallel_neutral_energy_flux).

NAMES.name: parallel_neutral_diamagnetic_velocity
NAMES.short: Parallel component of the diamagnetic drift velocity for neutral particles, defined on the generalized grid in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long:
The parallel neutral diamagnetic velocity is the projection of the neutral diamagnetic drift vector onto the direction of the magnetic field. For neutral particles, the diamagnetic drift is not a guiding-center drift as for charged species but arises from collisional momentum exchange with the ion fluid that carries the diamagnetic current. The parallel component is defined as $v_{\parallel,\,\mathrm{dia}}^{\mathrm{n}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia}}^{\mathrm{n}} \cdot \hat{b}$, where $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field and $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{dia}}^{\mathrm{n}}$ is the neutral diamagnetic velocity. This quantity is typically computed from fluid or kinetic transport models on unstructured grids and provides the neutral contribution to parallel momentum transport in the edge and scrape-off layer.

Cross-reference with [neutral_diamagnetic_velocity](name:neutral_diamagnetic_velocity) for the full vector quantity and with [parallel_ion_diamagnetic_velocity](name:parallel_ion_diamagnetic_velocity) for the charged-species counterpart.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the parallel component of the neutral diamagnetic velocity points in the direction of the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_neutral_energy_flux
NAMES.short: Parallel (field-aligned) component of the thermal energy flux carried by neutral particles in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long: The parallel neutral energy flux $Q_{\parallel,\mathrm{n}}$ is the projection of the total neutral thermal energy flux vector $\mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{n}}$ onto the magnetic field direction $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$, i.e. $Q_{\parallel,\mathrm{n}} = \mathbf{Q}_{\mathrm{n}} \cdot \hat{b}$. This quantity quantifies the rate of thermal energy transport by neutral atoms and molecules along the magnetic field, a key channel for heat transport in the scrape-off layer and divertor region where neutral densities are elevated.$Q_{\parallel,\mathrm{n}}$ is typically an output of edge-plasma transport codes such as SOLPS or included in the neutral particle model component of integrated modeling frameworks. It is distinguished from the total neutral energy flux by its alignment to the field and from the charge-state-specific flux by aggregating over all neutral charge states. Typical values in the divertor region can range from 0.1–10 MW m$^{-2}$, depending on the neutral density and temperature. See also the total [neutral_energy_flux](name:neutral_energy_flux), the charge-state-specific [parallel_neutral_state_energy_flux](name:parallel_neutral_state_energy_flux), and the electron counterpart [parallel_electron_energy_flux](name:parallel_electron_energy_flux).

NAMES.name: parallel_neutral_momentum_flux
NAMES.short: Parallel projection of the neutral particle momentum flux onto the magnetic field direction in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long: This quantity represents the component of the neutral momentum flux directed along the magnetic field lines, denoted $\Gamma_{n,\|} = \Pi_n \cdot \hat{b}$, where $\Pi_n$ is the neutral momentum flux density tensor and $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field. The parallel neutral momentum flux governs the toroidal and poloidal flow of neutral particles in the edge region and is essential for understanding momentum transport from the core to the scrape-off layer (SOL). It is a key term in the neutral momentum balance equation, coupling the neutral population to the ion and electron fluids through charge-exchange and ionization collisions. Typical magnitudes in the SOL of a diverted tokamak range from 10$^{-3}$ to 1 kg·m$^{-1}$·s$^{-2}$ depending on the neutral density and flow velocity. This quantity is computed self-consistently in edge transport codes (e.g., SOLPS, EMC3-EIRENE) and is closely related to the [parallel_ion_momentum_flux](name:parallel_ion_momentum_flux) for the ion channel and the total [parallel_momentum_flux](name:parallel_momentum_flux). The parent quantity is [neutral_momentum_flux](name:neutral_momentum_flux); the parallel component isolates the field-aligned contribution from the full tensor.

NAMES.name: parallel_neutral_state_energy_flux
NAMES.short: Parallel thermal energy flux carried by neutral particles in a given charge state along the magnetic field.
NAMES.long: This quantity describes the component of the neutral charge-state energy flux projected onto the direction parallel to the equilibrium magnetic field line, $Q_{\|,n}^{(\mathrm{state})} = \mathbf{Q}_{n}^{(\mathrm{state})} \cdot \hat{b}$, where $\mathbf{Q}_{n}^{(\mathrm{state})}$ is the energy flux of neutrals in a specific charge state and $\hat{b}$ is the unit vector along $\mathbf{B}$. It quantifies the thermal energy carried along field lines by neutral particles undergoing charge-exchange and elastic collisions, which is important for modeling edge transport and recycling. Typical magnitudes in the scrape-off layer of diverted tokamaks range from $0.1\,\text{kW}\,$ to $10\,\text{kW}\,$ per unit area, depending on the neutral density and temperature. The quantity is the parallel component of [neutral_state_energy_flux](name:neutral_state_energy_flux) and is related to the total neutral energy transport via [parallel_neutral_energy_flux](name:parallel_neutral_energy_flux), which sums over all charge states.

NAMES.name: parallel_total_ion_energy_flux
NAMES.short: Projection of the total energy flux from all ion species along the magnetic field direction, combining thermal and kinetic contributions.
NAMES.long: The parallel total ion energy flux $q_{i\parallel}^{\text{tot}}$ represents the component of the summed ion energy flux vector parallel to the equilibrium magnetic field. It is the sum $q_{i\parallel}^{\text{tot}} = \sum_s \left( q_{i s,\parallel}^{\text{th}} + q_{i s,\parallel}^{\text{kin}} \right)$ over all ion species $s$, where $q_{i s,\parallel}^{\text{th}}$ is the thermal (conductive) energy flux and $q_{i s,\parallel}^{\text{kin}}$ is the kinetic (convective) energy flux carried by the ion flow. This quantity is the parallel component of [total_ion_energy_flux](name:total_ion_energy_flux) and is central to scrape-off layer and divertor transport modeling, where the ion channel can carry a significant fraction of the power along the field line. Typical values in the SOL of a divertor tokamak range from 0.1 to 10 MW/m$^{-2}$, depending on the upstream density and heating power. The measurement or simulation of this flux requires resolving both the thermal pressure gradient and the parallel ion flow, often from kinetic or fluid transport codes that treat each charge state separately before summing.

NAMES.name: poloidal_anomalous_current_density
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the anomalous current density, representing the non-classical turbulent contribution to the poloidal current in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long: The poloidal anomalous current density $j_{\theta}^{\mathrm{anom}}$ is the projection of the anomalous current density vector onto the poloidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This component captures the turbulent non-classical current contribution driven by drift-wave or interchange instabilities, which is distinct from the collisional (Spitzer) and neoclassical current components. In the scrape-off layer, the poloidal anomalous current density can influence the radial electric field and poloidal flow damping, affecting edge turbulence saturation levels. Typical values in L-mode edge plasmas range from $10^3$ to $10^5$ A/m$^2$, depending on fluctuation amplitudes and the local plasma gradients. This quantity is linked to the full anomalous current density vector via the parent quantity `[anomalous_current_density](name:anomalous_current_density)` and is complemented by the `[toroidal_anomalous_current_density](name:toroidal_anomalous_current_density)` and `[radial_anomalous_current_density](name:radial_anomalous_current_density)` components.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current density points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the right-handed $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_conductivity
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the anisotropic electrical conductivity tensor, relating the poloidal current density to the poloidal electric field in a plasma. It describes the ability of the plasma to conduct electric current in the poloidal direction.
NAMES.long: The poloidal conductivity $\sigma_{\theta\theta}$ is the diagonal element of the conductivity tensor corresponding to the poloidal direction. In magnetized plasmas, the conductivity is highly anisotropic: the conductivity parallel to the magnetic field is orders of magnitude larger than the perpendicular (radial) conductivity. The poloidal component $\sigma_{\theta\theta}$ connects the poloidal electric field component $E_\theta$ to the poloidal current density $j_\theta$ via Ohm's law, $j_\theta = \sigma_{\theta\theta} E_\theta + \sigma_{\theta\phi} E_\phi + \sigma_{\theta\psi} E_\psi$, where $\sigma_{\theta\phi}$ and $\sigma_{\theta\psi}$ are off-diagonal Hall and Pfirsch-Schlüter terms. Typical values for the poloidal conductivity in tokamak edge plasmas range from 10^3 to 10^6 S/m (mho/m), depending on electron temperature and density profiles. The poloidal conductivity is relevant for modeling current drive, neoclassical transport, and MHD stability in the plasma edge. It is measured indirectly through probe arrays or inferred from equilibrium reconstructions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal current density $j_\theta$ flows in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ for a given poloidal electric field $E_\theta$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_electric_field
NAMES.short: Projection of the electric field vector onto the poloidal direction, given by $E_\theta = -\nabla_\theta \Phi$ from the electrostatic potential.
NAMES.long: The poloidal electric field is the component of the electric field vector resolved along the poloidal coordinate $\theta$ on a flux surface. It is defined as the negative gradient of the electrostatic potential $\Phi$ in the poloidal direction: $E_\theta = -\frac{1}{R \left| \nabla \theta \right|} \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial \theta}$, where $R$ is the major radius. This field is crucial for driving poloidal particle drifts, affecting impurity transport, and determining the radial electric field through the force balance equation $E_r = v_\theta B_\phi - v_\phi B_\theta + \frac{1}{Z_i e n_i} \nabla_r p_i$. Typical edge values range from 0.1 to 10 kV/m in H-mode pedestals, measured indirectly via Doppler backscattering or inferred from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy. See also the toroidal counterpart [toroidal_electric_field](name:toroidal_electric_field) and the governing relation with [poloidal_magnetic_field](name:poloidal_magnetic_field) in the radial force balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $E_\theta$ points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_electron_beta_at_pedestal_top
NAMES.short: Ratio of electron thermal pressure to poloidal magnetic field pressure, evaluated at the top of the pedestal region where the pressure gradient is maximal.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal electron beta at the pedestal top is defined as:

$$
\beta_{\theta, e}^{\text{ped}} = \frac{2 \mu_0 p_e}{B_{\theta}^2}
$$

where $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \: \mathrm{H \, m^{-1}}$ is the permeability of free space, $p_e$ is the electron thermal pressure (in Pa), and $B_{\theta}$ is the poloidal magnetic field magnitude (in T). The quantity is evaluated at the top of the pedestal, i.e., at the radial location where the electron pressure gradient is maximal in the edge transport barrier. The radial coordinate used in the evaluation is the normalized poloidal flux $\psi_N$, as defined by the IMAS flux convention. Typical values in H-mode plasmas range from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-1}$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_electron_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the effective convective velocity for electron particle transport, representing the poloidal advection of the electron density profile.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal electron convection velocity is the poloidal component $v_{\theta,e}^{\text{conv}}$ of the effective velocity field that advects electron density in the particle transport equation. In the continuity equation $\partial_t n_e + \nabla \cdot (n_e \mathbf{v}^{\text{conv}}_e) = S_e$, this poloidal component governs cross-field transport in the poloidal direction. It is typically inferred from transport modeling on unstructured edge grids, complementing the total velocity $[\text{electron\_convection\_velocity}](name:electron_convection_velocity)$. In the edge plasma, poloidal convective velocities are often on the order of 1-100 m/s, significantly smaller than the toroidal flow but critical for determining density profiles and pedestal structure.

Cross-reference the total vector via $[\text{electron\_convection\_velocity}](name:electron_convection_velocity)$ and the corresponding ion quantity $[\text{poloidal\_ion\_velocity\_due\_to\_convection}](name:poloidal_ion_velocity_due_to_convection)$ for comparison of species-dependent convection.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal component points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_velocity_due_to_convection
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the effective ion velocity arising from convective transport processes in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal ion convection velocity $v_{\theta, \mathrm{conv}}$ is the projection of the total convective velocity for ion transport onto the poloidal direction, perpendicular to both the radial and toroidal axes. It quantifies the poloidal advection of ion particles, momentum, and energy due to macroscopic plasma flows such as those driven by neoclassical effects or turbulent eddy transport. This quantity is a component of the vector field defined by [ion_velocity_due_to_convection](name:ion_velocity_due_to_convection). In the edge and scrape-off layer, typical poloidal convection speeds range from tens to hundreds of m/s, depending on the collisionality and plasma rotation profile. It is diagnosed through transport code analysis or inferred from poloidal distribution of ion fluxes.

Related quantities include the radial counterpart [radial_ion_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_convection_velocity) and the [ion_momentum_flux](name:ion_momentum_flux) which characterizes the associated momentum transport.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the convection velocity is in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from the outboard midplane).

NAMES.name: poloidal_ion_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the diamagnetic drift velocity for an ion charge state, arising from pressure gradients perpendicular to the magnetic field.
NAMES.long: The poloidal ion diamagnetic drift velocity $v_{\theta}^{\text{dia}}$ is the poloidal projection of the diamagnetic drift velocity $\mathbf{v}_{\text{dia}} = (\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p_i) / (n_i Z_i e B^2)$, where $p_i$ is the ion pressure, $n_i$ is the ion density, $Z_i$ is the charge state, $e$ is the elementary charge, and $B = |\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic field magnitude. This quantity represents the poloidal component of the total diamagnetic drift vector for a single ion species and is the poloidal projection of the parent quantity [ion_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:ion_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). It is distinguished from perpendicular (radial) and toroidal components by its direction along the poloidal angle and is a key player in determining the poloidal rotation balance and radial electric field in the edge pedestal and scrape-off layer. Typical values in the edge of H-mode tokamak plasmas range from a few hundred m/s to several km/s, driven by the steep pressure gradients of the pedestal. The poloidal component is routinely inferred from charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) measurements or predicted by neoclassical transport codes. Sibling components include [radial_neutral_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:radial_neutral_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and [toroidal_neutral_diamagnetic_velocity](name:toroidal_neutral_diamagnetic_velocity), while the perpendicular pressure gradient that drives it is related to [ion_diamagnetic_velocity](name:ion_diamagnetic_velocity) and [current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the drift velocity points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ (towards the outboard midplane).

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_state_velocity
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the flow velocity for neutral particles in a specific quantum state, resolved relative to the magnetic field direction.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal neutral state velocity $v_{\theta, \text{n}}^{\text{state}}$ is the component of the neutral particle velocity vector perpendicular to the toroidal direction and lying within the poloidal plane. It describes the poloidal drift of neutrals in a particular charge state, which is essential for modeling edge plasma fueling and neutral transport. This quantity is part of the [neutral_state_velocity](name:neutral_state_velocity) vector, which also includes parallel and radial components. Typical poloidal velocities in the edge region range from $10^2$ to $10^4$ m/s, depending on charge-exchange and ionization rates. Measurement is typically inferred from spectroscopic diagnostics or 2D neutral fluid simulations.

Related standard names include [poloidal_neutral_velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_velocity) for charge-state-averaged flow and [poloidal_ion_state_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_state_velocity) for ion species.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal component points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_neutral_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the diamagnetic drift velocity for neutral species, driven by the pressure gradient perpendicular to the magnetic field.
NAMES.long: The poloidal component $v_{\theta, \rm dia} = \mathbf{v}_{\rm dia} \cdot \hat{\theta}$ of the neutral diamagnetic drift velocity $\mathbf{v}_{\rm dia}$. For neutral particles coupled to the plasma through collisions or charge exchange, the diamagnetic drift arises from the force balance $\nabla p_n = \mathbf{j}_n \times \mathbf{B}$, where $p_n$ is the neutral pressure in Pa, $\mathbf{j}_n$ is the equivalent current density in A/m$^2$, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T. In the edge plasma, this poloidal component contributes to the cross-field transport of neutral particles and influences the rotation dynamics of the neutral background. Typical poloidal diamagnetic velocities for neutrals range from $10^{-2}$ to $10^{1}$ m/s in the scrape-off layer, depending on the neutral pressure gradient and magnetic geometry. This quantity is the neutral counterpart of [$\text{poloidal\_ion\_velocity\_due\_to\_diamagnetic\_drift}$](name:poloidal_ion_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and the poloidal projection of the parent quantity [$\text{neutral\_velocity\_due\_to\_diamagnetic\_drift}$](name:neutral_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the drift points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ (clockwise in the poloidal plane when viewed from above for standard tokamak coordinates).

NAMES.name: radial_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Radial component of the bulk plasma velocity arising from convective transport processes.
NAMES.long:
The radial convection velocity $v_{\mathrm{conv},r}$ represents the radial component of the bulk fluid velocity associated with advective transport. This quantity characterizes the radial movement of the bulk plasma due to convective processes, such as those driven by turbulent eddies or neoclassical flows. The radial convection velocity is related to the radial particle flux $\Gamma_r = n v_{\mathrm{conv},r}$, where $n$ is the bulk plasma density. In the edge and scrape-off layer, typical radial convection velocities range from 10 to 1000 m/s, driven by edge-localized modes (ELMs), blobs, and turbulence. Model-based transport codes infer $v_{\mathrm{conv},r}$ by combining measured density and particle flux profiles. The radial component is defined in the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, projected onto the direction of the outward major radius $R$.

Cross-references: See the parent quantity [convection_velocity](name:convection_velocity) for the full vector definition. Compare with the charge-state-resolved [radial_ion_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_convection_velocity) for ion-specific transport, and [poloidal_ion_velocity_due_to_convection](name:poloidal_ion_velocity_due_to_convection) for the poloidal component. For the transported energy, see [radial_total_ion_energy_flux](name:radial_total_ion_energy_flux).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the convection velocity is directed outward in the major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: radial_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Radial component of the current density driven by the diamagnetic drift in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long:
The radial diamagnetic drift current density $j_{\mathrm{dia},r}$ is the component of the diamagnetic drift current density $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}} = (\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p) / B^2$ along the radial direction, where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field (T) and $p$ is the total plasma pressure (Pa). This component arises from the imbalance between ion and electron diamagnetic drifts in the presence of radial pressure gradients, and is a key contributor to the radial current balance in the edge and scrape-off layer. It is typically inferred from equilibrium reconstruction or measured by Langmuir probes and is essential for modeling the radial electric field and confinement transitions.

Typical values in the edge of a diverted tokamak are on the order of 1–100 kA·m$^{-2}$, depending on the local pressure gradient and magnetic geometry. Related quantities include [current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), [poloidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), and [toroidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows outward in the major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: radial_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity
NAMES.short: Radial component of the current density driven by perpendicular viscosity in the edge plasma, arising from radial gradients in the parallel ion flow.
NAMES.long: This quantity represents the radial current density $j_{r,\text{visc},\perp}$ that arises from perpendicular viscosity in the edge plasma. In the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the radial component is along the $\hat{R}$ direction (the direction of increasing major radius). Perpendicular viscosity, associated with collisional transport across the magnetic field, generates a radial current when there are radial gradients in the parallel ion flow velocity $v_{\|}$ or in the plasma rotation. The current density appears in the radial force balance and can play a role in edge plasma rotation braking and momentum transport. Typical magnitudes in the edge region of tokamaks range from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{2}\,\text{A}\,\text{m}^{-2}$, depending on the steepness of edge gradients and the collisionality regime. It is measured indirectly via analysis of edge flow profiles or modeled using neoclassical or gyro-viscous theory. The radial component is part of the perpendicular viscosity current density tensor; see also the toroidal counterpart.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_momentum_source
NAMES.short: Radial component of the volumetric momentum source density vector applied to the plasma, representing the net force per unit volume in the major-radius direction. This source accounts for momentum transfer from external actuators, such as neutral beam injection or radio-frequency waves, to the plasma in the cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long: The radial momentum source density $S_{p,R}$ (units: kg·m⁻²·s⁻²) is the component along the major radius axis $R$ of the volumetric momentum source density vector $\mathbf{S}_p$ applied to the plasma. It is defined as $S_{p,R} = \mathbf{S}_p \cdot \hat{R}$, where $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector in the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. $S_{p,R}$ represents the net force per unit volume on the plasma in the $R$-direction due to external actuators, such as neutral beam injection, radio-frequency wave heating, or pellet injection. Typical values in fusion devices range from 0.1 to 10 N/m³ for neutral beam injection and significantly larger values for pellet injection. In the edge plasma, the radial momentum source influences the radial electric field and impurity transport, while the toroidal component is described by `toroidal_momentum_source`. The ion and neutral contributions to radial momentum transport are captured by `ion_momentum_flux` and `neutral_momentum_flux`, respectively.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net force on the plasma points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.short: Radial component of the momentum diffusion coefficient for neutral particles in the edge plasma, describing diffusive transport of neutral momentum in the radial direction relative to the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long: The radial neutral momentum diffusion coefficient characterizes the diffusive transport of neutral particle momentum along the radial coordinate $r$ (or $\rho$, the normalized toroidal flux radius) in the edge plasma region. It quantifies how gradients in neutral momentum lead to a radial flux of momentum. Typical values range from $10^{-2}$ to $10^1$ m$^2$ s$^{-1}$ depending on plasma density, neutral pressure, and collisionality. This coefficient is a key input for fluid neutral models and is often derived from kinetic calculations or empirical fits. In the IMAS edge transport model, this radial component is one scalar per element of the grid subset, distinct from perpendicular components described in `toroidal_neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient` and `poloidal_neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient`.
NAMES.sign: Positive when momentum diffuses from regions of higher to lower radial neutral momentum density in the direction of increasing $r$.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Radial component of the diamagnetic drift velocity for neutral species, driven by the coupling of neutral particles to the plasma pressure gradient across the magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The radial component $v_{\text{dia},R}^{\text{neutral}}$ of the neutral diamagnetic drift velocity arises from collisional or charge-exchange coupling between the neutral population and the magnetized plasma. The diamagnetic drift is perpendicular to both the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ and the pressure gradient $\nabla p$, and its radial projection quantifies cross-field advection of neutral particles in the edge and scrape-off layer. The full velocity vector is given by $\mathbf{v}_\text{dia} = (\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p_\text{neutral}) / (Z_i e n_\text{neutral} B^2)$ in SI, where $p_\text{neutral}$ is the neutral pressure and $n_\text{neutral}$ the neutral density; the radial component $v_R$ isolates the $R$-directed contribution in the $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. This quantity is related to the parent [neutral_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:neutral_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and parallels the [toroidal_neutral_diamagnetic_velocity](name:toroidal_neutral_diamagnetic_velocity) for the poloidal component. Typical radial neutral drift velocities range from 10–100 m/s in the SOL to 1–10 km/s near the separatrix, strongly influencing fueling and impurity transport. Cross-referencing the radial profiles with [ion_diamagnetic_velocity](name:ion_diamagnetic_velocity) reveals the differential neutral–ion drift that drives charge-exchange momentum transfer.

This quantity is obtained from gyrofluid or kinetic neutral models that solve the coupled neutral–plasma transport equations, or diagnosed via charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy on neutral beams coupled to collisional–radiative modeling.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the velocity points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: radial_velocity_due_to_convection
NAMES.short: Radial component of the convective velocity for momentum transport in the edge plasma. This scalar describes the advective radial motion carrying momentum in the scrape-off layer and pedestal, distinct from diffusive or diamagnetic contributions. Positive when directed outward in major radius R (away from the magnetic axis).
NAMES.long:
The radial velocity due to convection represents the radial component $v_r^{\text{conv}}$ of the effective convection velocity in the momentum transport equation. It governs the advective radial transport of momentum in the scrape-off layer and pedestal, typically derived from gyro-fluid or reduced-MHD edge models. In the radial force balance, this velocity appears alongside diffusive and diamagnetic contributions.

The radial convection velocity is often obtained from edge transport simulations (e.g., SOLPS, EMC3-EIRENE) or reduced models parameterizing turbulent pinch effects. Typical magnitudes range from 1–100 m/s in the confined edge to several hundred m/s in the far scrape-off layer, depending on the plasma collisionality and fluctuation-driven transport.

See also the parent vector quantity [velocity_due_to_convection](name:velocity_due_to_convection) for the full vector, [radial_convection_velocity](name:radial_convection_velocity) for mass transport, and the charge-state-resolved counterparts [radial_ion_convection_velocity](name:radial_ion_convection_velocity) and [radial_ion_state_momentum_velocity](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when directed outward in major radius $R$ (away from the magnetic axis).

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Safety factor at the outboard midplane intersection with the separatrix, a standard MHD stability parameter for the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
The safety factor $q$ at the plasma boundary describes the helicity of magnetic field lines on the last closed flux surface, defined as $q = \partial \Phi_{\rm tor} / \partial \Phi_{\rm pol}$ where $\Phi_{\rm tor}$ and $\Phi_{\rm pol}$ are the toroidal and poloidal magnetic fluxes, respectively. This quantity is a critical indicator of edge stability; low edge $q$ values (approaching 2) can trigger peeling-ballooning modes and edge-localized modes (ELMs) that govern pedestal confinement and divertor heat loads. Typical values at the separatrix are in the range $q_{95} = 3$–$5$ for H-mode tokamaks, with the exact value depending on the plasma current, toroidal field, and shaping. It is routinely computed from equilibrium reconstruction (e.g., EFIT, LIUQE) using external magnetic measurements and internal profile constraints.

Related quantities: [safety_factor](name:safety_factor) evaluated at 95% flux surface, [minimum_safety_factor](name:minimum_safety_factor) as an MHD stability indicator, and [safety_factor_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:safety_factor_at_internal_transport_barrier) for transport barrier studies.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic field lines are left-handed with respect to the plasma current direction, which is standard for tokamaks in the IMAS $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_pressure_at_pedestal
NAMES.short: Thermal (Maxwellian) component of the electron pressure at the pedestal height location, obtained from edge profile fitting and characterizing the steep-gradient region of the H-mode pedestal.
NAMES.long:
The thermal electron pressure at the pedestal height is defined as $p_{e\,\text{therm}} = n_e k_B T_e$, where $n_e$ and $T_e$ are the local electron density and temperature of the Maxwellian population, and $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant. This quantity isolates the thermal component from any non-thermal contributions (e.g., fast electrons), providing the pressure that contributes to the total pressure gradient used in MHD stability analyzes of the pedestal. The pedestal height, typically identified at the radial location of the maximum pressure gradient, determines the local H-mode pedestal performance and the stored energy; typical values range from 0.1 to 50 kPa in present tokamaks depending on confinement regime and heating power. It is routinely inferred from Thomson scattering or other edge diagnostics combined with equilibrium reconstruction. The thermal electron pressure at the pedestal relates directly to the pedestal width via [electron_pedestal_width](name:electron_pedestal_width) and to the peak gradient via [gradient_of_electron_pressure_at_pedestal](name:gradient_of_electron_pressure_at_pedestal).

See also the total electron pressure at the pedestal [electron_pressure](name:electron_pressure) and the corresponding density [electron_density_at_pedestal](name:electron_density_at_pedestal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the Maxwellian electron pressure produces an outward force, consistent with the usual definition of kinetic pressure.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_pedestal_energy
NAMES.short: Ion contribution to the pedestal stored thermal energy, derived from an mtanh fit of the ion temperature and density profiles.
NAMES.long: The thermal stored energy of the ion pedestal, $W_{\text{th},i}^{\text{ped}}$, represents the ion contribution to the total pedestal thermal energy and is calculated as the volume integral of the thermal ion pressure over the pedestal region. It is derived from an mtanh (modified hyperbolic tangent) fit to the ion temperature and density profiles in the edge plasma, which parameterizes the pedestal height, width, and position. This quantity, together with [thermal_electron_pedestal_energy](name:thermal_electron_pedestal_energy), determines the total pedestal stored energy, a key parameter for edge-localized mode (ELM) stability and pedestal structure analysis. Typical values for the ion pedestal energy in H-mode tokamak plasmas range from 0.1 to 1 MJ, depending on machine size, heating power, and plasma conditions. The pedestal energy is inferred from profile diagnostics (e.g., Thomson scattering, charge exchange recombination spectroscopy) and equilibrium reconstruction, and is routinely used in pedestal databases and ELM prediction models.

NAMES.name: toroidal_conductivity
NAMES.short: The component of the electrical conductivity tensor corresponding to current driven along the toroidal direction.
NAMES.long: The toroidal component $\sigma_{\phi\phi}$ of the conductivity tensor quantifies the plasma's ability to conduct electric current in the geometric toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$ of the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This component is distinct from [parallel_conductivity](name:parallel_conductivity) which acts along the magnetic field line, and is relevant for modeling current redistribution and resistive dissipation in axisymmetric configurations. It is typically evaluated from neoclassical transport coefficients or derived self-consistently in edge/SOL simulations on unstructured generalized grids, complementing [radial_conductivity](name:radial_conductivity) and [poloidal_conductivity](name:poloidal_conductivity). Typical values in the edge plasma range from $10^3$ to $10^6\;\Omega^{-1}\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, decreasing with lower electron temperature and increasing collisionality.

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the current density arising from the diamagnetic drift due to perpendicular pressure gradients.
NAMES.long: The toroidal diamagnetic current density $j_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}}$ is the projection of the diamagnetic current density vector onto the toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It arises from the perpendicular pressure gradient in a magnetized plasma, given by $j_{\phi,\mathrm{dia}} = \frac{(\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p) \cdot \hat{\phi}}{B^2}$, where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field and $p$ is the total thermal pressure. This current contributes to the equilibrium force balance in tokamak edge plasmas and is a key component of the bootstrap current drive mechanism. Typical values reach tens of kA.m$^{-2}$ in the pedestal region of H-mode plasmas. This quantity is the toroidal component of the total diamagnetic current density vector $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ described by [current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). The poloidal counterpart is [poloidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). Viscous-driven toroidal currents are described by [toroidal_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) and [toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the current density driven by heat-viscous forces arising from the traceless part of the stress tensor.
NAMES.long: The toroidal heat-viscosity current density $j_{\phi}^{\rm hv}$ is the toroidal projection of the current density $\mathbf{j}^{\rm hv}$ produced by the heat-viscous stress tensor $\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\rm hv}$, which originates from the collisionally coupled parallel heat flux in the magnetized plasma. This non-inductive current contributes to the total toroidal current density in the edge plasma and is typically computed from fluid transport codes that solve the momentum balance including neoclassical viscous forces. The toroidal component is obtained as $j_{\phi}^{\rm hv} = \mathbf{j}^{\rm hv} \cdot \hat{\phi}$, where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the toroidal direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Related quantities include [toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) and [toroidal_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity), which describe the toroidal components driven by the parallel and perpendicular parts of the viscous stress tensor, respectively.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the current density resulting from the parallel viscous force in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal component $j_{\phi,\|
u} = \mathbf{j}_{\|
u} \cdot \hat{\phi}$ quantifies the projection of the parallel-viscosity-driven current density $\mathbf{j}_{\|
u}$ onto the geometric toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$. This current arises from neoclassical parallel-force balance: when the ion pressure tensor becomes anisotropic along the magnetic field, the resulting parallel viscous force drives a current that flows predominantly along field lines. The toroidal component links the viscous momentum transport to the toroidal current density profile in the edge plasma. Typical edge values are in the range $10^3\!-\!10^5$ A/m$^2$, depending on the local pressure gradient and collisionality. It is evaluated from fluid/MHD edge models or inferred from neoclassical transport analysis.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $j_{\phi,\|\nu}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.short: Toroidal (toroidal-angle-directed) flow velocity of the helium-3 ion population at the pedestal location.
NAMES.long: The toroidal helium-3 velocity $v_{\phi,\,^3\mathrm{He}}$ quantifies the toroidal rotation of the $^3\mathrm{He}^{1+}$ ion population in the pedestal region, and is a key parameter for understanding edge momentum transport, the H-mode pedestal structure, and impurity confinement. It is primarily measured via charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) by analyzing the Doppler shift of the $^3\mathrm{He}$ spectral emission lines, which directly yields the toroidal component of the flow velocity relative to the magnetic field direction. In tokamak pedestals, typical values range from a few km/s to tens of km/s, and the rotation shear can influence the stability of edge-localized modes. Compare with the value at the magnetic axis ([toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_magnetic_axis)) and at the separatrix ([toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_separatrix](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_separatrix)). The local helium-3 density is given by [helium_3_density_at_pedestal](name:helium_3_density_at_pedestal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above).

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_source_rate
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the volumetric momentum source density for a given ion charge state in the edge plasma governing ion rotation evolution.
NAMES.long: The toroidal ion source rate $S_{m,\phi,i}$ represents the volumetric density of momentum transferred to a specific ion charge state in the $\phi$ direction. It acts as a source or sink term in the toroidal momentum balance equation for that ion population, $\partial_t (m_i n_i v_{\phi,i}) + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_{\phi,i} = S_{m,\phi,i}$, where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $n_i$ the density, and $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{\phi,i}$ the momentum flux. This term can arise from neutral-beam injection, intrinsic rotation drives, collisional friction between species, or turbulent fluctuations. The quantity is defined on the generalized grid (GGD) subsets of the edge plasma and is typically inferred from integrated modeling codes. It complements the total momentum source from all species, [ion_source_rate](name:ion_source_rate), and the neutral counterpart [toroidal_neutral_source_rate](name:toroidal_neutral_source_rate). Units are kg·m⁻¹·s⁻², equivalent to momentum per unit volume per unit time (N·m⁻³).

NAMES.name: toroidal_neon_velocity_at_pedestal
NAMES.short: Time-averaged toroidal flow velocity of neon impurity ions at the top of the pedestal region in the plasma edge, consistent with the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.
NAMES.long: The toroidal velocity of neon impurity ions at the pedestal top is defined as $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ne}} = \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ne}} \cdot \hat{\phi}$, where $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{Ne}}$ is the neon ion velocity vector and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the toroidal direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system. This velocity is typically inferred from spectroscopic measurements of Doppler shifts in neon spectral lines, assuming the neon ions are thermalized with the bulk deuterium plasma. Typical values in the pedestal region of tokamaks range from a few tens to several hundred km/s in the co-current or counter-current direction, depending on the plasma rotation state and the injection of neutral beams. The measurement context includes edge charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) or passive spectroscopy using neon lines (e.g., Ne X at 12.13 nm).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal component of the neon velocity vector is in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above the machine).

NAMES.name: vertical_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Vertical component of the current density arising from the diamagnetic drift of the bulk plasma, driven by the pressure gradient perpendicular to the magnetic field.
NAMES.long: The vertical current density $j_{Z,\mathrm{dia}} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}} \cdot \hat{Z}$ is the projection of the diamagnetic drift current density $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia}} = (\mathbf{B} \times \nabla p)/B^2$ onto the vertical $Z$-axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ coordinate system, where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field and $p$ is the total plasma pressure. This component is physically relevant in the edge and scrape-off-layer (SOL) regions where poloidal asymmetry in the pressure gradient and magnetic geometry can produce a net vertical current, contributing to the radial force balance and influencing divertor heat flux distribution. The vertical current density is typically inferred from edge equilibrium reconstructions or kinetic profile measurements combined with the local magnetic field geometry. It is closely related to the parent quantity [current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and complements other component-specific quantities such as [radial_neutral_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:radial_neutral_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic current density vector has a component in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$ (upward).

NAMES.name: vertical_current_density_due_to_inertial
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) component of the current density arising from the ion polarization drift in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long: The vertical component $j_{\text{inertial},Z}$ of the inertial current density vector represents the projection onto the $+\hat{Z}$ axis of the current driven by the ion polarization drift $\mathbf{j}_{\text{inertial}} = (m_i n_i / B^2) \, d\mathbf{E}_\perp / dt$. This component arises from the time-varying perpendicular electric field and contributes to the radial force balance in the edge plasma, particularly during transient events such as edge-localized modes (ELMs). Typical magnitudes in the pedestal region range from 1 to 100 kA/m² for medium-size tokamaks. The full vector is described by [current_density_due_to_inertial](name:current_density_due_to_inertial); the radial counterpart is [radial_current_density_due_to_inertial](name:radial_current_density_due_to_inertial).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current density flows in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$ (upward in the machine cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame).

NAMES.name: vertical_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) component of the current density driven by the perpendicular component of the ion viscous stress tensor in the edge and scrape-off layer plasma.
NAMES.long:
The vertical current density $j_{\perp\nu,Z}$ is the projection of the perpendicular viscosity-driven current density vector onto the vertical ($Z$) axis of the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It represents the rate of charge transport in the height direction resulting from gyroviscous and perpendicular viscous forces in the edge plasma, where strong radial gradients in the parallel ion flow generate a perpendicular viscous stress. This component is measured in Ampere per square meter and is particularly relevant for MHD stability and radial force balance in the pedestal and scrape-off layer, where poloidal asymmetries can produce significant vertical currents. It is the vertical complement to [radial_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity), together providing the full poloidal-plane component of the perpendicular viscosity-driven current. Typical edge values range from 0.1 to 10 kA per square meter in H-mode tokamak plasmas, with the vertical component peaking in regions of strong poloidal variation of the parallel flow.

See [current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) for the parent magnitude vector, and [vertical_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) for the analogous component driven by heat viscosity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current density flows in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$ (upward in the machine frame).

NAMES.name: area_of_reflectometer_antenna
NAMES.short: Physical cross-sectional area of the aperture of the antenna that emits the probing millimeter-wave beam in a reflectometer diagnostic. This is the geometric area of the antenna aperture and does not include beam or coupling efficiency factors.
NAMES.long: The physical cross-sectional area of the antenna aperture determines the spatial resolution and power handling of the probing millimeter-wave beam in a reflectometer system. For a typical horn antenna, the aperture area is approximately the product of the horn's width and height at the radiating face, while for a lens-coupled antenna it is the clear aperture area of the lens. Typical values range from $10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}^2$ (for small waveguide-fed horns) to $10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}^2$ (for large imaging arrays). This area is a positive scalar; it is distinct from the effective area, which incorporates antenna gain and ohmic losses. In IMAS, the antenna surface is stored in the reflectometer_profile data structure as a 2-D surface geometry, and the area is derived from that geometry.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of a point on a flux surface used to define a diagnostic line of sight.
NAMES.long:
The major radius $R$ coordinate, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, of a point lying on a specified flux surface that defines a diagnostic line of sight. This geometric coordinate locates the diagnostic sightline endpoint with respect to the tokamak symmetry axis. It is used together with the vertical coordinate $Z$ and toroidal angle $\phi$ to fully specify the three-dimensional measurement path for diagnostics such as interferometry, polarimetry, and ECE. Typical values range from 1.0 to 1.2 m in the plasma core of ASDEX Upgrade to 4.0-8.0 m in ITER. See [major_radius_of_diagnostic_antenna](name:major_radius_of_diagnostic_antenna) and [major_radius_of_strike_point](name:major_radius_of_strike_point) for related geometric definitions.

Related standard names include [major_radius_of_x_point](name:major_radius_of_x_point) for the separatrix X-point and [major_radius_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:major_radius_of_sensor_attachment_point) for sensor line-of-sight endpoints.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the point lies at a larger major radius than the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_reflectometer_antenna
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of the center of the detection antenna aperture in a fluctuation reflectometer.
NAMES.long: The major radius $R_{\rm ant}$ (cylindrical $R$ coordinate) locates the center of the aperture of the antenna that receives the reflected millimeter-wave beam in a fluctuation reflectometer. This coordinate is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame of the tokamak, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis. Typical values range from $R_{\rm ant} \approx 1.5\,\text{m}$ to $3.0\,\text{m}$, depending on the radial position of the reflectometer chord. The antenna position is a fixed geometric property of the diagnostic and is used together with the toroidal angle coordinate, given by [toroidal_angle_of_reflectometer_antenna](name:toroidal_angle_of_reflectometer_antenna), to define the full spatial location of the antenna. The aperture area is quantified by [area_of_reflectometer_antenna](name:area_of_reflectometer_antenna).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R$ increases outward from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: minor_radius_of_ece_channel
NAMES.short: Radial location of the cold resonance layer in the tokamak midplane for an electron cyclotron emission (ECE) channel, defined as the major radius where the electron cyclotron frequency matches the channel center frequency.
NAMES.long: The minor radius of an ECE channel represents the radial position of the cold resonance layer in the poloidal plane, measured along the midplane from the magnetic axis to the cold resonance point. It is defined in the cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame as the distance from the magnetic axis to the intersection of the resonance layer with the outboard midplane, projected onto the Z = 0 plane. This quantity is computed from the magnetic field strength B (typically toroidal) and the ECE channel center frequency f via the cold resonance condition: f = e B / (2π mₑ), where e is the elementary charge and mₑ is the electron mass. Typical values range from a few centimeters to several tens of centimeters, depending on the machine size and the magnetic field profile. The minor radius is always positive and increases monotonically from the magnetic axis (ρ = 0) to the plasma boundary (ρ = a).

NAMES.name: normalized_perpendicular_wave_vector
NAMES.short: Dimensionless component of the normalized wave vector perpendicular to the background magnetic field along an electron cyclotron emission (ECE) beam path.
NAMES.long: The normalized perpendicular wave vector $k_{\perp,\mathrm{norm}} = (k_{\perp})/(k_0)$ gives the component of the wave vector transverse to the magnetic field direction $\mathbf{B}$, scaled to the vacuum wavenumber $k_0 = \omega/c$. Here $\omega$ is the ECE channel center angular frequency and $c$ the speed of light. This quantity governs the perpendicular refractive index $N_\perp = k_{\perp,\mathrm{norm}}$ and controls the beam width evolution via diffraction in the cold-plasma dispersion relation. Typical values for ECE channels in tokamaks range from $10^{-2}$ to $0.5$, increasing with poloidal field shear and beam divergence. Evaluated along the ray path from beam-tracing codes, it determines the spatial resolution of the ECE measurement perpendicular to the flux surfaces. The sibling quantity [normalized_parallel_wave_vector](name:normalized_parallel_wave_vector) describes the parallel component; together they satisfy $k_{\parallel,\mathrm{norm}}^2 + k_{\perp,\mathrm{norm}}^2 = N^2$ (where $N$ is the total refractive index).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the perpendicular wave vector component points in the direction of increasing minor radius projected onto the plane perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the Doppler reflectometer measurement position, identifying the flux surface probed by the channel.
NAMES.long:
The normalized poloidal flux coordinate $ho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}}$ maps the Doppler reflectometer measurement position onto the magnetic equilibrium, indicating which flux surface the probed cut-off layer lies on. It is defined as $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}} = \sqrt{(\psi(R,Z) - \psi_0) / (\psi_b - \psi_0)}$, where $\psi(R,Z)$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the measurement location, $\psi_0$ is the flux at the magnetic axis, and $\psi_b$ is the flux at the last closed flux surface. This coordinate is dimensionless and ranges from 0 on the magnetic axis to 1 at the plasma boundary. The measurement position is determined from the frequency-dependent cold resonance condition and ray tracing of the Doppler reflectometer probing beam. Typical probed values span $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}} \sim 0.2$–$0.9$ for turbulence measurements.

Related quantities include [normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_ece_channel_emission_position](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_ece_channel_emission_position) for ECE diagnostics and [poloidal_angle_of_reflectometer_antenna](name:poloidal_angle_of_reflectometer_antenna) for the antenna orientation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the measurement position lies on a flux surface with poloidal flux increasing away from the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_ece_channel_emission_position
NAMES.short: Normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the cold-resonance emission position of an ECE diagnostic channel, mapping the measurement location onto the equilibrium flux-surface grid.
NAMES.long: The normalized toroidal flux coordinate $ho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \sqrt{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}} / \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,LCFS}}}$ evaluated at the cold-resonance layer where the ECE channel center frequency matches the local electron cyclotron frequency $ω = e B / m_e$. This coordinate locates the emission position within the plasma on the flux-surface grid that spans $ho = 0$ at the magnetic axis to $ho = 1$ at the last closed flux surface (LCFS). For optically thick second-harmonic X-mode ECE in conventional tokamaks, the emission position shifts outward in $ho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ as the toroidal magnetic field increases. The radial resolution is typically $Δ \rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} \approx 0.01$ to 0.05. See `[normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate)` for the definition of the coordinate itself and `[normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_ece_channel_emission_position](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_ece_channel_emission_position)` for the poloidal counterpart.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the normalized toroidal flux coordinate increases outward from the magnetic axis toward the LCFS.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_wave_vector_of_ece_channel
NAMES.short: Dimensionless toroidal component of the wave vector, normalized to its magnitude, along an electron cyclotron emission beam path.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal wave vector component is defined as $k_\phi / |\mathbf{k}|$, where $k_\phi$ is the toroidal wavenumber and $|\mathbf{k}|$ is the magnitude of the wave vector. This quantity characterizes the fraction of wave propagation directed along the toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$, providing information on the directional structure of the beam or ray. It is computed from beam tracing calculations for electron cyclotron emission (ECE) diagnostics to model wave propagation through the plasma. Typical values range from near zero for predominantly radial propagation to unity for purely toroidal propagation.

See also [toroidal_wave_vector](name:toroidal_wave_vector) for the unnormalized component and [normalized_perpendicular_wave_vector](name:normalized_perpendicular_wave_vector) for the perpendicular counterpart.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $k_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_reflectometer_antenna
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle coordinate of the center of the reflectometer detection antenna in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle $\phi$ of the reflectometer antenna defines the toroidal position of the measurement location used for profile or fluctuation reflectometry. In the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, the angle is measured from a reference toroidal direction, increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$. The antenna center is typically the geometric center of the aperture or waveguide opening that couples the probing millimeter-wave beam into or out of the plasma.

The toroidal coordinate is a key geometric parameter for the reflectometer channel, alongside the [poloidal\_angle\_of\_reflectometer\_antenna](name:poloidal_angle_of_reflectometer_antenna) and the major radius, which together define the beam's launch or detection point. Combined with the antenna beam pattern, this coordinate determines the toroidal localization of the reflectometer measurement and is used in ray-tracing or beam-tracing codes to model the probing wave propagation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the angle increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: diamagnetic_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Statistical weight factor assigned to the diamagnetic flux constraint in equilibrium reconstruction, controlling its relative contribution to the least-squares cost functional.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic flux $\Phi_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the poloidal flux contribution arising from the plasma diamagnetic current, which reduces the toroidal magnetic field inside the plasma relative to the vacuum field. The weight $w_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is a dimensionless multiplicative factor in the $\chi^2$ cost function of equilibrium reconstruction, setting the relative importance of the diamagnetic flux measurement against all other constraints. A weight of unity applies the nominal measurement variance; larger values up-weight the constraint when systematic effects (e.g., eddy currents, calibration drift) are underestimated. Typical values for modern tokamaks are of order 1, with adjustments spanning 0.1–10 depending on measurement reliability and the reconstruction's sensitivity to the diamagnetic signal. This weight works alongside [weight_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:weight_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) and other constraint weights to determine the equilibrium solution.

The companion constraint data is the diamagnetic flux measurement itself, which is compared with the reconstructed diamagnetic flux derived from the equilibrium. The poloidal component [poloidal_diamagnetic_magnetic_flux](name:poloidal_diamagnetic_magnetic_flux) isolates the poloidal projection of this diamagnetic effect. Cross-reference with [normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_constraint_position](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_constraint_position) when the constraint is applied at a specific radial location.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic flux constraint is active in the reconstruction cost functional.

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Electron number density at a spatial location used as a constraint in equilibrium reconstruction, representing either a measured or reconstructed value.
NAMES.long:
The electron density $n_e$ at the specified measurement position serves as a local constraint in equilibrium reconstruction codes, providing pointwise information about the plasma density profile. This quantity can represent either a measured value from a diagnostic system (e.g., Thomson scattering, reflectometry, or interferometry) or the value calculated from the reconstructed equilibrium at the same spatial location.

Typical values in tokamak plasmas range from $10^{19}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ in the scrape-off layer to $10^{20}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ in the core of high-density H-mode discharges. The density at the measurement position is compared with the reconstructed value in the equilibrium fitting process to evaluate the $
chi^2$ cost functional.

See also: [toroidal_current_density_at_constraint_position](name:toroidal_current_density_at_constraint_position) for the analogous current constraint, and [electron_density_at_divertor_target](name:electron_density_at_divertor_target) for the density in the divertor region.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron number density is finite (the density is inherently a non-negative quantity).

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the total magnetic field magnitude, defined as the mean of |B| over a flux surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity represents the flux-surface average of the total magnetic field magnitude, computed as $\langle |B| \rangle = \frac{1}{V'} \oint |B| \, \frac{d\theta}{\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla \theta}$ where $V' = dV/d\psi$ is the flux-surface volume derivative. It is always positive irrespective of the sign convention for the magnetic field direction. In tokamak equilibria, the flux-surface averaged field varies radially, typically decreasing from the inboard to the outboard side; values range from $1\,\text{T}$ to $6\,\text{T}$ in present devices along the minor radius. This quantity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction (e.g., EFIT, LIUQE) and is related to the safety factor through $q = \frac{1}{2\pi} \oint \frac{B_\phi}{|\nabla\psi|} \, d\theta$. See [flux_surface_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:flux_surface_magnetic_field_magnitude) for a closely related quantity with an alternative label, and [magnetic_field_magnitude](name:magnetic_field_magnitude) for the unequally-weighted value at a point on a flux surface.

The flux-surface average is a key ingredient in neoclassical transport theory, appearing in expressions for the bootstrap current and the neoclassical conductivity. For a given equilibrium, the on-axis value $\langle |B| \rangle_{\psi=0}$ matches the vacuum toroidal field $B_0$ scaled by the major radius ratio, while at the plasma edge it approaches the total field at the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic field magnitude is defined as the Euclidean norm of the magnetic field vector.

NAMES.name: magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Maximum magnitude of the total magnetic field on each flux surface, determining the minimum possible value of the magnetic field strength encountered by a particle on that surface.
NAMES.long: The magnetic field magnitude maximum $B_\mathrm{max}(\psi)$ on a given flux surface is the largest value of $|\mathbf{B}|$ along the poloidal circumference. This quantity governs the mirror ratio $R_\mathrm{mirror} = B_\mathrm{max}/B_\mathrm{min}$ of the magnetic well, which is a key parameter for trapped-particle confinement and neoclassical transport: particles with pitch angle $\xi = v_\parallel/v$ satisfying $|\xi| < \sqrt{1 - B_\mathrm{min}/B_\mathrm{max}}$ become trapped in the magnetic mirror. $B_\mathrm{max}$ is routinely obtained from equilibrium reconstruction codes (EFIT, LIUQE) and can be validated by ECE diagnostics resolving the cyclotron resonance layer. Typical core values in diverted tokamaks range from 1 T (low-field side) to 6 T (high-field side) depending on the plasma cross-section elongation and triangularity. See also [magnetic_field](name:magnetic_field) for the full vector field, [flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field](name:flux_surface_averaged_magnetic_field) for the surface-averaged magnitude, and [magnetic_field_magnitude](name:magnetic_field_magnitude) for the local field modulus at a point.

NAMES.name: magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux at a flux loop sensor location, calculated from the reconstructed equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
The reconstructed poloidal magnetic flux at a flux loop sensor is the value of $\psi$ computed from the Grad–Shafranov equilibrium solution at the $(R, Z, \phi)$ coordinates of the loop. It is used as a target in the least-squares cost functional of the equilibrium reconstruction, where it is compared with the measured flux loop signal to constrain the plasma current profile and boundary shape. The quantity is closely related to the [poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop) (the measured counterpart) and to other magnetic diagnostics such as [poloidal_field_coil_current](name:poloidal_field_coil_current) that enter the same reconstruction. Typical values for the poloidal flux range from 0–10 Wb on axis to 0–5 Wb at the boundary, depending on the plasma current and the major radius of the machine.

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Normalized radial derivative of the safety factor evaluated at the magnetic axis, a key MHD stability parameter in the plasma core.
NAMES.long:
The magnetic shear at the magnetic axis is defined as $s(\rho_{\rm tor}=0) = (\rho_{\rm tor}/q)\,dq/d\rho_{\rm tor}$ evaluated in the limit of vanishing toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\rm tor}$. In this expression $q$ is the safety factor and $\rho_{\rm tor}$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate. The magnetic axis value sets the innermost boundary condition for the interior shear profile and controls the stability of ideal and resistive MHD modes including sawtooth oscillations. In typical H-mode tokamak plasmas $s_0$ is near zero or slightly positive, whereas negative central shear (reversed shear) can suppress sawtooth activity and improve confinement. This quantity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction codes such as EFIT or LIUQE and is closely related to [magnetic_shear_at_separatrix](name:magnetic_shear_at_separatrix) at the plasma boundary.

The radial derivative of the safety factor governs the field-line winding rate and determines the strength of magnetic flux surface compression in the core region.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $q$ increases with increasing minor radius.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_closest_wall_point
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of the point on the plasma-facing first wall that is closest to the plasma separatrix.
NAMES.long:
The major radius $R_{\mathrm{cw}}$ of the closest wall point quantifies the radial proximity of the plasma boundary to the first-wall surface within a given poloidal cross-section. This quantity is used in equilibrium reconstruction to define the wall-limiting surface and in disruption modeling to assess halo-current contact locations. Typical values range from 1.5 to 2.5 m in medium-size tokamaks and up to 6.2 m for ITER. The closest-wall point is identified by minimizing the Euclidean distance between the separatrix and all first-wall outline points in the $R$--$Z$ plane.

See also [vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point) for the corresponding $Z$ coordinate and [major_radius_of_x_point](name:major_radius_of_x_point) for another key boundary radius.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the coordinate is measured in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_current_center
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of the plasma current centroid, defined as the flux-surface average of the toroidal current density weighted by major radius.
NAMES.long: The current center major radius $R_{\mathrm{cc}}$ is the $R$ coordinate of the centroid of the toroidal plasma current density distribution. It is computed as $R_{\mathrm{cc}} = \frac{\iint j_\phi R \, dS}{\iint j_\phi \, dS}$, where $j_\phi$ is the toroidal current density (A/m²) and $dS$ is a poloidal cross-section area element. This quantity locates the effective radial position of the net toroidal current $I_p$ and is used in equilibrium reconstruction to constrain the current profile. Typical values in a medium-size tokamak range from the magnetic axis major radius (≈1.6–3.0 m) out to the separatrix; in diverted plasmas it lies inside the geometric center. It is inferred from magnetic measurements via equilibrium codes such as EFIT or LIUQE. See also $[\text{major radius of X-point}](name:major_radius_of_x_point)$ for the separatrix geometry and $[\text{poloidal magnetic flux}](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux)$ for the flux coordinate system.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R_{\mathrm{cc}}$ lies in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_geometric_axis
NAMES.short: Major radius (R) coordinate of the plasma geometric axis, computed as the arithmetic mean of the maximum and minimum R coordinates of the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long: The major radius of the geometric axis, $R_{\text{geo}} = (R_{\text{max}} + R_{\text{min}})/2$, locates the horizontal center of the plasma boundary contour in the tokamak poloidal plane. This quantity serves as a primary descriptor of plasma position within the vacuum vessel and is routinely extracted from equilibrium reconstruction (e.g., EFIT, LIUQE) or directly from the plasma boundary contour. Typical $R_{\text{geo}}$ values are 1.6–3.0 m for medium-size tokamaks and 6.2 m for ITER. The geometric axis differs from the magnetic axis by the Shafranov shift, which can reach 10–30 cm in high-β plasmas; compare with [major_radius_of_magnetic_axis](name:major_radius_of_magnetic_axis) and [major_radius_of_current_center](name:major_radius_of_current_center).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the coordinate increases in the direction of increasing $R$ (outward from the machine symmetry axis) in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Magnetic axis location in the tokamak poloidal plane, defined by the major radius coordinate R_axis where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
$R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the major radius $R$ of the magnetic axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, corresponding to the innermost point of the nested flux-surface topology where $\nabla\psi = 0$ and the poloidal magnetic field vanishes. In tokamak equilibrium reconstruction, $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is found by locating the extremum of $\psi$ and is constrained by magnetics diagnostics, motional-Stark-effect measurements, and X-ray imaging. Typical values range from 2.8–3.1 m (JET) to 6.2 m (ITER) and are correlated with the plasma current centroid via $[current\,center](name:major_radius_of_current_center)$ and the geometric axis via $[geometric\,axis](name:major_radius_of_geometric_axis)$. The vertical coordinate is given by $[Z_{\mathrm{axis}}](name:vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis)$.

See also $[\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis)$ for the flux reference.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ lies radially outward from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of the reference point defining the distance between the plasma boundary and the first wall in an equilibrium reconstruction.
NAMES.long:
The major radius $R_{\mathrm{gap}}$ of the reference point used to define the plasma boundary gap, a control parameter for the distance between the separatrix and the first wall in tokamaks. This coordinate is part of a set of gap definitions that describe the plasma position and shape relative to the surrounding vessel, and is derived from equilibrium reconstruction (e.g., EFIT, LIUQE). Together with the vertical coordinate $Z_{\mathrm{gap}}$ (see `vertical_coordinate_of_gap_reference_point`), it defines the location of a specific gap measurement used in real-time plasma position control and pulse scheduling. Typical values for $R_{\mathrm{gap}}$ range from 1.5 to 3.0 m for medium-size tokamaks (e.g., DIII-D, ASDEX Upgrade) and up to 6.2 m for ITER, depending on the vessel geometry and the gap reference point. This quantity is also closely related to the major radius of the separatrix and the plasma boundary (see `major_radius_of_separatrix`).

See also the plasma boundary gap reference defined by the poloidal flux geometry and the corresponding `vertical_coordinate_of_gap_reference_point`.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the gap reference point is at a larger major radius than the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_strike_point
NAMES.short: Major radius (R) coordinate of the point where the secondary separatrix intersects the divertor target plate.
NAMES.long:
The major radius of the strike point is the $R$ coordinate, in the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, of the intersection between the secondary separatrix (divertor leg) and the divertor target plate. This quantity is critical for divertor heat load management, as the strike point position determines the peak heat flux deposition area. It is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction using magnetic diagnostics and is used together with $\texttt{major\_radius\_of\_magnetic\_axis}$ and $\texttt{major\_radius\_of\_x\_point}$ to characterize the plasma boundary geometry. Typical strike point major radii lie in the range 1.5–3.0 m for medium-size tokamaks, depending on the divertor configuration and magnetic equilibrium.

See also $\texttt{major\_radius\_of\_closest\_wall\_point}$ for the first wall intersection coordinate, and $\texttt{distance\_of\_secondary\_separatrix}$ for the radial separation between inner and outer strike points.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the strike point lies at a major radius $R > 0$ in the cylindrical frame.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_x_point
NAMES.short: Major radius (R) coordinate of the secondary X-point of a double-null divertor configuration, where the poloidal magnetic field vanishes on the secondary separatrix.
NAMES.long:
The major radius of the secondary X-point, $R_{X2}$, locates the poloidal-field null on the secondary separatrix in a double-null equilibrium. Both the primary and secondary X-points satisfy $\mathbf{B}_p = 0$, where $\mathbf{B}_p$ is the poloidal magnetic field. The secondary X-point is typically the lower or upper null opposite the primary null, and its radial position affects divertor heat-flux sharing and magnetic geometry. $R_{X2}$ is determined from equilibrium reconstruction codes (e.g., EFIT) that solve the Grad--Shafranov equation, with typical values of $1.5$–$3.0\,\mathrm{m}$ in medium-size tokamaks. Larger major radius of the secondary X-point shifts the outer divertor leg outward, increasing the outer strike-point radius.
