See also [major radius of magnetic axis](name:major_radius_of_magnetic_axis) for the innermost flux-surface location and [major radius of strike point](name:major_radius_of_strike_point) for the divertor-target intersection.

Measurement of $R_{X2}$ relies on magnetic probe arrays, flux loops, and poloidal-field coil currents used as constraints in equilibrium reconstruction. Typical uncertainty is $\pm 0.01$–$0.02\,\mathrm{m}$ in well-diagnosed plasmas. The secondary X-point may be absent in single-null configurations, where the secondary separatrix lies entirely outside the plasma. A matched quantity for the primary null is [major radius of X-point](name:major_radius_of_x_point) (without the 'secondary' qualifier) — the present name is used only for the second null in double-null or snowflake equilibria.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R_{X2}$ increases in the direction of the geometric major radius $+R$ in the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: minimum_safety_factor
NAMES.short: Minimum value of the safety factor across the plasma radial profile, a key MHD stability parameter.
NAMES.long: The minimum safety factor $q_{\mathrm{min}}$ is the lowest value of $q(\psi)$ across the radial profile of a tokamak plasma, where $q$ is the ratio of toroidal to poloidal magnetic field line turns per circuit around the flux surface. It governs the core ideal MHD stability: when $q_{\mathrm{min}} < 1$, sawtooth oscillations are triggered, and values near a rational integer can destabilize resonant tearing modes. In a typical H-mode discharge, $q_{\mathrm{min}}$ lies between 1.0 and 2.0, and is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic measurements together with internal constraints such as the motional Stark effect. See also [safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis](name:safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis) and [safety_factor_at_inside_flux_surface](name:safety_factor_at_inside_flux_surface).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the standard safety factor $q$ is positive, i.e., the field-line helicity is right-handed in the $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: parallel_total_plasma_current_density
NAMES.short: Projection of the total plasma current density vector onto the direction parallel to the local magnetic field in the poloidal plane.
NAMES.long: The parallel component of the total plasma current density, $j_{\parallel} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{total}} \cdot \mathbf{b}$, where $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the total magnetic field. This quantity accounts for all current sources — ohmic, bootstrap, and auxiliary current drive — providing the field-aligned current that flows along flux surfaces and generates the poloidal magnetic field. Typical values in the core of a burning plasma range from 0.1 to 1.0 MA/m², decreasing toward the scrape-off layer. The parallel current density is essential for MHD equilibrium force balance $\nabla p = \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}$ and determines the poloidal field structure via Ampère's law. It is routinely reconstructed from magnetic measurements combined with kinetic profile constraints using Grad–Shafranov solvers. See also the radial component [radial_total_plasma_current_density](name:radial_total_plasma_current_density) and the parent vector quantity [total_plasma_current_density](name:total_plasma_current_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above).

NAMES.name: plasma_inductance
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic energy stored in the plasma current channel, expressed as an inductance via $L_p = 2E_{mag}/I_p^2$.
NAMES.long: The plasma inductance quantifies the magnetic energy stored in the poloidal field generated by the toroidal plasma current $I_p$. It is defined as $L_p = 2 E_{mag} / I_p^2$, where $E_{mag} = \frac{1}{2}\int \psi \, j_{\phi} \, dS$ is the poloidal magnetic energy integrated over the plasma poloidal cross-section, $\psi$ (Wb) is the poloidal magnetic flux, and $j_{\phi}$ (A/m²) is the toroidal current density. This global scalar is distinct from the normalized internal inductance $l_i$, which is a dimensionless shape factor used in MHD stability analysis. The plasma inductance is typically inferred from equilibrium reconstruction codes (e.g., EFIT) and is closely related to the [mutual_inductance_of_flux_loop_due_to_induction](name:mutual_inductance_of_flux_loop_due_to_induction) that couples the plasma to external diagnostics. Typical values for medium-size tokamaks range from 0.5–2 μH, depending on the current profile peaking and plasma geometry. The inductance increases as the current profile becomes more peaked (larger $l_i$) and decreases as the plasma becomes more hollow.

NAMES.name: plasma_resistance
NAMES.short: Effective bulk electrical resistance of the plasma column, relating the toroidal loop voltage to the total toroidal plasma current through Ohm's law.
NAMES.long:
The global plasma resistance $R_p$ quantifies the total resistive dissipation of the toroidal current in the plasma column. It is defined via the integral relation $R_p = \int \mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{j} \, dV \,/\, I_p^2$, where $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric field, $\mathbf{j}$ is the current density, and $I_p$ is the total toroidal plasma current [toroidal_total_plasma_current](name:toroidal_total_plasma_current). This resistance is dominated by the Spitzer resistivity $\eta \propto Z_{\text{eff}} \, T_e^{-3/2}$ and is therefore a sensitive function of the core electron temperature $T_e$ and effective ion charge $Z_{\text{eff}}$. Typical values range from 1–10 $\mu\Omega$ in high-temperature H-mode plasmas to tens of $\mu\Omega$ in L-mode, directly determining the Ohmic heating power [ohmic_power](name:ohmic_power) deposited in the plasma. The plasma resistance is inferred from the measured loop voltage and plasma current during the current flat-top phase of a discharge.

The global resistance is a lumped parameter distinct from the local resistivity profile and is complementary to the [mutual_inductance_of_flux_loop_due_to_induction](name:mutual_inductance_of_flux_loop_due_to_induction) in the circuit equation of the plasma column.
NAMES.sign: Positive for passive resistive dissipation when toroidal loop voltage and plasma current are aligned.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle
NAMES.short: Angular coordinate parameterizing positions along a flux surface in the poloidal plane, measured from the low-field-side midplane.
NAMES.long: The poloidal angle $\theta$ is an angular coordinate in the poloidal plane, measured from the outboard midplane of a given flux surface. It is a fundamental coordinate for describing plasma equilibrium and for mapping flux-surface quantities, such as pressure and current density. The poloidal angle is typically defined in the range $[0, 2\pi)$ or $(-\pi, \pi]$, increasing in the direction from the outboard midplane toward the lower divertor region. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the poloidal angle is measured in radians originated at the outboard midplane (where $R > R_\text{axis}$, $Z = Z_\text{axis}$), providing a natural label for the poloidal location on a flux surface. The poloidal angle is related to the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi_\text{pol}$ and the safety factor $q$ through the differential relation $d\psi_\text{pol}/d\theta = -I(\psi_\text{pol})/(2\pi q(\psi_\text{pol}))$, where $I(\psi_\text{pol})$ is the diamagnetic function. Common ranges span $[0, 2\pi)$ for full poloidal coverage. Related standard names include [poloidal_magnetic_flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) for the flux-surface label, [safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis](name:safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis) for the field-line helicity parameter, and [straight_field_line_poloidal_angle](name:straight_field_line_poloidal_angle) for the flux-aligned version.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the angle increases clockwise in the poloidal plane, which corresponds to increasing direction of the toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_field_coil_current
NAMES.short: Measured electric current in a poloidal field coil used as a constraint in equilibrium reconstruction.
NAMES.long:
The measured current $I_{\text{PF}}$ in a poloidal field coil is a critical input constraint for axisymmetric equilibrium reconstruction codes, which solve the Grad–Shafranov equation to determine the plasma boundary and internal current distribution. These measurements, obtained from calibrated current transducers on each PF coil circuit, provide essential boundary conditions that constrain the poloidal magnetic flux generated by the external coil set. Typical values range from tens of kiloamperes in the central solenoid to several kiloamperes in equilibrium shaping coils, depending on the tokamak size and operating scenario. The reconstructed PF coil currents are compared against these measured values to form a χ² cost function that quantifies the fit quality, alongside constraints from magnetic probes and flux loops. See [passive_structure_current](name:passive_structure_current) for the analogous quantity in passive structures.

The reconstructed counterpart [weight_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:weight_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) (for magnetic probes) demonstrates the analogous statistical weighting applied in the equilibrium reconstruction cost function.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction that generates a positive poloidal magnetic flux within the plasma region.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: The poloidal component of the magnetic field vector, providing the field that confines the plasma in the poloidal cross-section, generated primarily by the plasma current.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal magnetic field $B_\theta = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{\theta}$ is the projection of the total magnetic field vector onto the poloidal direction. In a tokamak, the poloidal field is essential for the nested-flux-surface topology that confines the plasma; it is produced by the toroidal plasma current $I_p$ and is related to the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ gradient by $B_\theta = -|\nabla \psi|/R$. The poloidal field direction determines the pitch of the helical magnetic field lines and controls MHD stability through the safety factor $q = d\Phi/d\psi$. Typical on-axis values are near zero, while the poloidal field increases to 0.2–2 T at the plasma boundary in present-day tokamaks. The poloidal field is inferred from external magnetic probe arrays mounted at the vessel wall and is a primary constraint in equilibrium reconstruction codes such as EFIT and LIUQE.

See the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ components [radial_magnetic_field](name:radial_magnetic_field) and [toroidal_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), as well as the scalar magnitude [magnetic_field_magnitude](name:magnetic_field_magnitude). The poloidal magnetic flux [poloidal_magnetic_flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) is the integral of this component over a toroidal surface.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal field points from the inboard to the outboard midplane on the low-field side.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux, the scalar flux-surface label defined by integrating the poloidal magnetic field over a toroidal cross-section delimited by the flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ is a fundamental flux-surface label in 2D axisymmetric equilibrium, defined for a flux surface enclosing the magnetic axis as the flux of the magnetic field through a toroidal cross-section bounded by that surface. Together with the toroidal magnetic flux $\Phi$, it completes the magnetic-flux description of the equilibrium, and its gradient $
abla \psi$ defines the poloidal magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{pol} = 
abla \phi 	imes 
abla \psi / (2\pi)$, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle. The poloidal flux decreases monotonically from the magnetic axis to the separatrix in a conventional tokamak, with typical separatrix values of 5–20 Wb in medium-size devices. It serves as a radial coordinate for profiles of plasma quantities (density, temperature, safety factor) and is reconstructed from external magnetic measurements combined with equilibrium codes. The safety factor $q = d\Phi/d\psi$ is the local helicity of magnetic field lines, directly linking $\psi$ to MHD stability. See the parent quantity [magnetic_flux](name:magnetic_flux) and the sibling [toroidal_magnetic_flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux), as well as the spatially localized [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_internal_transport_barrier).

Typical core values range from 0 Wb at the magnetic axis to 5–20 Wb at the separatrix in diverted tokamaks such as JET and DIII-D, scaling with the plasma current and major radius.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal magnetic field lines are oriented to give a diamagnetic plasma response for a positive toroidal plasma current.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_minimum_safety_factor
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux evaluated at the radial location where the safety factor reaches its minimum value across the plasma profile.
NAMES.long: The poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ is the flux of the poloidal magnetic field through a surface of constant toroidal angle, serving as the fundamental flux surface label in axisymmetric equilibrium. At the location where the safety factor $q(r)$ attains its minimum $q_{\mathrm{min}}$, this quantity $\psi(q_{\mathrm{min}})$ provides the flux coordinate of the most MHD-sensitive radial zone. In conventional tokamak H-modes, $q_{\mathrm{min}}$ typically lies near $\psi / \psi_{\mathrm{sep}} \approx 0.5$–$0.7$, with $\psi_{\mathrm{sep}}$ the poloidal flux at the separatrix; the radial position of $q_{\mathrm{min}}$ strongly influences sawtooth stability and the onset of neoclassical tearing modes. This flux value is routinely extracted from equilibrium reconstruction (EFIT, LIUQE) and is paired with [minimum_safety_factor](name:minimum_safety_factor) to define the $q$-profile minimum. See also [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) and [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_separatrix](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_separatrix) for the bounding references of the radial flux coordinate. The quantity is COCOS-dependent: under the standard IMAS right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $\psi$ is defined such that $B_{\mathrm{pol}} = (1/R)\, \nabla \psi \times \hat{\phi}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\psi$ decreases from the magnetic axis to the plasma boundary for a plasma current $I_p$ flowing in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short: Poloidal component of the magnetic flux threading a flux loop sensor, equal to the loop voltage integrated in time.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal magnetic flux through a flux loop sensor is the integral of the inductive voltage induced in the loop, $Ψ_{\text{loop}} = \int V_{\text{loop}} \, dt$. This flux is dominated by the poloidal field generated by the plasma current and external poloidal field coils, with contributions from eddy currents in passive structures. It serves as a fundamental constraint in equilibrium reconstruction codes, such as EFIT or LIUQE, that solve the Grad-Shafranov equation. Typical flux values range from 1 to 10 Wb in medium-size tokamaks. For a loop located inside the vacuum vessel, the measured flux includes both the plasma contribution and the flux from induced currents in the vessel wall.

The measured value [magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop](name:magnetic_flux_of_flux_loop) is compared with the reconstructed value in the equilibrium solution; the mutual inductance [mutual_inductance_of_flux_loop](name:mutual_inductance_of_flux_loop) relates the flux to currents in poloidal field coils. The poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) and at the separatrix [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_separatrix](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_separatrix) provide normalization references.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flux through the loop is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $φ$.

NAMES.name: radial_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Radial component of the magnetic field vector on the 2D poloidal grid, representing the projection onto the major-radius direction of the cylindrical coordinate system.
NAMES.long: The radial magnetic field $B_R = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{R}$ is the projection of the magnetic field vector onto the radial ($\hat{R}$) axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ coordinate system. In the confined plasma region, $B_R$ describes the poloidal magnetic field's contribution to the equilibrium force balance $\nabla p = \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}$, and it is a key output of Grad-Shafranov equilibrium reconstruction codes such as EFIT or LIUQE. Typical values range from a few tens of mT in the plasma core to several hundred mT near the separatrix in medium-size tokamaks. The sign indicates the direction of the field component relative to increasing major radius $R$; this is convention-dependent and must be understood from the reconstruction setup. The full magnetic field vector is represented by the parent quantity [magnetic_field](name:magnetic_field), with companion components [poloidal_magnetic_field](name:poloidal_magnetic_field) and a toroidal component [toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis).

NAMES.name: safety_factor
NAMES.short: Safety factor q evaluated at the 95% poloidal flux surface, a standard global MHD stability indicator.
NAMES.long: The safety factor $q_{95} = d\Phi_{\rm tor}/d\Phi_{\rm pol}$ evaluated at the surface enclosing 95% of the poloidal magnetic flux is a key dimensionless ratio of toroidal to poloidal field line turns. This edge quantity is routinely used in tokamak operations to assess proximity to the $q=2$ and $q=3$ rational surfaces that seed tearing modes and the $q=3/2$ neoclassical tearing mode threshold; typical H-mode values range from 3 to 5. $q_{95}$ is derived from equilibrium reconstruction (e.g., EFIT, LIUQE) using external magnetic measurements and internal profile constraints. The quantity is positive by convention; the sign of $q$ follows the sign of the toroidal plasma current in the $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. See also [safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis](name:safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis) for the core value and [poloidal_magnetic_flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) for the underlying flux coordinate.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Safety factor (q) at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the nested flux surfaces where the poloidal magnetic field vanishes.
NAMES.long: The safety factor at the magnetic axis, $q_0 = q(\psi=0)$, is defined as $q = d\Phi_{\text{tor}} / d\Phi_{\text{pol}}$ evaluated at the magnetic axis, where $\Phi_{\text{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux (in Wb) and $\Phi_{\text{pol}}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux (in Wb). $q_0$ is a critical MHD stability parameter; in conventional tokamak H-mode plasmas $q_0$ is typically near unity (0.9–1.2), and values below unity drive sawtooth instabilities. It is routinely inferred from motional Stark effect (MSE) measurements or equilibrium reconstruction codes, cross-referenced with [safety_factor](name:safety_factor) at the edge and [magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis](name:magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis). The [major_radius_of_magnetic_axis](name:major_radius_of_magnetic_axis) gives the spatial location of this point.
NAMES.sign: Positive for conventional tokamak operation with plasma current in the direction of increasing toroidal angle.

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Safety factor measured at a specific diagnostic location and used as a constraint in equilibrium reconstruction.
NAMES.long: The safety factor $q(R,Z,\phi) = d\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}/d\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}$ quantifies the helicity of magnetic field lines on a flux surface upto an arbitrary point. This particular instance records the value of $q$ at a diagnostic measurement position, representing a measured constraint for equilibrium reconstruction. The measured $q$ at a local position is typically obtained from motional Stark effect (MSE) diagnostics, Zeeman polarimetry, or high-resolution Thomson scattering, with typical core values of $q_0 \sim 0.9$–$1.1$ and $q_{95} \sim 3$–$5$ in H-mode tokamak operation. The constraint contrasts with the safety factor at the magnetic axis, $[\mathrm{safety\,factor\,at\,magnetic\,axis}](name:safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis)$, which defines the innermost limit.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal magnetic field and plasma current directions produce a field-aligned coordinate system with $q > 0$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_beta
NAMES.short: Ratio of the volume-averaged total plasma pressure to the toroidal magnetic field pressure, derived from MHD equilibrium reconstruction.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal beta $\beta_t = 2\mu_0 \langle p \rangle / B_{\phi,0}^2$ quantifies the efficiency of the magnetic confinement, where $\langle p \rangle$ is the volume-averaged perpendicular plasma pressure and $B_{\phi,0}$ the toroidal magnetic field at the plasma center. This dimensionless ratio is a key figure of merit for confinement quality, with typical values ranging from 0.001 in early tokamaks to above 0.05 in modern high-performance regimes. It is routinely computed from equilibrium reconstruction codes (e.g., EFIT) that constrain the pressure profile using external magnetic measurements and kinetic profile data. The quantity is the toroidal component of the vector beta, defined as $[\beta_t](name:poloidal_beta) \equiv [\beta](name:beta) \cdot \hat{\phi}$. 

For a related measure using the poloidal field, see `[poloidal_beta](name:poloidal_beta)`. The value is closely tied to the `[safety_factor](name:safety_factor)` profile through the MHD equilibrium force balance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the volume-averaged pressure is positive.

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_density_at_constraint_position
NAMES.short: Toroidal current density at specified spatial positions used as a constraint in equilibrium reconstruction codes.
NAMES.long: The toroidal current density $j_\phi(R,Z)$ on a set of discrete spatial positions (``constraint positions'') defined by their $R$ and $Z$ coordinates. These positions are distinct from the equilibrium reconstruction grid and are used to enforce agreement between the reconstructed current profile and independent current-density measurements (e.g. from MSE or current wires). The quantity is a scalar value at each position; the full toroidal current-density profile is obtained by integrating over the plasma cross-section. Typical core values range from $10^5$--$10^7$ A/m$^2$ in medium-size tokamaks. The constraint positions are defined in [major_radius_of_constraint_position](name:major_radius_of_constraint_position).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above).

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the magnetic field, evaluated at a reference major radius and used for normalizing quantities in local gyrokinetic simulations.
NAMES.long: The toroidal magnetic field $B_\mathrm{tor}$ is the projection of the total magnetic field vector onto the geometric toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ coordinate system. In tokamaks, $B_\mathrm{tor}$ is the dominant field component, set primarily by the toroidal field coils scalings as $B_\phi \propto 1/R$. This quantity serves as a normalizing scale for dimensionless parameters in local gyrokinetic simulations, such as the normalized gyroradius $\rho_* = \rho_\mathrm{tor}/a$, where $\rho_\mathrm{tor} = m_i v_\mathrm{th} / (e B_\mathrm{tor})$ is the thermal ion Larmor radius. Typical values at the reference radius range from 1 to 6 T for current devices (e.g., 2.0 T at $R_0 = 1.7$ m in DIII-D, 5.2 T at $R_0 = 6.2$ m in ITER). The reference major radius is typically the magnetic axis or geometric center, chosen to match the local gyrokinetic simulation domain. See also [toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis) for the value at the magnetic axis, and [magnetic_field](name:magnetic_field) for the total vector field.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the field direction coincides with the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above).

NAMES.name: toroidal_total_plasma_current_density
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the total plasma current density vector on the poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long: The toroidal total plasma current density $j_{\phi}^{\mathrm{plasma}} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{total}} \cdot \hat{\phi}$ is the projection of the total plasma current density vector onto the geometric toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$ in the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It represents the local net current density carried by all plasma species (electrons and ions) in the toroidal direction, encompassing ohmic, bootstrap, and auxiliary current drive contributions. This quantity is defined on the poloidal grid and is reconstructed from equilibrium codes constrained by magnetic measurements (e.g., motional Stark effect, polarimetry) and kinetic profile data. Typical values in the plasma core range from 0.1 to 1 MA/m² for medium-size tokamaks, peaking on-axis and decreasing toward the edge. The radial integral of $j_{\phi}^{\mathrm{plasma}}$ over the poloidal cross-section yields the total plasma current $I_p$. See also the [radial_total_plasma_current_density](name:radial_total_plasma_current_density) and [parallel_total_plasma_current_density](name:parallel_total_plasma_current_density) components, as well as the parent vector quantity [total_plasma_current_density](name:total_plasma_current_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $j_{\phi}$ flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above the device).

NAMES.name: total_plasma_current
NAMES.short: The net toroidal electric current flowing through the plasma column, measured for use as a constraint in magnetic equilibrium reconstruction.
NAMES.long: The total plasma current $I_p$ is the net toroidal current carried by the confined plasma, typically measured by a Rogowski coil encircling the vessel. It is a primary global parameter that determines the poloidal magnetic field through Ampère's law and directly influences the safety factor profile and MHD stability. Typical values range from 0.5–3.0 MA in present-day tokamaks to 15 MA for ITER. The measured value of $I_p$ enters the least-squares cost functional in equilibrium reconstruction codes such as EFIT or LIUQE, where it constrains the poloidal flux solution. The reconstructed quantity is [plasma_current](name:plasma_current), while the toroidal component is explicitly resolved as [toroidal_total_plasma_current](name:toroidal_total_plasma_current).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net toroidal current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle (counter-clockwise viewed from above).

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the point on the first wall that lies closest to the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z_{\mathrm{wall,min}}$ of the first-wall point nearest to the plasma boundary defines the closest approach of the wall in the poloidal plane. This geometric quantity is used to assess plasma-wall clearance, evaluate heat-flux deposition patterns, and constrain halo-current paths during disruptions. The coordinate is measured in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ increases vertically upward.

The radial companion [major_radius_of_current_center](name:major_radius_of_current_center) similarly locates the plasma current centroid, while the boundary shape is referenced via [vertical_coordinate_of_limiter](name:vertical_coordinate_of_limiter) for limiter contact considerations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the closest wall point lies above the midplane ($Z=0$).

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the arithmetic mean of the plasma boundary's maximum and minimum Z coordinates, defining the vertical midpoint of the poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long: The vertical coordinate of the geometric axis defines the midpoint of the plasma boundary in the $Z$ direction of the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, computed as $Z_{\rm geo} = (Z_{\max} + Z_{\min}) / 2$ from the boundary contour. This geometric descriptor is independent of the magnetic equilibrium and provides a robust reference for plasma position control and shape analysis. In tokamak scenarios with a well-aligned plasma, $Z_{\rm geo}$ closely tracks the magnetic axis height $[Z_{\rm axis}](name:vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis)$, but may deviate substantially during vertical displacement events or strong shaping. Typical core plasmas have $Z_{\rm geo}$ within $\pm 0.3$ m of the vacuum vessel midplane for medium-size devices. The companion radial coordinate is $[R_{\rm geo}](name:major_radius_of_geometric_axis)$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the geometric axis lies above the $Z = 0$ reference plane (the machine midplane).

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_limiter
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the active limiter contact point that defines the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z_{\mathrm{lim}}$ of the active limiter point at the plasma boundary in the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This point defines the outermost extent of the confined plasma where it contacts the limiter surface, governing heat-flux deposition and plasma-wall interaction. The value is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction or from magnetic measurements that identify the limiter contact location.

Typical values span $\pm moid$ of the vessel vertical height, e.g., $\sim\pm 2\,\mathrm{m}$ in ITER. Compare with [vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point) for the nearest wall element and [gap_at_separatrix](name:gap_at_separatrix) for the distance to the limiter.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the active limiter contact point lies above the midplane ($Z > 0$).

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Vertical height (Z coordinate) of the magnetic axis, defined as the point where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long: The magnetic axis is the location of the extremum of the poloidal magnetic flux in the poloidal plane; its vertical coordinate $Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ positions the plasma centroid vertically. $Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is a primary actuator-controlled quantity in plasma position feedback and must be maintained within narrow limits to avoid wall contact. Typical values range from $Z=0\,\mathrm{m}$ for a centered plasma to $\pm 0.3\,\mathrm{m}$ in tilted or off-axis equilibrium reconstructions. It is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction codes (e.g. EFIT, LIUQE) that solve the Grad–Shafranov equation. See also [major_radius_of_magnetic_axis](name:major_radius_of_magnetic_axis) for the corresponding radial coordinate and [vertical_coordinate_of_x_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point) for the vertical height of the divertor X-point.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic axis lies above the equatorial plane ($Z=0$) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the point where the secondary separatrix intersects the divertor target plate in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long: The vertical coordinate of the strike point $Z_{\mathrm{SP}}$ defines the height on the divertor target where the plasma exhaust strikes during steady-state operation. This geometric quantity is extracted from equilibrium reconstruction and is critical for designing divertor geometry and controlling heat flux deposition. Typical values range from $Z \approx -1.5$ to $-2.0\,\mathrm{m}$ in ITER for lower single-null configurations, while in current machines like DIII-D or ASDEX Upgrade $Z_{\mathrm{SP}}$ falls within $\pm 0.2\,\mathrm{m}$ of the target location. The strike point is identified as the intersection of the separatrix magnetic surface with the divertor plate, and its vertical coordinate directly determines the poloidal flux expansion and thus the peak heat load. See also [major_radius_of_strike_point](name:major_radius_of_strike_point) for the radial coordinate of the same location, and [vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_separatrix](name:vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_separatrix) for the full separatrix outline.
NAMES.sign: Positive when above the midplane ($Z=0$) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_x_point
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the primary X-point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, locating the poloidal field null point of a diverted magnetic equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the primary X-point defines the height $Z_{\mathrm{X}}$ of the magnetic field null (Br = Bz = 0) on the main separatrix in a diverted tokamak configuration. This X-point location determines the vertical position of the divertor entrance and strongly influences the scrape-off layer geometry, heat flux distribution to the divertor targets, and H-mode pedestal stability. The coordinate is measured in the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with $Z$ increasing upward from the machine midplane.

Typical values for the primary X-point vertical coordinate range from $Z_{\mathrm{X}} \approx \pm 0.1$ m (lower single-null) to $\pm 0.5$ m (highly elongated shapes) below or above the midplane in medium-size tokamaks, depending on the poloidal field coil currents and plasma shaping. In ITER, the primary X-point is planned to lie approximately $\pm 0.5$ m from the midplane. The X-point position is routinely reconstructed from magnetic diagnostics via equilibrium codes (e.g., EFIT, LIUQE) and can be controlled in real time by the plasma control system.

See also [vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis) for the magnetic axis height, and [major_radius_of_x_point](name:major_radius_of_x_point) for the horizontal coordinate of the X-point.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the X-point is located above the machine midplane (i.e., $Z > 0$).

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Component of the magnetic field vector along the vertical (Z) axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ coordinate system.
NAMES.long:
The vertical magnetic field $B_Z$ is the projection $\mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{Z}$ of the total magnetic field vector onto the geometric vertical direction. In a tokamak, the poloidal field is the sum of the vertical and radial components; $B_Z$ is essential for determining the flux-surface geometry and plasma equilibrium, as the poloidal flux function $\psi$ satisfies $
abla \psi 	imes 
abla \phi \cdot \hat{Z} = R B_Z$. Typical values range from $\pm 0.1-1\,\mathrm{T}$ in the poloidal plane of medium-size tokamaks, reaching zero at the magnetic axis (where $
abla \psi = 0$) and extremal values near the X-point. The vertical field provides the restoring force that maintains plasma position; it is measured by magnetic pick-up coils or inferred from equilibrium reconstruction codes. The sign of $B_Z$ is tied to the plasma current direction and the orientation of the toroidal field. See also [radial_magnetic_field](name:radial_magnetic_field), [toroidal_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), and the full vector quantity [magnetic_field](name:magnetic_field).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z$ points in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction (upward along the machine vertical axis).

NAMES.name: ion_atomic_mass
NAMES.short: Mass of the dominant ion species element in atomic mass units (u).
NAMES.long: The ion atomic mass, typically expressed in unified atomic mass units (u), identifies the element of the primary ion species in a fusion plasma. For example, deuterium plasma has an atomic mass of approximately 2.014 u. This quantity is essential for calculating the ion thermal velocity, sound speed $c_s = \sqrt{Z_i k_B T_e / m_i}$, and the Larmor radius, where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $Z_i$ is the charge state, $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant, and $T_e$ is the electron temperature. The atomic mass is directly related to the isotope, as seen in [atomic_mass_of_isotope](name:atomic_mass_of_isotope), and is typically determined by the plasma fueling or impurity content.

NAMES.name: plasma_duration
NAMES.short: Duration of the confined plasma phase within a pulse. Starts at plasma breakdown and ends at loss of confinement, defined as the interval of measurable plasma current.
NAMES.long: Plasma duration is the total time from the moment of plasma breakdown (formation of the first closed flux surfaces with significant ionization) to the instant when the plasma loses confinement and transitions into a non-confined state. The end of the interval is determined by a rapid decrease in plasma current or stored energy below a diagnostic threshold, marking the loss of magnetic or kinetic confinement. Typical values for tokamaks range from hundreds of milliseconds to several minutes, while stellarators may sustain steady-state plasmas for many minutes. This quantity is fundamental for assessing energy confinement time, pulse reliability, and operational limits. It is derived from diagnostics such as plasma current ($I_p$) and diamagnetic stored energy ($W_\mathrm{dia}$), which provide unambiguous markers of confinement termination. The duration corresponds to the interval where $I_p(t) > I_\mathrm{thresh}$ or $W_\mathrm{dia}(t) > 0$, with thresholds set according to facility-specific criteria.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the confined phase interval is measured in forward chronological time.

NAMES.name: plasma_volume
NAMES.short: Total spatial volume enclosed by the plasma boundary surface, encompassing the confined plasma region.
NAMES.long: The total plasma volume is the 3D spatial region bounded by the last closed flux surface (LCFS) or the plasma-facing wall. It is a fundamental geometric parameter derived from equilibrium reconstruction, computed by integrating the volume element $dV = 2\pi R\, dR\, dZ$ over the poloidal cross-section within the boundary. Typical volumes range from $1\text{–}100\,\text{m}^3$ for medium-size tokamaks to $840\,\text{m}^3$ for ITER. This quantity relates to [volume_of_flux_surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface), which gives the volume enclosed by each magnetic flux surface rather than the total confined region.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the enclosed spatial region is finite and oriented in the standard right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: count_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Signed turn count of a poloidal magnetic field probe coil, encoding both the number of turns and the winding direction via sign.
NAMES.long: The signed turn count of a poloidal magnetic field probe coil combines the absolute number of wire turns with a sign that encodes the winding sense relative to the probe's orientation. This sign convention is essential for correctly reconstructing the poloidal magnetic field from the measured induced voltage via $V = -N \, d\Phi/dt$, where $N$ is the turn count (including sign) and $\Phi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux through the coil's effective area. Typical absolute turn counts range from tens to hundreds for in-vessel poloidal field probes; the sign is set during installation or calibration. The sign convention directly mirrors that of $[\text{count\_of\_toroidal\_magnetic\_field\_probe}](name:count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe)$ and serves as a key calibration parameter for equilibrium reconstruction and plasma shape control.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the winding direction follows the right-hand rule about the probe's positive normal direction as defined by the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Signed turn count of a toroidal magnetic field probe coil, encoding both the number of turns and the winding direction via sign
NAMES.long: A poloidal array of localized induction coils oriented to measure the local toroidal component of the magnetic field. Each probe records the loop integral $\oint \vec{A} \cdot d\vec{l}$ around its open area, but the measured voltage is proportional to $N \cdot \frac{d\Phi}{dt}$, where $N$ is the signed number of turns. The sign convention arises from the right-hand rule: a positive $N$ means that a positive rate of change of toroidal flux ($\Phi_\phi$) produces a positive electromotive force (voltage) in the probe. Typical turn counts range from 1 to 100 for individual probes, with larger $|N|$ increasing signal strength but also loading the circuit. A change in winding direction flips the sign, encoding the physical orientation of the coil relative to the $(R, \phi, Z)$ cylindrical basis.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the winding direction yields a positive voltage for increasing $\Phi_\phi$ in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Magnetic field component perpendicular to a reference direction, typically the local equilibrium field. Computed as the root-sum-square of contributing field components, assuming orthogonality.
NAMES.long: The perpendicular magnetic field $B_{\perp}$ is the component of the total magnetic field orthogonal to a specified reference direction, most often the local equilibrium magnetic field. It arises from stray magnetic fields and eddy currents induced in conducting structures, and is computed as $B_{\perp} = \sqrt{B_{\text{stray}}^2 + B_{\text{eddy}}^2}$, under the assumption that the stray and eddy contributions are mutually orthogonal. In plasma initiation, $B_{\perp}$ influences electron magnetization and avalanche ionization; typical acceptable values during breakdown are below 1–5 mT in large tokamaks. This quantity complements the toroidal and poloidal magnetic field components.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the component points in the direction of increasing coordinate in the right-handed $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_field_due_to_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic field response at each probe location due to a unit current in a passive conducting loop, used for electromagnetic coupling analysis.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal magnetic field coupling from passive axisymmetric conductor loops to poloidal field probe measurements quantifies the linear response of the poloidal field probes to currents induced in passive structures. This quantity forms a coupling matrix $M_{ij}$ where each element gives the poloidal field at probe $i$ per unit current in passive loop $j$, defined as $B_{\text{pol},i} = M_{ij} I_{\text{passive},j}$. The coupling matrices encode the electromagnetic mutual inductance between passive structures and poloidal field probes, typically computed from vacuum field solutions or direct inductance calculations, and are essential for real-time plasma position control and equilibrium reconstruction. This quantity differs from [mutual_inductance_of_flux_loop](name:mutual_inductance_of_flux_loop) by directly providing poloidal field values rather than flux linkages, and complements [current_of_passive_loop_due_to_induction](name:current_of_passive_loop_due_to_induction) by specifying the resulting fields.

The coupling values are geometry-dependent and typically range from $10^{-8}$ to $10^{-4}$ T/A for medium-scale tokamaks, depending on probe proximity and loop size, with larger values for probes near passive structures. See [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) and [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_separatrix](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_separatrix) for related poloidal magnetic flux quantities.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal magnetic field produced by a positive passive loop current points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle in the $(R, \phi, Z)$ reference frame.

NAMES.name: area_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Cross-sectional area of the conductor or structural element forming a passive axisymmetric loop.
NAMES.long: The cross-sectional area $A$ of a passive loop element determines the loop's electrical resistance $R = \rho L / A$ (where $\rho$ is the conductor resistivity and $L$ the element length) and thus the characteristic eddy-current decay time $\tau = L / R$. Passive loops are electrically conducting structures, such as vacuum-vessel segments or stabilizing shells, in which plasma transients induce current without an external power supply. Typical cross-sectional areas range from $10^{-4}\,\text{m}^2$ for thin-wall stabilizing shells to $10^{-1}\,\text{m}^2$ for thick vacuum-vessel sections. The area enters magnetic-field diffusion calculations and the coupling between passive structures and active coils. See the related quantities [current_of_passive_loop_due_to_induction](name:current_of_passive_loop_due_to_induction) for the induced current and [major_radius_of_passive_loop](name:major_radius_of_passive_loop) for the element's radial position.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the cross-section is oriented such that the surface normal points in the direction of the current path along the loop's contour.

NAMES.name: area_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Cross-sectional area of the conductor within a non-axisymmetric toroidal field coil, used for estimating coil resistance and thermal capacity.
NAMES.long: The cross-sectional area of the conductor within a non-axisymmetric toroidal field coil, such as an ELM control coil. This area is measured in a plane perpendicular to the local conductor direction and is used to compute the coil's electrical resistance, current density, and thermal behavior. For rectangular or circular conductors, the area is derived from the conductor's geometric dimensions (width and height or radius). The typical range is on the order of $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}^2$ for poloidal field and ELM control coils, depending on the fusion device size and coil design. The area affects the coil's inductance and heating during operation.

NAMES.name: effective_count_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Signed effective number of conductor turns in a passive loop element, encoding the winding direction via the sign.
NAMES.long:
The signed effective turn count $N_{\text{eff}}$ of a passive loop element quantifies both the number of conductor turns and the winding direction, where a positive sign indicates current flow in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above). The absolute value is the effective number of turns contributing to the magnetic coupling with active coils; the sign is required for consistent summation of induced currents in circuit models. The effective count may differ from the physical turn count when geometric or skin-effect corrections apply.

This quantity is used together with the [area_of_passive_loop](name:area_of_passive_loop) and [resistance_of_passive_loop](name:resistance_of_passive_loop) for eddy-current calculations. A related concept for active coils is described by [effective_count_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:effective_count_of_poloidal_field_coil).
NAMES.sign: Positive when current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop conductor, defining the boundary of the hollow conductor core.
NAMES.long: The inner radius $r_{\text{inner}}$ describes the radial extent of the hollow interior of a passive loop conductor's circular or annular cross-section, measured from the conductor's local axis. For a solid (non-hollow) conductor, this value is zero. Together with the [outer_radius_of_passive_loop](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop), it defines the conductor's cross-sectional area and thus its electrical conductance and inductive coupling with the plasma and active coils. The loop's electrical [resistance_of_passive_loop](name:resistance_of_passive_loop) scales with the cross-sectional area derived from these radii. Typical values for in-vessel passive stabilizing loops range from 0.01 m to 0.1 m, depending on the conductor material (copper, beryllium, or steel) and the required eddy-current decay time.
NAMES.sign: Positive for all physically valid conductors; the inner radius is geometrically positive semi-definite and always less than or equal to the outer radius.

NAMES.name: length_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Length of the parallelogram side of an oblique trapezoidal cross-section of a passive loop element, inclined at angle beta with respect to the height axis. This side defines the slanted edge of the loop's cross-sectional geometry.
NAMES.long: The length of the parallelogram side inclined at angle beta ($\beta$) with respect to the height axis in an oblique trapezoidal cross-section model of a passive loop element. This geometric parameter describes the slanted edge of the loop's cross-section, where $\beta$ is measured from the vertical (height) axis in the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The angle $\beta$ typically ranges from 0 to 90 degrees, with $\beta = 0$ corresponding to a vertical side and $\beta = 90^\circ$ to a horizontal side. This length is a key input for calculating the loop's electrical resistance and inductance, which influence eddy current dynamics during plasma disruptions. Positive orientation follows the direction of increasing $\beta$ (counter-clockwise from the height axis in the cross-sectional plane).

NAMES.name: magnetic_field_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Scalar magnetic field magnitude used as the independent variable for evaluating the relative permeability of an iron core segment from its material lookup table. This field quantifies the applied magnetic flux density B in the core segment and is paired with corresponding relative permeability values to define the nonlinear B-H curve.
NAMES.long: The magnetic field of an iron core segment provides the discrete set of magnetic flux density values $B$ (in tesla) that form the independent-variable axis of the $(B,\mu_r)$ lookup table characterizing the nonlinear magnetic response of the core material. For each entry in this array, the corresponding relative permeability $\mu_r = B/(\mu_0 H)$ is specified, enabling the core's inductance and saturation behavior to be updated in circuit models as a function of the applied field. Typical values range from $0\,\mathrm{T}$ to approximately $2\,\mathrm{T}$ for common ferromagnetic materials. The relationship between the magnetic field and the magnetic flux density is $B = \mu_0 \mu_r H$, where $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{N/A^2}$ is the vacuum permeability.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the field magnitude is measured as a positive scalar, consistent with the direction of positive flux in the core segment.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: The major radius R of the first point of a thick-line polygon element defining the cross-section of an axisymmetric ferritic component, such as a ferromagnetic insert or structural insert. This establishes the radial position from which the full geometry is defined in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long: The major radius $R$ is the cylindrical coordinate of the starting vertex of a thick-line polygon representing the cross-section of a ferritic element, such as a ferromagnetic insert or structural component. This quantity sets the radial location of the reference vertex, from which the full element geometry is built. $R$ is measured in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the distance from the machine symmetry axis. For axisymmetric ferritic components in tokamaks, typical values range from 1 to 4 meters, varying with radial placement inside the vacuum vessel. This geometric parameter is analogous to the major radius used for other device components, such as poloidal field coils and iron core segments.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the first point lies at a larger major radius than the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of the annular cross-section center of a transformer iron core segment.
NAMES.long:
The major radius $R_{\mathrm{seg}}$ defines the radial position of the center of a rectangular or trapezoidal iron core segment in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This geometric parameter sets the centroid of the segment's cross-section, which is critical for computing the magnetic circuit properties of the iron core transformer, including its reluctance, saturation, and flux linkage. The annular geometry is assumed to be axisymmetric, with the major radius locating the annulus center. Typical values range from centimeters to meters depending on the tokamak design (e.g., ~祭 1–2 m for medium-size devices).

See [height_of_iron_core_segment](name:height_of_iron_core_segment) for the vertical extent and [major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) for a similar geometric quantity applied to PF coils.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured outward from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Cylindrical major radius coordinate of the second point defining a thick-line cross-section element of a passive loop.
NAMES.long:
The major radius $R$ of the second point specifies the radial coordinate, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, of one endpoint of a straight-line segment describing the cross-section geometry of a passive loop conductor. This point pairs with the first point (stored in a sibling standard name) to define the radial and vertical extent of the loop element, which is essential for computing mutual inductances and induced eddy currents during plasma disruptions or fast transients. Passive loops are typically made of high-conductivity materials (e.g., copper) and are used for passive stabilization and vertical control in tokamaks; their major radii range from several meters in large devices like JET to smaller values in compact experiments. The quantity is obtained from engineering design drawings or equilibrium reconstruction of the passive structure.

See also [major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) for the analogous geometric coordinate applied to active poloidal field coils, and [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil) for the vertical dimension of a coil cross-section.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the point is located at a larger major radius than the machine symmetry axis ($R=0$).

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Major radius (R) coordinate defining a discrete element endpoint along the toroidal field coil conductor path in the cylindrical frame.
NAMES.long:
The major radius $R$ of a toroidal field coil conductor element endpoint specifies the radial distance from the machine symmetry axis ($Z$) to an individual turn segment within the winding pack. These $R$ coordinates, together with the corresponding $Z$ and $\phi$ values, define the full 3-dimensional geometry of each coil element in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The positions are used to construct the conductor path for circuit analysis; typical $R$ values for TF coils range from 0.5 m (inboard leg) to 9 m (outboard return leg) in large tokamaks. See also [major_radius_of_passive_loop](name:major_radius_of_passive_loop) and [major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) for analogous geometry definitions.

Measurement is direct from coil design geometry; all coordinates are defined in the machine architectural frame.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the element endpoint lies radially outward from the machine axis.

NAMES.name: maximum_magnetic_field_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: The maximum magnitude of the magnetic field on the conductor surface of a poloidal field coil, used to evaluate field-dependent current limits for the coil. This positive scalar quantifies the peak total magnetic field strength over the coil winding pack.
NAMES.long:
The maximum magnetic field on the poloidal field coil conductor surface is defined as $B_{\mathrm{max}} = \max_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{C}} |\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{total}}(\mathbf{r})|$, where $\mathcal{C}$ denotes the conductor surface of the coil winding pack and $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{total}} = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{self}} + \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{external}}$ is the vector sum of the coil's self-field and external fields from other coils, passive structures, and the plasma. The magnitude $|\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{total}}|$ is always non-negative; $B_{\mathrm{max}}$ carries no directional component.

The quantity sets the operating point for superconducting strand performance, as the critical current density $J_c(B,T)$ degrades with increasing field. Typical values range from 2 T for outer shaping coils to 12 T for the central solenoid in ITER-class devices. The field magnitude is obtained from electromagnetic equilibrium reconstruction or finite-element coil models. This value is used as the parameter for evaluating field-dependent critical current limits in superconducting magnet design, serving as the abscissa for field-dependent current tables.

Associated uncertainty depends on the reconstruction quality, coil geometry, and plasma scenario; for high-fidelity models, relative uncertainty can be a few percent. The relationship between $B_{\mathrm{max}}$ and plasma equilibrium is mediated by the poloidal flux, linking to [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis] for flux-surface geometry and [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_separatrix] for boundary context.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Outer radius of an annular cross-section ferritic element in the axisymmetric machine model.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius $R_{\mathrm{out}}$ defines the radial extent of an annular cross-section ferritic element in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Together with the inner radius, it determines the radial thickness of the annulus, which affects the magnetic circuit properties such as reluctance and saturation characteristics. This geometric parameter is used in electromagnetic modeling of axisymmetric ferritic components, including iron core segments and passive structural elements.

Typical values range from centimeters to meters depending on the ferritic component, with larger values for transformer iron cores and smaller values for ferromagnetic inserts. This quantity is geometrically independent of the plasma state. See also [inner_radius_of_passive_loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop), [outer_radius_of_passive_loop](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop), and [major_radius_of_ferritic_element](name:major_radius_of_ferritic_element) for related radial definitions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radius extends outward from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Outer radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element in the poloidal field system.
NAMES.long: The outer radius defines the outermost radial extent of the conducting path in a passive loop, such as a toroidally-continuous stabilizing shell or a saddle-loop structure. Together with the [inner_radius_of_passive_loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) it sets the radial thickness of the annulus, which directly governs the loop's cross-sectional area $A = \pi (r_\text{out}^2 - r_\text{in}^2)$ and therefore its electrical resistance $R = \rho \ell / A$ (where $\rho$ is the resistivity and $\ell$ the total conductor length). Typical outer radii range from $0.2\,\text{m}$ in compact spherical tokamaks to $2.0\,\text{m}$ in large conventional devices. The quantity is obtained from engineering design specifications and is a static geometric input for eddy-current and circuit models in plasma equilibrium and stability simulations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured outward from the machine axis, increasing in the major-radius $R$ direction.

NAMES.name: resistance_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Ohmic electrical resistance of a passive axisymmetric conducting loop, such as the vacuum vessel or stabilizing shell, that carries induced eddy currents.
NAMES.long: The resistance $R_{\text{loop}}$ of a passive axisymmetric conductor determines the resistive decay time $\tau = L / R_{\text{loop}}$ of eddy currents induced by transient magnetic fields, where $L$ is the loop inductance. This quantity governs the passive stabilization of plasma vertical displacements and the penetration of poloidal magnetic flux through conducting structures during plasma initiation and disruptions. Typical resistance values range from micro-ohms for thick copper stabilizing shells to milliohms for stainless-steel vacuum vessels in medium-size tokamaks. The resistance depends on the conductor material resistivity and cross-sectional area (see [resistivity_of_passive_loop](name:resistivity_of_passive_loop) and [area_of_passive_loop](name:area_of_passive_loop)) and is a key input to circuit models for electromagnetic analysis. For structural design studies, the ohmic power dissipation $P = I^2 R_{\text{loop}}$ in the loop is evaluated together with $[current\_of\_passive\_loop\_due\_to\_induction](name:current_of_passive_loop_due_to_induction)$.

NAMES.name: resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Ohmic electrical resistance of a toroidal field coil winding pack, defining the resistive voltage drop and power dissipation for circuit analysis.
NAMES.long: The resistance $R_{\mathrm{TF}}$ of a toroidal field coil determines the resistive voltage drop $V = I R_{\mathrm{TF}}$ and ohmic power dissipation $P = I^{2} R_{\mathrm{TF}}$ for a given coil current $I$. In superconducting TF coils, the resistance is effectively zero under steady-state operation but becomes relevant during fast current ramps or quench events when the conductor transitions to the normal state. For normal-conducting coils, typical resistance values range from micro-ohms (large copper coils) to milliohms (compact water-cooled designs). This quantity is essential for coil power supply design, quench detection modeling, and estimates of resistive heating in the coil system. See also [current of passive loop due to induction](name:current_of_passive_loop_due_to_induction) for induced-current effects in conducting structures and [resistivity of plasma facing component](name:resistivity_of_plasma_facing_component) for the material-specific property of other tokamak components.

NAMES.name: temperature_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Temperature of the poloidal field coil conductor, used to evaluate the temperature-dependent current limits for quench protection and superconducting operation.
NAMES.long: The conductor temperature of a poloidal field (PF) coil determines the critical current density of the superconducting strands and the resistive margin against quench. In operation, the temperature must remain below the current-sharing temperature $T_{cs}$ to avoid flux flow and normal zone propagation. Typical operating temperatures range from 4.5 K for Nb$_3$Sn and NbTi coils up to 80 K for high-temperature superconductors, with allowable temperature rises of 1–3 K during a plasma pulse. This quantity is applied as the lookup coordinate for the maximum coil current limit, together with the peak magnetic field described in [maximum_magnetic_field_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:maximum_magnetic_field_of_poloidal_field_coil).

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of an outline point defining the cross-sectional geometry of a transformer iron core segment.
NAMES.long: The vertical coordinate $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame specifies the height of a vertex on the polygonal outline of an iron core segment's cross-section. This coordinate, together with the corresponding [major radius](name:major_radius_of_iron_core_segment) and [height](name:height_of_iron_core_segment), defines the 2-D shape used to compute magnetic circuit properties such as reluctance and saturation. Outline points are typically stored in ordered pairs $(R, Z)$ and trace the closed boundary of the segment cross-section, providing the geometric input for axisymmetric finite-element models of the transformer core.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the point lies above the equatorial plane ($Z > 0$).

NAMES.name: area_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Poloidal cross-sectional area of a magnetic flux surface in an axisymmetric plasma, used as a radial geometric metric for flux-surface-averaged transport calculations.
NAMES.long: The area $A(\psi)$ of a given flux surface is the area of the closed toroidal surface formed by rotating the poloidal contour around the machine symmetry axis. It is a fundamental geometric quantity for evaluating flux-surface-averaged quantities such as particle and energy confinement times. In a tokamak equilibrium, $A(\psi)$ is computed from the poloidal flux function and the coordinates $(R, \phi, Z)$ of the surface. Typical values range from about $1\,\mathrm{m}^2$ near the magnetic axis to over $100\,\mathrm{m}^2$ at the plasma boundary for a medium-sized tokamak. The area generally increases monotonically from the axis to the edge, but local variations can occur due to shaping effects such as elongation or triangularity. This quantity is closely related to the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the surface.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flux surface is oriented outward from the magnetic axis, following the right-hand rule in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: bootstrap_current_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged bootstrap current density profile evaluated immediately after a sawtooth crash, representing the neoclassical current driven by the pressure gradient.
NAMES.long: The bootstrap current density $j_{\mathrm{bs}} = \langle \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{bs}} \cdot \mathbf{B} \rangle / B_0$ is the neoclassical current driven by gradients in plasma pressure and temperature in a toroidally confined plasma. It arises from the asymmetry between trapped and passing particles in a magnetic field with non-uniform strength, and is a key component of the total plasma current in tokamaks, contributing to steady-state operation. After a sawtooth crash, the central pressure gradient is reduced, leading to a characteristic flattening of the bootstrap current profile inside the inversion radius. This quantity is routinely computed in transport simulations and equilibrium reconstructions, typically ranging from $0.1 \, \mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$ in the far edge to several $\mathrm{kA\,m^{-2}}$ in the core of high-performance H-mode plasmas. It is related to the total parallel current density through $j_{\parallel} = j_{\mathrm{ohmic}} + j_{\mathrm{bs}} + j_{\mathrm{CD}}$, where $j_{\mathrm{CD}}$ is the current driven by external heating and current drive systems. See also [parallel_current_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash](name:parallel_current_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash) and [ohmic_current_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash](name:ohmic_current_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the bootstrap current density flows in the direction of the total plasma current (increasing toroidal angle $\phi$).

NAMES.name: current_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash_due_to_bootstrap
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged neoclassical bootstrap current density profile evaluated immediately after a sawtooth crash.
NAMES.long: The bootstrap current density $j_{\rm bs} = \langle \mathbf{J}_{\rm bs} \cdot \mathbf{B} \rangle / B_0$ is a neoclassical current driven by the radial pressure gradient in a toroidal plasma, where $\mathbf{J}_{\rm bs}$ is the bootstrap current density vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, $B_0$ is the toroidal magnetic field on axis, and $\langle \cdot \rangle$ denotes the flux-surface average. This quantity represents $j_{\rm bs}$ evaluated on the flux-surface grid immediately following a sawtooth crash, a period when the core pressure gradient is strongly reduced by the internal reconnection event)Skip—typically $j_{\rm bs}$ is small near the axis and rises with the pressure gradient toward the pedestal region. After the crash, the bootstrap current density profile reshapes as the pressure gradient rebuilds, and it is closely linked to the total parallel current density $[\text{parallel\_current\_density\_at\_post\_sawtooth\_crash}]$ and the ohmic current density $[\text{ohmic\_current\_density\_at\_post\_sawtooth\_crash}]$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the bootstrap current flows in the same direction as the total toroidal plasma current (counter-clockwise when viewed from above).

NAMES.name: diffusion_coefficient_at_neoclassical_tearing_mode_center
NAMES.short: Enhanced diffusion coefficient added to the transport equations to model the increased radial transport induced by a magnetic island at the center of a neoclassical tearing mode.
NAMES.long:
The diffusion coefficient $D_{\mathrm{NTM}}$ represents the anomalous cross-field transport enhancement caused by a magnetic island in a neoclassical tearing mode (NTM). It appears in the 1-D radial diffusion equation for the electron density, $n_e$,

\[
\frac{\partial n_e}{\partial t} = \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \left( r D_{\mathrm{total}} \frac{\partial n_e}{\partial r} \right),
\]

where $D_{\mathrm{total}} = D_{\mathrm{background}} + D_{\mathrm{NTM}}$, with $D_{\mathrm{background}}$ the neoclassical or turbulent diffusion in the absence of the mode. $D_{\mathrm{NTM}}$ is localized around the island's O-point, typically following a Gaussian or top-hat radial profile with a full width proportional to the island width, $w_{\mathrm{island}}$. Typical values range from $10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}$ in the outer plasma to $10^{1}\,\mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}$ near the pedestal, depending on local island width and collisionality. The coefficient is derived from the modified Rutherford equation or from experimental fits to the electron density profile flattening observed by ECE or reflectometry.

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash
NAMES.short: Total electron number density in the plasma core measured immediately after a sawtooth crash, including both thermal and non-thermal electrons.
NAMES.long:
This quantity represents the total electron number density at the plasma core, evaluated within a few microseconds after a sawtooth crash. Sawtooth crashes, commonly observed in tokamak plasmas, are MHD instability events that periodically flatten the core profiles. During the crash, core particles and energy are redistributed outward. The post-crash electron density is determined from the flattening of the density profile after the sawtooth inversion radius, providing information on particle transport and confinement in the plasma core. The density includes all electron populations (thermal and non-thermal) and is referenced from the sawteeth data entry.

Typical values in fusion-grade devices range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, depending on plasma conditions such as density, current, and heating methods. The measurement relies on core diagnostics like Thomson scattering or interferometry, sampled at times immediately after sawtooth-induced crashes. The post-crash density is usually lower than the pre-crash peak due to the expulsion of particles from the core region.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the measured electron density is real and non-negative (physical density).

NAMES.name: fast_electron_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash
NAMES.short: Number density of suprathermal electrons in the plasma core immediately following a sawtooth crash, comprising only the non-thermal population.
NAMES.long: The fast electron number density $n_{\mathrm{e,fast}}$ quantifies the density of supra-thermal (non-Maxwellian) electrons generated by mechanisms such as lower-hybrid or electron-cyclotron current drive, avalanche processes, or runaway acceleration. In the post-sawtooth-crash phase, the reconnection event redistributes the current density and flattens the core profiles, leading to a transient evolution of $n_{\mathrm{e,fast}}$ that is critical for modeling the sawtooth cycle and the subsequent current profile relaxation. Typical values in the core of a sawtoothing tokamak range from $10^{17}$ to $10^{19}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$, depending on the auxiliary heating power and the efficiency of fast-electron generation. This quantity is closely related to the total electron density $[\text{electron\_density\_at\_post\_sawtooth\_crash}](name:electron_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash)$ and to the anisotropic pressure carried by the fast population $[\text{parallel\_fast\_electron\_pressure\_at\_post\_sawtooth\_crash}](name:parallel_fast_electron_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash)$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the suprathermal electron density is greater than zero (physical number density is a non-negative scalar).

NAMES.name: frequency_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode
NAMES.short: Rotation frequency of the magnetic island associated with a neoclassical tearing mode, measured in the laboratory frame.
NAMES.long: The frequency $f_{\mathrm{NTM}}$ of a neoclassical tearing mode (NTM) quantifies the rotation rate of the helical magnetic island in the laboratory frame. This rotation is driven primarily by the bulk plasma flow, including toroidal rotation and the $E \times B$ drift, and is Doppler shifted from the mode eigenfrequency in the plasma rest frame. Typical NTM frequencies range from a few kHz to tens of kHz in tokamaks, depending on the plasma toroidal rotation velocity and the radial location of the island. In the rotating frame of the island, the tearing mode is marginally unstable, governed by the modified Rutherford equation. The frequency is routinely inferred from magnetic pickup coils (Mirnov coils) or from electron cyclotron emission (ECE) radiometry, which modulate as the island rotates past fixed diagnostic lines of sight. The quantity is closely related to the $[\text{phase}](name:phase)$ evolution of the detected signal and to the $[\text{toroidal mode number}](name:toroidal_mode_number_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode)$ of the instability.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the mode rotates in the direction of the ion diamagnetic drift (counter-clockwise viewed from above).

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_halo_boundary
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of the outboard boundary between the confined plasma and the halo region during a disruption.
NAMES.long: The major radius of the halo boundary defines the radial coordinate $R_{\mathrm{halo}}$ of the interface separating the confined plasma from the halo region, where open field lines carry large halo currents during the thermal and current quench phases of a disruption. This interface is typically identified as the outboard separatrix of the last closed flux surface at the time of the peak halo current, and its radial position influences both the path length and the inductance of the halo current circuit. Measured from equilibrium reconstructions that resolve the evolving magnetic geometry during the disruption; typical $R_{\mathrm{halo}}$ values span 1.5–3.0 m in medium-size tokamaks, moving outward as the plasma displaces vertically and contracts. Related geometric parameters include the vertical coordinate of the same boundary and the major radius of the strike point [major_radius_of_strike_point](name:major_radius_of_strike_point) on the divertor targets, together with the major radius of the first wall [major_radius_of_wall](name:major_radius_of_wall) which bounds the halo region at the outer side.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured outward from the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_wall
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of a user-defined point on the tokamak wall, used in disruption halo current path analysis.
NAMES.long:
The major radius $R_{\text{wall}}$ of an active wall point is the $R$ coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame of a specific point on the tokamak wall. This point is used as a boundary for halo current path analysis during disruptions, where the plasma current continues to flow through the scrape-off layer and into the wall. The active wall point is typically one of a set of discrete points defining the wall contour, and its major radius is extracted for geometric calculations in disruption simulations. Typical $R$ values range from 0.5 to 5 m, depending on the tokamak's inner and outer wall radii. Cross-reference with `[major_radius_of_current_center](name:major_radius_of_current_center)` for the plasma current centroid and `[poloidal_current_over_halo_region](name:poloidal_current_over_halo_region)` for the associated current.

Major radius coordinate of a user-defined point on the tokamak wall, used in disruption halo current path analysis.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R$ increases radially outward from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_inversion_radius
NAMES.short: Value of the normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the sawtooth inversion radius, the surface where the q profile equals unity and the reconnection event originates.
NAMES.long: The normalized toroidal flux coordinate $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} = \sqrt{\Phi/\Phi_{\mathrm{sep}}}$ evaluated at the sawtooth inversion radius $r_{\mathrm{inv}}$. This radial position marks the location where the safety factor $q = 1$ in a tokamak plasma and defines the boundary between the sawtooth mixing region (inside) and the unaffected outer plasma. The inversion radius is identified from soft-X-ray or electron-cyclotron emission (ECE) measurements as the radius where the sawtooth perturbation changes sign. In typical H-mode plasmas, $r_{\mathrm{inv}}$ lies at $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}} \approx 0.3\!-\!0.5$, with the exact value depending on plasma current and internal inductance. See also [normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_pedestal](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_pedestal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ increases radially outward from the magnetic axis to the separatrix.

NAMES.name: ohmic_current_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash
NAMES.short: Current density driven by the inductive toroidal electric field via Ohm's law, evaluated as radial profiles immediately after a sawtooth crash.
NAMES.long: The ohmic current density is the component of the current density driven by the inductive toroidal electric field generated during the current ramp-up or decay. It is defined via Ohm's law as $j_\mathrm{ohmic} = \sigma E_\phi$, where $\sigma$ is the parallel electrical conductivity and $E_\phi$ is the toroidal electric field. After a sawtooth crash, the central current density is partially flattened, and this quantity captures the subsequent re-distribution of the ohmic current.
