Typical values range from 0.1 to 10 MA/m² depending on the plasma conditions. The radial profile is evaluated on a flux-surface grid.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: ohmic_energy_over_halo_region
NAMES.short: Cumulative ohmic dissipation energy deposited in the halo region during a disruption.
NAMES.long: The ohmic energy in the halo region is the time integral of the ohmic heating power dissipated resistively by the poloidal or toroidal halo current flowing through the halo plasma during a disruption. This energy contributes to the total disruption energy balance and is a key input for assessing heat loads on plasma-facing components. The total ohmic energy is related to the ohmic power via $E_{\text{ohm,halo}} = \int P_{\text{ohm,halo}} \, dt$, where $P_{\text{ohm,halo}}$ is the instantaneous ohmic power. Typical values range from tens of kilojoules in small tokamaks to tens of megajoules in large devices like ITER. This quantity is estimated from resistive dissipation models using measured halo currents and estimated halo resistivity. See also [ohmic_power_over_halo_region_due_to_ohmic_dissipation](name:ohmic_power_over_halo_region_due_to_ohmic_dissipation) and the total [ohmic_energy](name:ohmic_energy) over the disruption.

NAMES.name: parallel_current_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged projection of the plasma current density vector onto the local magnetic field direction, evaluated immediately after a sawtooth crash.
NAMES.long: The parallel current density $j_\parallel = \langle \mathbf{j} \cdot \mathbf{B} \rangle / B_0$ is the flux-surface-averaged component of the electric current density along the equilibrium magnetic field, where $\langle \cdot \rangle$ denotes the flux-surface average, $\mathbf{j}$ is the current density vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field vector, and $B_0$ is the on-axis vacuum toroidal field. This quantity drives the local safety-factor evolution and determines the post-crash magnetic equilibrium. It is evaluated immediately after a sawtooth crash, during which magnetic reconnection flattens the core current profile, typically reducing the central current density. The post-crash parallel current density is reconstructed from motional Stark effect measurements or equilibrium codes such as EFIT and LIUQE. In tokamaks, the central value is on the order of 1–10 MA/m², depending on plasma current and size. This quantity complements the ohmic current density component at the same time slice.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flux-surface-averaged current flows along the direction of the equilibrium magnetic field, i.e., in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction for a standard tokamak with positive toroidal field.

NAMES.name: parallel_electric_field_at_post_sawtooth_crash
NAMES.short: Projection of the electric field vector onto the local magnetic field direction, evaluated immediately after a sawtooth crash.
NAMES.long: The parallel electric field $E_\parallel$ is given by $E_\parallel = (\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{B}) / |\mathbf{B}|$, where $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric field vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic field vector, and $|\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnitude of the local magnetic field. Evaluated at a time point immediately after a sawtooth crash, this quantity is typically derived from the loop voltage measurement and the local magnetic geometry. Typical values during the post-crash phase range from 0.01 to 0.1 V/m in present-day tokamaks. The local magnetic field is the total magnetic field at the measurement location, not a vacuum or reference field.

NAMES.name: parallel_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash
NAMES.short: Parallel component of the total plasma pressure tensor, summing all thermal and suprathermal species, evaluated after a sawtooth crash.
NAMES.long:
The parallel pressure $p_\parallel$ is the component of the anisotropic pressure tensor along the local magnetic field direction. It is computed as the sum of the parallel pressures of all thermal and suprathermal electron and ion species, incorporating contributions from both the Maxwellian and fast-particle populations. In the immediate aftermath of a sawtooth crash, the pressure anisotropy $p_\parallel - p_\perp$ reveals the interplay between fast-particle redistribution and MHD relaxation, with typical core values in the range 10–100 kPa for ITER-relevant scenarios. The quantity is reconstructed by combining equilibrium solvers with kinetic-profile measurements from Thomson scattering and charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy. Together with [perpendicular_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash](name:perpendicular_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash) it forms the full pressure tensor, while [thermal_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash](name:thermal_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash) gives the isotropic thermal component. 

This scalar quantity is always positive for a confined plasma; its sign convention references the direction of the resulting diamagnetic current density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plasma pressure acts to expand the flux surface outward.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash
NAMES.short: Perpendicular component of the total plasma pressure tensor, summed over all species, evaluated immediately after a sawtooth crash.
NAMES.long: The perpendicular pressure $p_\perp$ is the component of the anisotropic pressure tensor perpendicular to the local magnetic field direction, defined as $p_\perp = p_{\rm total} + (B^2/\mu_0)\Delta$ for a bi-Maxwellian distribution, where $\Delta$ measures the pressure anisotropy. This quantity sums the perpendicular contributions from thermal electrons, thermal ions, and suprathermal (fast) particle populations. Immediately after a sawtooth crash, the perpendicular pressure profile is flattened inside the mixing radius due to the magnetic reconnection event, with typical values ranging from tens of kPa on axis to a few kPa near the inversion radius. The perpendicular pressure is routinely inferred from equilibrium reconstruction constrained by magnetic and kinetic profile diagnostics, and together with the parallel pressure [parallel_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash](name:parallel_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash) it quantifies the degree of pressure anisotropy in the post-crash state.
NAMES.sign: Positive for compressive stress, representing an outward force, by the standard pressure sign convention.

NAMES.name: poloidal_mode_number_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode
NAMES.short: Poloidal mode number (m) characterizing the helicity of the magnetic island associated with a neoclassical tearing mode.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal mode number $m$ is the integer Fourier harmonic index describing how many toroidal circuits a magnetic field line makes per single poloidal transit of the magnetic island. For a neoclassical tearing mode, $m$ and the toroidal mode number $n$ $(n = m/q)$ together specify the resonant rational surface where $q = m/n$. Typical NTM mode numbers in tokamaks range from $m = 2$ to $m = 5$, with $m/n = 2/1$, $3/2$, and $4/3$ being commonly observed. The mode number is inferred from Mirnov coil arrays or ECE radiometry through toroidal and poloidal array correlation analysis.

See also [toroidal_mode_number_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode](name:toroidal_mode_number_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode) for the companion toroidal harmonic, and [frequency_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode](name:frequency_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode) for the island rotation frequency at the corresponding resonant surface.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $m$ increases with the poloidal harmonic index, with no dependence on the toroidal sign convention.

NAMES.name: radiated_power_over_halo_region_due_to_impurity_radiation
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic power radiated by electron collisions with impurity ions within the halo region during a disruption.
NAMES.long: This quantity represents the power lost through line radiation and bremsstrahlung as thermal electrons interact with impurity species (e.g., argon, neon, nitrogen) in the halo plasma region during a disruption event. The radiated power $P_{\rm rad,halo}^{\rm imp}$ is a critical term in the disruption power balance, helping to dissipate the plasma thermal energy and mitigate heat loads on plasma-facing components. Typical values in ITER-scale disruptions range from tens to hundreds of megawatts, depending on the injected impurity concentration and the halo region volume. The radiated power is related to the electron density $n_e$, the impurity density $n_{\rm imp}$, and the electron temperature $T_e$ through the radiation function $L(T_e)$: $P_{\rm rad,halo}^{\rm imp} = \int_{\rm halo} n_e n_{\rm imp} L(T_e) \, dV$. This quantity is a subset of the total radiated power during a disruption, complementing the core-plasma radiated power from [radiated_power_due_to_impurity_radiation](name:radiated_power_due_to_impurity_radiation) and the ohmic dissipation in [ohmic_power_over_halo_region_due_to_ohmic_dissipation](name:ohmic_power_over_halo_region_due_to_ohmic_dissipation). The power balance is sign-invariant (always non-negative).

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_critical_momentum_due_to_hot_tail
NAMES.short: Critical momentum threshold for hot-tail runaway electron generation, given by the momentum above which collisional drag is overcome by the electric field during the thermal quench.
NAMES.long: The critical momentum for the hot-tail runaway electron generation mechanism defines the threshold momentum $p_{\mathrm{crit}}^{\mathrm{HT}}$ above which a suprathermal electron from the high-energy tail of the post-thermal-quench distribution can overcome collisional drag and become a runaway electron. The hot-tail mechanism is the dominant runaway seed source during a tokamak disruption when the electron temperature drops rapidly, leaving a suprathermal population that can be accelerated by the induced toroidal electric field. The critical momentum scales inversely with the cold-electron density and the electric field strength during the current quench; typical values in ITER-relevant disruption scenarios range from $0.1\,m_e c$ to $1.0\,m_e c$, corresponding to kinetic energies of $5$–$500$ keV. This quantity is closely related to the [critical electric field](name:critical_electric_field), which defines the Dreicer threshold for bulk-electron runaway. The hot-tail seed population is distinct from the avalanche multiplication process and is a critical input to disruption mitigation strategies.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_density
NAMES.short: Number density of the runaway electron population, representing electrons that have undergone continuous acceleration to relativistic energies in the presence of a strong electric field.
NAMES.long:
The runaway electron density $n_{\mathrm{RE}}$ quantifies the number of relativistic electrons per unit volume that are no longer confined by collisions and are continuously accelerated by the toroidal electric field. In tokamak disruptions, runaway electron densities can reach $10^{18}$–$10^{20}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, with corresponding current densities up to several MA/m$^2$. The density is obtained from fluid models of the runaway dynamics (e.g., solving the kinetic equation for the runaway distribution) or from diagnostic measurements such as synchrotron radiation imaging and hard X-ray cameras. The radial profile of $n_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is critical for assessing local heat loads and for estimating the total runaway current during disruptions. This quantity is related to the density of thermal electrons via $n_e = n_{\mathrm{thermal}} + n_{\mathrm{RE}}$ and to the runaway current through $j_{\mathrm{RE}} = e n_{\mathrm{RE}} c$ for fully relativistic electrons.

The density is closely linked to [runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer) which describes the primary generation mechanism, and is distinguished from the volume-averaged density [volume_averaged_runaway_electron_density](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_density) by its local, radial-profile nature.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the number of runaway electrons per unit volume is measured.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_kinetic_energy
NAMES.short: Total relativistic kinetic energy stored in the runaway electron population, summed over all electrons in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The total runaway electron kinetic energy $E_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the sum over all runaway electrons of the single-electron relativistic kinetic energy:

\[
E_{\mathrm{RE}} = \sum_i (\gamma_i - 1) m_e c^2
\]

where $\gamma_i = 1/\sqrt{1 - v_i^2/c^2}$ is the Lorentz factor of the $i$-th electron. For a typical runaway electron with energy 10–30 MeV, the Lorentz factor ranges from 20 to 60. In large tokamaks such as ITER, the total stored energy can reach tens of megajoules, implying a population of $\sim 10^{14}$–$10^{15}$ electrons.

This quantity is a global measure of the free energy available for a potential disruption event, directly relevant to assessing the threat of runaway-electron-driven damage.

Typical value range: for present tokamaks, $E_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is at most a few megajoules; for ITER scenarios with significant runaway generation, it can exceed 20 MJ.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the total kinetic energy of the runaway electron population increases relative to a reference state.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_fast_ion
NAMES.short: Volumetric rate of runaway electron generation via knock-on collisions between fast ions and thermal electrons, evaluated at fixed normalized radial coordinate.
NAMES.long: This source rate quantifies the fast-ion knock-on mechanism, where a high-energy ion collides with a thermal electron. The electron gains sufficient momentum to overcome the critical velocity for runaway acceleration dash; the process transforms kinetic energy from the fast-ion population into seed runaway electrons. The rate $S_{\mathrm{RE}}^{\mathrm{fast\,ion}}$ is computed as an integral over the fast-ion velocity distribution: $S_{\mathrm{RE}}^{\mathrm{fast\,ion}} = n_{\mathrm{fast}} \int \sigma_{\mathrm{knock\,on}}(v_{\mathrm{fast}}, v_{\mathrm{e}})\, f_{\mathrm{fast}}(v_{\mathrm{fast}})\, d^3 v_{\mathrm{fast}}$, where $n_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast-ion density, $\sigma_{\mathrm{knock\,on}}$ is the knock-on cross-section (typically modeled using the Møller or Bhabha scattering formulas), and $f_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the normalized fast-ion velocity distribution. In a deuterium-tritium plasma, fusion-born alpha particles with energy $E_{\alpha} = 3.5\,\mathrm{MeV}$ are a dominant fast-ion source, producing seed runaway electrons with typical energies in the MeV range. The rate is computed as a radial profile (at fixed normalized radial coordinate, e.g., $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$) from the fast-ion distribution obtained by neutral beam injection, ion cyclotron resonance heating, or fusion reactions. Typical values near the plasma core can reach $10^{17}\,{\mathrm{m}}^{-3}\,{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$ in high-power discharges. This rate is a primary mechanism for seed runaway electron generation and is linked to the Dreicer mechanism; when the knock-on seed exceeds the Dreicer rate, the runaway population can be dominated by avalanche amplification.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net rate produces runaway electrons from the fast-ion knock-on process.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_fusion
NAMES.short: Volumetric generation rate of runaway electrons resulting from the tritium beta decay reaction in a deuterium-tritium plasma.
NAMES.long: This quantity represents the source rate of runaway electrons produced by the tritium beta decay process. In a D-T fusion plasma, tritium nuclei undergo beta decay with a half-life of 12.32 years, emitting an electron and an antineutrino: $\mathrm{T} \rightarrow {}^3\mathrm{He} + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e$. The emitted beta electron has a continuous energy spectrum up to 18.6 keV, and a fraction of these electrons can become runaway if the local electric field exceeds the critical threshold $E_c$. The source rate scales with the tritium density $n_{\mathrm{T}}$ as $S_{\mathrm{RE}}^{\beta} = n_{\mathrm{T}} / \tau_{\beta}$, where $\tau_{\beta}$ is the tritium beta decay time constant. Typical values in a burning D-T plasma with $n_{\mathrm{T}} \sim 10^{20} \, \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ are on the order of $10^{5} \, \mathrm{m}^{-3}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, much smaller than primary Dreicer or hot-tail sources. This beta-decay source is most relevant for long-pulse burning plasmas where tritium inventory accumulates, such as ITER. Measurements of the associated tritium density and decay products are used to constrain this source term. See also [runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer) and [runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail) for other generation mechanisms.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail
NAMES.short: Volumetric generation rate of runaway electrons due to the hot-tail mechanism, where a rapidly cooling Maxwellian tail traps suprathermal electrons during a thermal quench.
NAMES.long: The hot-tail mechanism is the dominant primary generation process for runaway electrons during a plasma disruption. When the bulk electron temperature collapses on a timescale shorter than the collisional slowing-down time of electrons at a few times the thermal velocity, the high-energy tail of the velocity distribution function is left behind as a suprathermal population that can then be accelerated to runaway energies by the induced electric field. The hot-tail source rate $S_{\mathrm{HT}}$ enters the runaway electron density evolution equation as $\partial n_{\mathrm{RE}}/\partial t = S_{\mathrm{Dreicer}} + S_{\mathrm{HT}} + S_{\mathrm{avalanche}}$, where each term accounts for a distinct generation mechanism. This rate depends strongly on the initial electron temperature, the quench time, and the post-quench plasma parameters. The related total generation rate is [runaway_electron_source_rate](name:runaway_electron_source_rate), which sums all mechanisms, and the Dreicer-driven rate is [runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer). Typical hot-tail source rates can reach $10^{20}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ during the current quench in an ITER-scale disruption, far exceeding the Dreicer rate for fast thermal quenches.

NAMES.name: thermal_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash
NAMES.short: Scalar thermal pressure of the Maxwellian electron population, evaluated in the plasma core immediately after a sawtooth crash.
NAMES.long: The thermal electron pressure $p_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ quantifies the kinetic pressure contributed by the thermal (Maxwellian) electron population. In the post-sawtooth-crash state, the central pressure profile is flattened inside the inversion radius due to the redistribution of plasma energy. Typical core values in a tokamak range from a few tens of kilopascals (e.g., 10–100 kPa in medium-size devices like JET or DIII-D) up to several hundred kPa in ITER-like plasmas. This quantity is reconstructed from kinetic profile diagnostics (Thomson scattering, electron cyclotron emission) and is related to the electron density and temperature via $p_{e,\mathrm{th}} = n_e k_B T_e$ for a Maxwellian distribution. See also the total retained pressure in [total_ion_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash](name:total_ion_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash) and the fast-electron contribution in [parallel_fast_electron_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash](name:parallel_fast_electron_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the kinetic pressure is compressive, representing a net outward force against the confining magnetic field.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_phase
NAMES.short: Instantaneous angular frequency of a neoclassical tearing mode, defined as the rate of change of its measured phase in the laboratory reference frame.
NAMES.long: The time derivative of the phase, $d\phi/dt$, represents the instantaneous angular frequency of a neoclassical tearing mode (NTM). This frequency, often denoted as $f = d\phi/(2\pi dt)$ in hertz, measures how fast the mode rotates in the laboratory frame. For a mode with toroidal mode number $n$, the angular frequency is related to the plasma toroidal rotation frequency $\Omega = d\phi_{\text{plasma}}/dt$ via the dispersion relation $d\phi/dt = n\Omega$ (i.e., $f = n\Omega/2\pi$), where $\Omega$ is the angular frequency of the rotating plasma. Typical values range from a few kilohertz to tens of kilohertz in tokamaks, depending on the plasma rotation and the mode's toroidal mode number. This quantity is derived from magnetic pickup coils, electron cyclotron emission, or soft X-ray diagnostics, which measure the mode's phase evolution.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the phase increases in time, corresponding to mode rotation in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the total current density on the poloidal cross-section, evaluated immediately after a sawtooth crash.
NAMES.long: The toroidal current density $j_\phi = \langle J_\phi / R \rangle / \langle 1/R \rangle$ is the flux-surface-averaged projection of the plasma current density vector onto the geometric toroidal direction $\hat{\phi}$. Immediately after a sawtooth crash, the current density profile is flattened inside the inversion radius as the central $q$ profile resets above unity, redistributing the core current toward the periphery. This quantity is commonly derived from equilibrium reconstructions constrained by magnetic diagnostics, Motional Stark Effect measurements, or polarimetry. Typical core values range from 0.1 to 1 MA/m$^2$ and depend on the plasma current, safety factor profile, and the magnitude of the sawtooth crash. The post-crash current density is closely related to the parallel current density [name:parallel_current_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash] and the ohmic component [name:ohmic_current_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash] that re-establishes the central current after the event.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $j_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above).

NAMES.name: toroidal_mode_number_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode
NAMES.short: Integer toroidal periodicity (n) of the magnetic island chain associated with a neoclassical tearing mode.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal mode number $n$ quantifies the number of complete toroidal transits of the magnetic island chain as the safety factor $q$ varies across a rational surface, where $q = m/n$. It is determined from Mirnov coil arrays or ECE imaging by analyzing the toroidal phase relationship of the magnetic perturbation. In typical tokamak plasmas, NTM toroidal mode numbers range from $n=1$ (core modes) to $n=3$ or higher (edge modes). The poloidal counterpart is the [poloidal mode number of neoclassical tearing mode](name:poloidal_mode_number_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode) $m$, and together they define the island helicity and rational surface location. The [frequency of neoclassical tearing mode](name:frequency_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode) and [toroidal flux radius of neoclassical tearing mode](name:toroidal_flux_radius_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode) further characterize the island dynamics.

$n$ is sign-invariant for a given tearing parity — only the absolute value determines the island helicity; the sign convention is preserved for consistency with Fourier decomposition of the perturbed magnetic field.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the field perturbation rotates in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_total_plasma_current_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged toroidal current density of the total plasma immediately after a sawtooth crash.
NAMES.long: The toroidal current density $j_{\phi}^{\text{total}}$ represents the flux-surface average of the total toroidal current density, defined as $j_{\phi}^{\text{total}} = \langle J_{\phi} / R \rangle / \langle 1 / R \rangle$, where $J_{\phi}$ is the local toroidal current density and $R$ is the major radius. This quantity is evaluated immediately after a sawtooth crash, capturing the redistribution of current in the core following the internal reconnection event. Typical post-crash values in the core of a tokamak are in the range 0.1–1.0 MA·m$^{-2}$, depending on plasma current and density profiles, and the profile is commonly inferred from equilibrium reconstruction using magnetic measurements combined with motional Stark effect (MSE) or polarimetry constraints. The total current density is the sum of ohmic, bootstrap, and non-inductive contributions, and it is distinguished from individual component contributions such as [ohmic_current_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash](name:ohmic_current_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash) and [bootstrap_current_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash](name:bootstrap_current_density_at_post_sawtooth_crash).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above).

NAMES.name: vertical_current_density
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) component of the total current density vector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) coordinate system.
NAMES.long: The vertical current density $j_Z = \mathbf{j} \cdot \hat{Z}$ is the projection of the total current density vector onto the vertical axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ is the height above the tokamak midplane. It represents the net charge flow per unit area in the vertical direction and is a fundamental component of the vector [current_density](name:current_density). This quantity is routinely computed in equilibrium reconstruction and MHD stability analysis from magnetic measurements or inferred from diagnostic data; in axisymmetric configurations, the vertical component is related to the poloidal current stream function. Typical values in the edge region of diverted tokamak plasmas range from 0.1 to 10 kA·m$^{-2}$, depending on the plasma regime and the presence of halo currents during disruptions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$ (upward).

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_runaway_electron_current_density
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged parallel current density of the runaway electron population.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged runaway electron current density quantifies the total electric current carried by fast electrons undergoing relativistic runaway in a plasma, averaged over the entire plasma volume. It is defined as $j_{\text{RE, vol}} = \frac{1}{V}\int_V\langle \mathbf{j}_{\text{RE}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}} \rangle\,dV$, where $\langle \mathbf{j}_{\text{RE}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}} \rangle$ is the flux-surface-averaged parallel runaway current density and $V$ is the total plasma volume. This global measure represents the net contribution of runaway electrons to the toroidal current and is critical for assessing disruption mitigation requirements, as beam currents can reach several mega-amperes in ITER-class devices. The value is typically derived by integrating radial profiles from kinetic simulations or disruption reconstructions, linking to [runaway_electron_kinetic_energy](name:runaway_electron_kinetic_energy) and [critical_electric_field](name:critical_electric_field).

Typical values during tokamak disruptions range from $10^5$ to $10^7$ A/m$^2$ depending on avalanche multiplication and electric field strength.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the runaway electron parallel current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above).

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged volumetric generation rate of runaway electrons due to the hot-tail mechanism, representing the primary seed source during a thermal quench.
NAMES.long: The hot-tail mechanism generates runaway electrons when the electron temperature drops rapidly during a thermal quench, leaving a high-energy tail of the Maxwellian distribution that outruns the rising collisional drag. This quantity is the volume-averaged production rate $\langle d n_{\mathrm{RE}} / dt \rangle = (1/V) \int_V S_{\mathrm{hot\,tail}}(r) \, dV$, where $S_{\mathrm{hot\,tail}}$ is the local hot-tail source rate in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The hot-tail seed is typically strongest in the early disruption phase before secondary amplification by the avalanche mechanism becomes dominant; characteristic values for ITER-scale disruptions range from $10^{18}$ to $10^{21}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, depending on the quench rate and initial temperature. This quantity is a volume-averaged version of [runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail) and complements the total production rate given by [volume_averaged_runaway_electron_source_rate](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_source_rate). Measurement relies on hard X-ray and gamma-ray diagnostics during disruptions combined with transport simulations.

NAMES.name: width_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode
NAMES.short: Full radial width of the magnetic island associated with a neoclassical tearing mode (NTM).
NAMES.long:
The full island width $W$ of a neoclassical tearing mode is the radial extent of the magnetic island chain, measured from the innermost to the outermost separatrix of the O-point. A magnetic island causes a flattening of the local pressure and temperature profiles, degrading plasma confinement. The saturated island width for a neoclassical tearing mode is determined by a balance of the perturbed bootstrap current, polarization current, and stabilizing effects such as flow shear. The island width is measured using diagnostic techniques like electron cyclotron emission (ECE) imaging or soft X-ray tomography; typical islands in medium-size tokamaks range from a few centimeters to tens of centimeters in radial width. This quantity is closely related to $[\text{toroidal flux radius at the NTM}](name:toroidal_flux_radius_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode)$ and the $[\text{island rotation frequency}](name:frequency_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode)$.

In plasmas where the island is seeded by sawtooth events or other MHD activity, the $[\text{onset island width}](name:width_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode_onset)$ provides the initial condition for nonlinear evolution. The poloidal mode number $m$ is captured by $[\text{poloidal mode number of the NTM}](name:poloidal_mode_number_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode)$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic island is present and has a finite radial extent, zero when no island exists.

NAMES.name: area_of_langmuir_probe
NAMES.short: Physical surface area of a Langmuir probe collector pin that is exposed to the plasma and collects charged particles.
NAMES.long: The exposed surface area $A_{\rm probe}$ of a Langmuir probe pin determines the ion and electron current collected by the probe.  The ion saturation current $I_{\rm sat} = e n_e c_s A_{\rm probe}$ depends linearly on this area, where $e$ is the elementary charge, $n_e$ is the electron density, and $c_s$ is the ion sound speed.  The effective collection area may differ from the geometric area due to sheath expansion, shadowing by nearby structures, or the probe orientation relative to the magnetic field.  Typical probe areas in tokamak edge studies range from $10^{-6}\,{\rm m}^2$ (fine pins) to $10^{-4}\,{\rm m}^2$ (larger collectors).  This quantity is the geometric area exposed to the plasma; the companion `[electron_density](name:electron_density)` and `[parallel_heat_flux](name:parallel_heat_flux)` are inferred from the measured currents using this area.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the surface normal points in the direction of increasing coordinate for that surface element.

NAMES.name: area_of_reciprocating_probe
NAMES.short: Physical surface area of a reciprocating Langmuir probe collector that is exposed to the plasma and collects charged particles.
NAMES.long:
The surface area of a reciprocating probe collector determines the collected ion saturation current $I_{\rm sat} = e n_e c_s A_{\rm eff}$ for a given electron density $n_e$ and sound speed $c_s$, where $e$ is the elementary charge. This area is typically treated as constant during a probe plunge, assuming negligible dependence on the magnetic field line angle. The effective collecting area may differ from the geometric surface area due to sheath expansion, shadowing, or the probe's orientation relative to the magnetic field. Typical reciprocating probe collector areas range from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-4}$ m$^2$ in tokamak scrape-off layer measurements. See also [area_of_langmuir_probe](name:area_of_langmuir_probe) for fixed Langmuir probes, and [electron_density](name:electron_density) for the quantity derived using this area.

The effective collecting area is often smaller than the geometric surface area, and corrections accounting for the probe's orientation relative to the magnetic field may be applied in data analysis. The exposed area is defined as the portion of the probe collector surface in direct contact with the plasma, excluding insulated or shielded regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the exposed surface area faces the plasma, defined as a positive scalar quantity.

NAMES.name: current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Electron emission current from the hot filament used to ionize residual gas molecules in a mass spectrometer, providing the source of ionizing electrons.
NAMES.long: The emission current is the electron current drawn from the heated filament cathode of a mass spectrometer (also known as a residual gas analyzer, RGA). This current controls the rate of electron-impact ionization of neutral gas molecules in the spectrometer's ion source. Typical values range from 0.1 to 10 mA, with higher currents increasing sensitivity at the cost of faster filament aging. The emission current must be stabilized against filament temperature drift to ensure reproducible ion currents at the detector. It is distinct from the collected ion current, which is the current measured at a specific mass channel (see [ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel](name:ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel)). The emission current and the detector high voltage (see [voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel)) together define the spectrometer operating point.

NAMES.name: ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Ion current measured by a mass spectrometer channel tuned to a specific atomic mass, used for neutral gas composition analysis.
NAMES.long: The ion current $I_{\mathrm{ion}}$ collected by a mass spectrometer channel (residual gas analyzer) measures the abundance of a specific gas species after electron-impact ionization. The channel is tuned to a particular mass-to-charge ratio $m/z$ via a quadrupole mass filter or magnetic sector, producing a current proportional to the partial pressure of that species. Typical currents range from $10^{-12}$ to $10^{-6}$ A depending on gas pressure, ionization efficiency, and detector gain. This measurement is commonly used for fuel composition monitoring, impurity tracking, and leak detection in fusion devices. See also [current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel](name:current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel) for the filament emission current and [voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel) for the detector bias setting.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_langmuir_probe
NAMES.short: Major radial coordinate (R) specifying the static position of a Langmuir probe in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The major radius $R_{\text{probe}}$ defines the radial distance from the machine symmetry axis to the fixed Langmuir probe position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This coordinate is established during probe installation and does not vary during plasma operation; it is critical for mapping the probe's measurements to the local flux-surface geometry. Typical values for reciprocating probes in the scrape-off layer range from $R_{\text{sep}} - 0.1$ m to $R_{\text{sep}} + 0.2$ m, where $R_{\text{sep}}$ is the separatrix major radius. The static position is measured directly during probe design or assembly; dynamic scans during a discharge are tracked separately by the reciprocating mechanism.

See also [vertical_coordinate_of_langmuir_probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_langmuir_probe) for the corresponding vertical coordinate and [major_radius_of_reciprocating_probe](name:major_radius_of_reciprocating_probe) for the dynamic position of a moving probe.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the probe is farther from the machine symmetry axis along the $+\hat{R}$ direction.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_reciprocating_probe
NAMES.short: Radial position coordinate in the IMAS right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame for a reciprocating probe collector during its plunge into the plasma edge.
NAMES.long:
The major radius $R$ of the reciprocating probe collector positions the probe within the tokamak poloidal cross-section, defining its radial location in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ coordinate system. During a plunge, the collector moves radially from the vessel wall through the scrape-off layer into the plasma edge; $R$ marks its instantaneous location along this trajectory, typically in the range $R = 1.5$–$2.5\,\text{m}$ for medium-size tokamaks. The vertical partner coordinate is given by [vertical_coordinate_of_reciprocating_probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_reciprocating_probe), while static probe positions are described by [major_radius_of_langmuir_probe](name:major_radius_of_langmuir_probe).

The collector $R$ is recorded during each plunging stroke and used together with the plunge depth to reconstruct the probe's trajectory relative to the separatrix, enabling measurement of the radial profiles of edge plasma quantities such as [electron_density](name:electron_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured radially outward from the machine symmetry axis in the $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: parallel_heat_flux
NAMES.short: Power flux density carried by particles and heat along the magnetic field line, measured by Langmuir probes in the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long: The parallel heat flux density $q_{\parallel}$ quantifies the thermal energy transported per unit area per unit time along the magnetic field direction. For a Langmuir probe, it is inferred from the measured ion saturation current and electron temperature using the relation $q_{\parallel} = \gamma k_B T_e j_{\text{sat}}$, where $\gamma \approx 7\!-\!8$ is the sheath heat transmission coefficient. In the scrape-off layer of diverted tokamaks, $q_{\parallel}$ at the outer midplane typically ranges from $1\!-\!100\;\text{MW}\,\text{m}^{-2}$, with the exact value depending on the upstream density and heating power. Together with the scrape-off layer heat flux decay length, $q_{\parallel}$ determines the divertor target peak heat load critical for power exhaust design. This quantity is the parallel component of the total [heat flux](name:heat_flux) and complements measurements of [electron density](name:electron_density) from the same probe.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the heat flows in the direction of increasing poloidal angle (i.e., along the magnetic field toward the outboard midplane).

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_langmuir_probe
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate (Z) of the collector of a reciprocating Langmuir probe in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, specifying its position relative to the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z_{\text{LP}}$ locates the Langmuir probe collector along the machine symmetry axis, measured from the midplane. It is essential for mapping probe measurements to flux surfaces, especially when the probe plunges across the scrape-off layer into the core plasma edge. Typical vertical positions range from $-1$ to $+1\,\text{m}$ for medium-size tokamaks. This coordinate is paired with $[\text{major\_radius\_of\_langmuir\_probe}](\text{name:major\_radius\_of\_langmuir\_probe})$ to define the full position in the $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Unlike the reciprocating probe variant $[\text{vertical\_coordinate\_of\_reciprocating\_probe}](\text{name:vertical\_coordinate\_of\_reciprocating\_probe})$, this quantity refers to a static probe installation without plunging motion.

The coordinate is measured in meters and is referenced to the machine geometry; it is independent of plasma conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the probe is located above the machine midplane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_reciprocating_probe
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate (cylindrical Z) of the reciprocating probe position in the right-handed IMAS cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long: The vertical coordinate $Z$ specifies the height of the reciprocating probe head or collector relative to the device midplane ($Z=0$) in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system where $Z$ increases upward. This coordinate, together with the major radius $R$ ([major_radius_of_reciprocating_probe](name:major_radius_of_reciprocating_probe)), defines the probe's position in the poloidal cross-section. The reciprocating probe is typically plunged radially into the edge plasma or scrape-off layer to measure local plasma parameters such as [electron_density](name:electron_density) and electron temperature; its vertical coordinate is critical for mapping measurements to flux surfaces and for analyzing radial profiles at a fixed poloidal angle.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the probe is positioned above the device midplane ($Z=0$).

NAMES.name: area_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: Geometric cross-sectional area of a diagnostic aperture that defines the entrance pupil for a camera, spectrometer, or bolometer channel.
NAMES.long:
The geometric surface area $A_{\text{ap}}$ of a diagnostic aperture opening is a fundamental parameter that defines the entrance pupil for an optical or particle diagnostic channel. Together with the line-of-sight geometry Proxy, it determines the etendue ($A_{\text{ap}} \cdot \Omega$) where $\Omega$ is the solid angle subtended by the aperture, governing the photon or particle collection efficiency of the diagnostic. This quantity is derived from the aperture's geometric data and is used across a wide range of fusion diagnostics including spectroscopy, bolometry, neutron, and imaging systems. Typical aperture areas range from $10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2$ for visible spectroscopy channels to $10^{-2}\,\text{m}^2$ for bolometer cameras. The geometric area described here must be distinguished from the effective area that accounts for aperture transmission and vignetting. See also [radius_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture), [area_of_optical_element](name:area_of_optical_element), and [area_of_reflectometer_antenna](name:area_of_reflectometer_antenna).

Measurement of the aperture opening area is typically performed during diagnostic construction using precision mechanical measurements or optical profilometry, with the value fixed for the duration of the diagnostic's operational lifetime.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the surface normal vector points outward from the diagnostic housing.

NAMES.name: area_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Surface area of a neutron detector hardware component, such as an active detection element or a collimating aperture, used to determine the geometric acceptance for incident neutron flux.
NAMES.long:
The surface area $A_\mathrm{det}$ of the neutron detector defines the geometric cross-section presented to the incident neutron flux and is a key parameter for calculating the detector's overall detection efficiency and solid angle of acceptance. Together with the detector's distance from the plasma and its collimation geometry, this area determines the fraction of the total neutron emission that is intercepted. Typical detector areas in fusion neutron diagnostics range from a few square centimeters for compact scintillation or diamond detectors to several hundred square centimeters for large fission chambers or activation foil assemblies. The quantity is distinct from the active area of any internal converter material, which is described by `[area_of_neutron_detector_converter](name:area_of_neutron_detector_converter)`.

Typical values in fusion diagnostics range from $10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}^2$ for small fiber-coupled detectors to $0.1\ \mathrm{m}^2$ for large neutron flux monitors, depending on the required count rate and spatial resolution.
NAMES.sign: Positive for all physically realizable detector surfaces, as area is a geometric property.

NAMES.name: area_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Active surface area of the converter material in a neutron detector, used to compute neutron-to-charged-particle conversion efficiency.
NAMES.long:
The area of the neutron detector converter defines the active surface through which incident neutrons interact with the converter material to produce charged particles (e.g., protons, tritons) via nuclear reactions such as $^6\mathrm{Li}(n,\alpha)^3\mathrm{H}$. Together with the [nuclear density](name:nuclear_density_of_neutron_detector_converter) and [volume](name:volume_of_neutron_detector_converter) of the converter, this area enters the detection efficiency calculation: $\eta = n \sigma A_{\mathrm{conv}} d_{\mathrm{conv}}$, where $n$ is the nuclear number density, $\sigma$ the relevant cross-section, $A_{\mathrm{conv}}$ the converter area, and $d_{\mathrm{conv}}$ the converter thickness. Typical converter areas for neutron cameras in present-day tokamaks range from 1-100 cm$^2$, depending on the detector design and required count-rate capability. This geometric parameter is determined during detector characterization and is stored for each detector channel.

The converter area is related to the detector's [geometric acceptance](name:area_of_neutron_detector), which additionally accounts for collimation and viewing geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the surface is oriented outward from the converter material toward the incident neutron flux.

NAMES.name: dead_time_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Minimum interval after a detected event during which the neutron detector cannot register a new event.
NAMES.long:
The dead time of a neutron detector is the shortest time separation between two successive detected events such that the second event can be registered. This interval arises from the finite response time of the detector and its electronics, limiting the maximum count rate and causing count losses at high neutron fluxes. In fusion plasmas, typical dead times range from 0.1 to several microseconds, depending on detector technology (e.g., fission chambers, scintillators, diamond detectors). The dead time model (non-paralyzable or paralyzable) must be applied when correcting measured count rates for these losses. The related quantity [time_of_neutron_detector](name:time_of_neutron_detector) gives the integration time per spectrum slice, which together with dead time determines the effective duty cycle.

Dead times are used in the count-rate correction formula $R = C / (1 - C \tau)$ for non-paralyzable detectors, where $R$ is the true count rate, $C$ the measured count rate, and $\tau$ the dead time.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the dead time interval is measured as a positive number of seconds.

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_emissivity
NAMES.short: Volumetric rate of 2.45 MeV neutrons produced by deuterium-deuterium fusion reactions in the plasma.
NAMES.long: The deuterium-deuterium (DD) emissivity $\epsilon_{\mathrm{DD}}$ is the volumetric reaction rate density for the D(d,n)$^3$He fusion branch, which produces a 2.45 MeV neutron and a $^3$He ion. It is given locally by $\epsilon_{\mathrm{DD}} = n_D \, n_D \, \langle \sigma v \rangle_{\mathrm{DD}} / (1+\delta_{12})$, where $n_D$ is the deuterium density, $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{\mathrm{DD}}$ is the Maxwellian-averaged reactivity for the DD reaction, and the factor $(1+\delta_{12})$ accounts for indistinguishability of identical reactants. This emissivity profile is routinely reconstructed from neutron camera measurements using tomographic inversion techniques. Core values in a high-performance deuterium plasma can reach $10^{16}$–$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$s$^{-1}$, depending on density and temperature. The total neutron source rate is obtained by integrating the emissivity over the plasma volume, giving the [deuterium_deuterium_source_rate](name:deuterium_deuterium_source_rate). For the DT fuel cycle, the analogous quantity is [deuterium_tritium_emissivity](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity). The [fusion_power](name:fusion_power) includes contributions from both DD and DT reactions.

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_fusion_power_density
NAMES.short: Volumetric power density released as kinetic energy of charged fusion products and 2.45 MeV neutrons from deuterium-deuterium fusion reactions in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The deuterium-deuterium fusion power density quantifies the local rate of energy release from D(d,n)$^{3}$He and D(d,p)$^{3}$H reactions. Its defining relation is $P_{\mathrm{DD}} = \frac{1}{1+\delta_{12}} n_D^2 \langle \sigma v \rangle_{\mathrm{DD}} E_{\mathrm{DD}}$, where $n_D$ (m$^{-3}$) is the deuterium density, $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{\mathrm{DD}}$ (m$^3$s$^{-1}$) the Maxwellian-averaged reactivity, $E_{\mathrm{DD}} \approx 7.3$ MeV the total energy released per D-D fusion branch after accounting for the two-channel branching ratio, and $1+\delta_{12}$ the statistical factor for identical reactants.

This quantity is reconstructed from neutron emission measurements (neutron flux monitors, activation foils) combined with equilibrium density and temperature profiles via a forward model of the reactivity. In the core of high-performance D plasmas, typical values range from $10^3$ to $10^5$ W/m$^3$.

The related standard name [deuterium_deuterium_emissivity](name:deuterium_deuterium_emissivity) gives the neutron production rate (particles per volume per time), while [deuterium_deuterium_source_rate](name:deuterium_deuterium_source_rate) integrates over the entire plasma volume. The deuterium-tritium counterpart is [deuterium_tritium_fusion_power_density](name:deuterium_tritium_fusion_power_density).

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_source_rate
NAMES.short: Total neutron emission rate from deuterium-deuterium fusion reactions in the plasma, summing contributions from thermal, beam-thermal, and beam-beam reactions.
NAMES.long: The deuterium-deuterium fusion source rate quantifies the total 2.45 MeV neutron production from $D(d,n)^3He$ reactions, integrated over all reaction channels (thermal-thermal, beam-thermal, and beam-beam). This rate is a key fusion performance metric, directly proportional to the deuterium density squared and the fusion reactivity $ ar{\langle\sigma v\rangle}_{DD}$ in the thermal plasma. Typical values range from $10^{12}$ to $10^{16}$ neutrons per second in medium-sized tokamaks with neutral beam injection, measured using neutron flux monitors (fission chambers, activation foils) and neutron cameras. The total rate is the sum of [thermal_source_rate](name:thermal_source_rate) and beam-driven components such as [deuterium_deuterium_beam_source_rate](name:deuterium_deuterium_beam_source_rate), and is a subset of the overall [source_rate](name:source_rate) from all fusion reactions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutron emission rate is directed outward from the plasma (net production).

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_emissivity
NAMES.short: Volumetric rate of 14.1 MeV neutrons produced by deuterium-tritium fusion reactions in the plasma.
NAMES.long: This quantity represents the local volumetric neutron emissivity $ rac{dN_{14.1}}{dV dt}$ from deuterium-tritium (DT) fusion, yielding 14.1 MeV neutrons. It is the product of the thermal reactivities and densities of the deuterium and tritium populations integrated over their velocity distributions, $	ext{Emissivity}_{	ext{DT}} = n_D n_T  rac{ ar{	au}v}{	ext{DT}}$, where $n_D$ and $n_T$ are the deuterium and tritium densities (in $	ext{m}^{-3}$) and $ ar{	au}v_{	ext{DT}}$ is the Maxwellian-averaged fusion reactivity (in $	ext{m}^3	ext{s}^{-1}$). Typical core values in ITER-baseline DT plasmas are $1	imes10^{17}$ to $1	imes10^{19}	ext{ m}^{-3}	ext{s}^{-1}$, with the peak near the magnetic axis. The emissivity profile is routinely reconstructed from line-integrated neutron measurements using tomographic inversion of arrays of neutron detectors (e.g., diamond detectors or liquid scintillators) and provides a source term for neutronics calculations. See [deuterium_deuterium_emissivity](name:deuterium_deuterium_emissivity) for the companion DD 2.45 MeV channel and [deuterium_tritium_source_rate](name:deuterium_tritium_source_rate) for the integrated total DT neutron rate.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_fusion_power_density
NAMES.short: Volumetric thermal power released by deuterium-tritium fusion reactions in a magnetically confined plasma.
NAMES.long: The deuterium-tritium fusion power density $P_{\mathrm{DT}} = n_{\mathrm{D}}n_{\mathrm{T}} \langle \sigma v \rangle_{\mathrm{DT}} E_{\alpha}$ quantifies the local heating power per unit volume from DT reactions, where $n_{\mathrm{D}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{T}}$ are the deuterium and tritium densities in m$^{-3}$, $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{\mathrm{DT}}$ is the Maxwellian-averaged DT fusion reactivity in m$^3$ s$^{-1}$, and $E_{\alpha} = 3.52\,\mathrm{MeV}$ is the energy of the fusion-born alpha particle. This quantity represents the dominant alpha-heating source in burning-plasma scenarios and is routinely reconstructed from 14.1-MeV neutron emissivity measurements via collimated neutron cameras or activation systems. In ITER-relevant DT plasmas with core densities of $10^{20}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ and temperatures near 10–20 keV, the peak fusion power density can approach several MW m$^{-3}$. The related quantity [deuterium_tritium_emissivity](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity) gives the volumetric rate of 14.1-MeV neutron production, while [deuterium_deuterium_fusion_power_density](name:deuterium_deuterium_fusion_power_density) describes the analogous quantity for DD reactions.

NAMES.name: energy_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Discrete neutron energy values defining the sampling points within an energy band of a neutron detector.
NAMES.long:
The energy-of-neutron-detector provides the discrete energy grid $E_i$ (in eV) that defines the sampling points within an energy band of a neutron detector system. These energy values serve as the independent variable for the energy-resolved neutron flux incident on the detector, enabling spectral discrimination between fusion neutron sources such as DD (2.45 MeV) and DT (14.1 MeV) reactions. The energy sampling is typically chosen to match the detector intrinsic energy resolution and the width of the energy band being measured. The associated energy-resolved measurement quantity is [neutron_flux](name:neutron_flux), which gives the neutron flux per energy interval at each sampling point.

Typical energy values range from 1 keV to 20 MeV for fusion neutron diagnostics, with finer sampling near the fusion peak energies to resolve the neutron spectrum shape.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the energy value increases with the index of the sampling array.

NAMES.name: gradient_of_neutron_flux
NAMES.short: Radial-poloidal cross-derivative of the neutron flux Green's function response matrix element, describing the spatial sensitivity of a detector to a unit ring source in the plasma.
NAMES.long: The gradient of neutron flux, $\nabla G_{ij}$, is the spatial derivative of the neutron flux per source neutron Green's function $G_{ij}$ with respect to the source position in the plasma. It quantifies how the detector response changes when the unit ring source is displaced radially or vertically, and is a key kernel quantity for tomographic reconstruction of the neutron emission profile from line-integrated measurements. In the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the cross-derivative $\partial^2 G_{ij} / (\partial R \, \partial Z)$ represents the mixed sensitivity; typical values are of order $10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{-4}$ for a compact neutron camera viewing a medium-size tokamak plasma. This quantity is computed from the same geometric and collimator model as the parent quantity [neutron_flux](name:neutron_flux), but differentiated analytically or numerically over the source grid, and is used in maximum-likelihood or Bayesian tomographic inversion algorithms.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_beam_tracing_point
NAMES.short: Major radius coordinate of the third defining point of a diagnostic line of sight in the cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long: The major radius $R_3$ of the third point that defines a diagnostic line of sight in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, completing the set of two points that specify a straight chord. This point lies on the ray path of a beam tracing diagnostic. It is used together with the first two points to fully define the geometry of the line of sight, enabling accurate calculation of the viewing direction and intersection with the plasma volume. Typical values span the tokamak minor-to-major radius range, e.g., 1.5--3.0 m for medium-size machines. The quantity is defined for each diagnostic beam tracing channel and can be obtained from the diagnostic engineering data. See [major_radius_of_measurement_position](name:major_radius_of_measurement_position) for the analogous first-point coordinate, and [toroidal_angle_of_line_of_sight](name:toroidal_angle_of_line_of_sight) for the toroidal orientation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the point lies at a larger major radius than the torus symmetry axis (R=0).

NAMES.name: neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Neutron flux from a unit fusion-reaction ring source, incident on the converter material in a neutron detector.
NAMES.long: The neutron flux $\Gamma_n$ (m$^{-2}$) quantifies the number of neutrons per unit area arriving at the converter layer of a neutron detector from a unit ring source (a thin toroidal shell) in the plasma. This flux is the Green's function element for the detector response, relating a localized fusion source to the signal at the converter. For typical DT plasmas, the flux from a unit source may be computed via ray tracing or Monte Carlo methods through the machine geometry. The flux is integrated over the [area_of_neutron_detector_converter](name:area_of_neutron_detector_converter) to obtain the total neutron rate incident on the detector. The nuclear interactions within the converter, which depend on its [nuclear_density_of_neutron_detector_converter](name:nuclear_density_of_neutron_detector_converter) and volume given by [volume_of_neutron_detector_converter](name:volume_of_neutron_detector_converter), determine the detection efficiency. This quantity is closely related to the [gradient_of_neutron_flux](name:gradient_of_neutron_flux), which describes the spatial derivative of the same Green's function. Typical neutron flux values at the detector position in a burning-plasma tokamak (e.g. ITER) range from $10^{12}$ to $10^{16}$ m$^{-2}$ for a 14.1 MeV DT source.

NAMES.name: temperature_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Thermodynamic temperature of the neutron detector hardware, influencing gain stability, noise characteristics, and calibration drift.
NAMES.long: The temperature of a neutron detector governs the thermal equilibrium of its constituent materials, directly affecting electronic noise, signal gain, and the detector's response to incident neutron flux. Temperature variations can cause drift in the detector's calibration, requiring corrections to maintain accurate fusion neutron yield measurements. Typical operating temperatures range from 300–350 K for detectors in tokamak environments, though active cooling may be used to stabilize conditions. Temperature measurements are used in conjunction with [temperature_of_neutron_detector_converter](name:temperature_of_neutron_detector_converter) to model the full detector system's thermal behavior. The quantity is a scalar field that is inherently sign-invariant, as thermodynamic temperature is always defined in Kelvin and never negative.

NAMES.name: volume_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Physical volume of the converter material in a neutron detector, used to calculate detection efficiency from the nuclear interaction cross-section.
NAMES.long: The converter volume $V_c$ is the geometric volume of the neutron-sensitive converter material within a neutron detector, typically a thin foil or layer of materials such as $^{235}$U, $^{238}$U, or $^{10}$B. This volume, combined with the nuclear density $n_c$ of the converter material, determines the total number of target nuclei ($N = n_c V_c$) available for neutron-induced reactions such as fission or (n,$\alpha$) capture. The detection efficiency of a neutron detector is directly proportional to the converter volume and the interaction cross-section, with typical converter volumes ranging from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-4}$ m$^3$ for fission chambers in fusion diagnostics. The converter volume is a fundamental input for calculating the detector response and calibrating the measured neutron flux. See also [nuclear_density_of_neutron_detector_converter](name:nuclear_density_of_neutron_detector_converter) and [temperature_of_neutron_detector_converter](name:temperature_of_neutron_detector_converter).
NAMES.sign: Positive for any physical volume.

NAMES.name: ammonia_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.short: Instantaneous injection rate of ammonia (NH3) molecules during gas puffing into the vacuum vessel.
NAMES.long:
The ammonia source rate quantifies the number of NH3 molecules injected per second through a dedicated gas-puff system. This rate is used to control the plasma composition for experiments involving nitrogen seeding, radiative cooling, or ammonia formation studies. The injection rate is typically commanded by the gas-injection controller and can be calibrated via pressure and flow measurements in the injection line. Typical values range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{22}$ molecules/s depending on the desired plasma density and impurity concentration.

Related quantities include the injection rates for other species such as [neon_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:neon_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection) and [argon_gas_source_rate](name:argon_gas_source_rate), which follow the same measurement and control principles.
NAMES.sign: Positive when gas is flowing into the vessel.

NAMES.name: atomic_mass_number
NAMES.short: Atomic mass number (total number of protons and neutrons) of the gas species element in an injection or pumping gas mixture.
NAMES.long: The atomic mass number $A$ (also called the mass number or nucleon number) is the total count of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of a specific isotope of the gas species. Together with the [atomic_number](name:atomic_number) (proton number $Z$), it uniquely identifies the nuclide — for example, $A=4$ with $Z=2$ specifies helium-4, while $A=3$ with $Z=2$ specifies helium-3. This quantity is used to characterize the injected or pumped gas composition in units of unified atomic mass units (u), where $1\,\text{u} = 1.660539 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}$. Typical values for fusion-relevant gasses range from $A=1$ (protium) through $A=4$ (helium-4), and up to $A=40$ (argon) for disruption-mitigation systems. The atomic mass number is distinct from the [atomic_number](name:atomic_number) (proton count) and from the isotope-resolved [ion_atomic_mass](name:ion_atomic_mass) used for plasma species.

NAMES.name: gas_source_rate_at_midplane
NAMES.short: Total instantaneous gas injection rate from all valves positioned near the equatorial midplane of the vacuum vessel, summed over all injected species.
NAMES.long:
This quantity aggregates the total instantaneous influx of gas into the plasma vessel from all injection systems located at the torus midplane (e.g., supersonic molecular beam injectors, gas puff modules). The midplane position is the primary location for core fueling and edge density control in many tokamak configurations, as the magnetic geometry couples this region directly to the plasma core.

Typical midplane injection rates span $10^{19}--10^{22}\;\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ depending on the plasma scenario (e.g., H-mode density ramp, disruption mitigation). This rate contributes to the total gas source rate due to injection, which sums over all spatial injection points. Specific species components are tracked by sibling names such as $\texttt{deuterium\_gas\_source\_rate\_of\_inlet}$ and $\texttt{argon\_gas\_source\_rate}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when gas flows into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: helium_3_source_rate_due_to_injection
NAMES.short: Instantaneous rate at which helium-3 atoms are injected into the vacuum vessel.
NAMES.long: The helium-3 source rate quantifies the number of $^3$He atoms introduced per unit time into the vacuum vessel via gas injection systems. This rate directly controls the concentration of helium-3 in the plasma, which influences fusion reactivity (e.g., $^3$He + D → $^4$He + p + 18.3 MeV) and plasma fueling. The injection rate is typically controlled by piezoelectric or solenoid valves and measured by calibrated flow meters, with typical values ranging from $10^{18}$ to $10^{21}$ s$^{-1}$ in present-day tokamaks. Maintaining a specified helium-3 source rate is essential for scenarios such as ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) minority heating or non-fusion tritium breeding studies. The quantity directly parallels [tritium_source_rate](name:tritium_source_rate) for tritium gas injection and is the helium-3 analog of [helium_4_gas_source_rate_due_to_injection](name:helium_4_gas_source_rate_due_to_injection).
NAMES.sign: Positive when helium-3 atoms are injected into the vessel, zero when no injection occurs.

NAMES.name: hydrogen_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.short: Instantaneous rate at which hydrogen atoms are injected into the vacuum vessel via gas puffing systems.
NAMES.long:
The hydrogen source rate quantifies the flux of atomic hydrogen injected into the vessel to fuel the plasma, control density profiles, or condition plasma-facing components. In tokamaks, hydrogen gas puffing is a primary fueling method, with injection rates typically ranging from 1×10^20 to 1×10^23 atoms/s depending on plasma regime and machine size. This rate is measured by flow meters on the gas injection system and is critical for particle balance studies alongside [deuterium_gas_source_rate_at_inlet_due_to_gas_injection](name:deuterium_gas_source_rate_at_inlet_due_to_gas_injection) and [tritium_source_rate](name:tritium_source_rate).

The source rate is directly related to the fueling efficiency, which may be estimated from the ratio of the core particle confinement time to the injection rate.
NAMES.sign: Positive when hydrogen flows into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: lithium_gas_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.short: Instantaneous rate of lithium atoms injected via gas puffing into the vacuum vessel.
NAMES.long:
The lithium gas source rate due to gas injection quantifies the number of lithium atoms per second introduced into the plasma vessel through a dedicated gas puffing system. This rate is used to model the fueling of the plasma with lithium, which can affect edge plasma conditions, heat flux mitigation, and plasma-facing component performance.

Typical values for lithium injection rates in present devices range from 10^18 s^-1 to 10^22 s^-1 depending on the discharge phase and desired lithium inventory. The rate is directly related to the total injected particle inventory via time integration.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flow of lithium atoms is directed into the plasma vessel.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_pellet
NAMES.short: Major radius (R) cylindrical coordinate of the position of a pellet used for plasma material injection.
NAMES.long:
The major radius $R$ of the pellet position is the radial coordinate in the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, measured from the machine symmetry axis to the pellet location. This coordinate determines the injection point of cryogenic pellets (e.g., for shattered pellet injection or fueling) and is critical for predicting pellet ablation dynamics and deposition profiles.

Typical pellet injection radii range from $R \approx 1.5$ m (inner wall) to $R \approx 3.0$ m (outer midplane) in medium-size tokamaks; in ITER, the major radius is approximately $6.2$ m. The radial location is routinely prescribed by the injector geometry or adjusted for dedicated experiments. See also [major_radius_of_launching_position](name:major_radius_of_launching_position) for the analogous coordinate of electron cyclotron launchers.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pellet position lies at $R > 0$, with the origin at the machine axis.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_pellet_path
NAMES.short: Major radius of the second point defining the straight-line trajectory of a pellet injection path in the cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, measured from the machine symmetry axis.
NAMES.long: The major radius of the pellet path second point is one of two positions that define the straight-line trajectory of a pellet as it is injected and before it ablates. The path is determined by a first point and a second point, both given in the cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, with the trajectory extending from the first through the second in the direction of travel. The major radius is the radial distance from the machine symmetry axis (Z-axis) to the second point, measured in meters. Typical values for the major radius range from 0.5 m to 3.0 m depending on device size and pellet injector location. This coordinate pair allows calculation of the pellet's velocity and direction of travel when combined with time-of-flight measurements. The second point is typically further along the trajectory than the first and is located near the plasma edge or beyond.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the second point is radially outward from the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: silane_source_rate_due_to_injection
NAMES.short: Instantaneous rate of silane molecules injected into the vacuum vessel via gas puffing systems for plasma-facing surface conditioning or diagnostic purposes.
NAMES.long: The silane source rate measures the number of silane (SiH$_4$) molecules per second introduced into the vacuum vessel from the gas injection system. Silane is used in tokamak operations for deposition of silicon coatings on plasma-facing components or for plasma chemistry studies. Typical injection rates range from $10^{18}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ to $10^{22}\ \text{s}^{-1}$, depending on the conditioning regime and diagnostic requirements. In the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the rate is a scalar quantity and does not depend on direction. The value is positive when silane flows into the vacuum vessel.

NAMES.name: temperature_of_port
NAMES.short: Bulk fluid temperature at the inlet or outlet port of a balance-of-plant component.
NAMES.long: The fluid temperature at a balance-of-plant component port defines the thermal state of the working fluid (coolant) as it enters or exits the component, such as a heat exchanger, pump, or valve. This temperature is a key thermodynamic state variable, used together with the fluid pressure to determine the specific enthalpy and, combined with the mass flow rate, to compute the thermal power transferred across the port. In the power-plant thermal cycle, the port temperature is measured by thermocouples or resistance temperature detectors (RTDs) at the pipe flange or manifold. Typical fluid temperatures range from 30–60°C in the low-pressure side of the heat rejection loop to 300–500°C in the primary coolant loop of a fusion power plant. The port temperature is closely related to the [pressure_of_port](name:pressure_of_port), which together define the fluid equation of state, and to the [thermal_power_of_port](name:thermal_power_of_port) calculated from the temperature difference across the component.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_pellet
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle coordinate of a pellet's position in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, defining the poloidal-plane location of any point along its injection trajectory.
NAMES.long: The toroidal angle $\phi$ specifies the azimuthal position of a pellet relative to the machine symmetry axis in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ coordinate system. This coordinate is used to define the location of the pellet at its launch point, during flight, or at the shattering position along the injection path, depending on the context. The toroidal angle is a critical geometric parameter for shattered pellet injectors and other fueling systems, as it determines the toroidal alignment of the injected material with the plasma and affects the resulting deposition and mixing. Typical values span the full $0$–$2\pi$ range toroidally, with the injection launch point often located on the low-field side or a specific sector. This quantity is related to the full position vector and can be paired with the [major_radius_of_pellet](name:major_radius_of_pellet) coordinate to locate the pellet in the poloidal plane. See also the [toroidal_angle_of_pellet_path](name:toroidal_angle_of_pellet_path) for the launch-point-specific variant.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above the torus (along the $+\hat{Z}$ direction).

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_pellet_path
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle of the launch point of a pellet injection trajectory in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal angle $\phi$ of the first point of the pellet path geometry, measured in the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The angle increases in the counter-clockwise direction when viewed from above (i.e., from the $+\hat{Z}$ direction). Typical values span the full range $[0, 2\pi)$ radians.

For reference, see the sibling standard name `toroidal_angle` and the corresponding DD path `pellets/time_slice/pellet/path_geometry/first_point/phi`.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_shattered_pellet
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle coordinate of the location along a shattered pellet injection path where the pellet fractures into fragments.
NAMES.long: The toroidal angle $\phi_{\mathrm{SP}}$ (in radians) identifies the shattering position along a shattered pellet injector (SPI) path in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This position determines the toroidal location where the injected pellet breaks apart, releasing a spray of solid fragments that then ablate along the remaining trajectory; the shattering location influences the deposition pattern and the resulting density perturbation.  Typical shattering positions for SPI systems in present-day tokamaks (DIII-D, JET) and planned for ITER are located in the outer half of the plasma cross-section, with $\phi_{\mathrm{SP}}$ spanning the full $0$–$2\pi$ range depending on the injector port.  This quantity is used together with [major_radius_of_pellet_path](name:major_radius_of_pellet_path) and [vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector](name:vertical_coordinate_of_neutral_beam_injector) to fully define the SPI geometry, and is complementary to [toroidal_angle_of_pellet_path](name:toroidal_angle_of_pellet_path) which records the launch point rather than the fracture point.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the shattering position lies in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: tritium_source_rate
NAMES.short: Instantaneous rate at which tritium atoms are injected into the plasma vessel.
NAMES.long:
The tritium source rate quantifies the number of tritium atoms introduced per unit time into the vacuum vessel through gas injection systems. This quantity is critical for controlling the tritium inventory, fueling requirements, and fusion power production in deuterium-tritium (D-T) burning plasmas. The injection rate is typically regulated by piezoelectric valves or fast gas injectors, with flow rates monitored by pressure and temperature measurements upstream of the injection point.

This quantity is directly related to the deuterium fueling rate via [deuterium_gas_source_rate_of_inlet](name:deuterium_gas_source_rate_of_inlet), which shares the same units and functional role. The total gas injection across all species is captured by [total_gas_source_rate_due_to_injection](name:total_gas_source_rate_due_to_injection). For neon or other impurity species, analogous quantities such as [neon_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection](name:neon_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection) follow the same physical definition.
NAMES.sign: Positive when tritium atoms flow into the plasma vessel from the gas injection system.

NAMES.name: xenon_source_rate_due_to_gas_injection
NAMES.short: Instantaneous rate at which xenon atoms are injected into the vacuum vessel via gas puffing systems.
NAMES.long: Xenon is a high-Z noble gas used as a radiating species in tokamak experiments to control divertor heat flux and mitigate edge localized modes (ELMs). The source rate quantifies the number of xenon atoms per second introduced into the vacuum vessel from gas injection hardware, typically piezo-electric valves or regulated gas puffs. Typical values range from $10^{18}$ to $10^{21}$ atoms per second, depending on the injection scenario (e.g., short-pulse ELM pacing vs. steady-state radiative cooling). The rate is measured at the injection point before any ionization or transport; it does not account for wall recycling or pumping losses. This quantity is distinct from the neutral influx rate, which may include reflected or desorbed atoms.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_diagnostic_antenna
NAMES.short: Major radius (R) coordinate of the second endpoint defining the line of sight for a diagnostic system.
NAMES.long:
The major radius coordinate $R$ of the second point on a diagnostic line of sight positions the far endpoint of the viewing chord in the IMAS right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This quantity is used to define the trajectory of the sightline from the first point (typically the entry point into the vessel) to the second point (the far end, e.g., opposing wall or far-field location). The coordinate is specified in the same equatorial-plane geometry used for all line-of-sight diagnostics such as bolometers, spectrometers, and visible cameras, ensuring consistent ray tracing across systems. Typical values range from 1.5 m to 2.5 m for the major radius of the second point in medium-size tokamaks, depending on the port location and viewing geometry. See also [major radius of sensor attachment point](name:major_radius_of_sensor_attachment_point) for the entry-point coordinate.

The second point, together with the first point, defines a straight line in space through which the diagnostic observes the plasma. The accuracy of this coordinate directly affects the spatial localization of measurements such as electron density and temperature profiles.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the second point lies at a larger major radius than the machine symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: ion_state_energy_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination
