NAMES.short: Power flux density incident on the wall surface, carried by ions in a given charge state and associated with volume recombination processes.
NAMES.long: This quantity represents the energy flux density $\Gamma_E = n_i^{Z+} \, v_\perp \, E_{\rm rec}$ incident on the plasma-facing wall, where $n_i^{Z+}$ is the density of ions in charge state $Z+$, $v_\perp$ is the perpendicular impact velocity, and $E_{\rm rec}$ is the energy released per recombination event. It is computed by fluid or kinetic edge codes (e.g., SOLPS, EMC3-EIRENE) from the recombination rate coefficient and the local ion energy. Typical values range from $10^3$ to $10^6$ W/m$^2$ in detached divertor conditions, where volumetric recombination dominates. This flux is distinguished from the kinetic energy flux (see `[state_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall](name:state_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall)`) which excludes the recombination contribution. Compare also with `[parallel_ion_state_energy_flux](name:parallel_ion_state_energy_flux)` for the parallel component along the magnetic field.

NAMES.name: ion_state_particle_flux_at_wall
NAMES.short: Net particle flux density of ions in a given charge state incident on wall surfaces.
NAMES.long: The ion state particle flux at the wall represents the rate at which ions of a specific charge state impact the plasma-facing wall per unit area, typically directed along the magnetic field lines or due to cross-field transport. This quantity is a key metric for quantifying net wall erosion, material migration, and tritium retention in fusion devices. Measured units are particles per square meter per second (m⁻²·s⁻¹). Typical values in the scrape-off layer of tokamaks range from 10²¹ to 10²⁴ m⁻²·s⁻¹, with higher fluxes near the divertor. The flux for a given charge state is related to the line-integrated density and flow velocity via $\Gamma_{Z} = n_{Z} \cdot v_{\parallel}$, where $n_{Z}$ is the ion density of that charge state and $v_{\parallel}$ is the parallel flow velocity. This quantity complements the total ion particle flux, as in [ion_particle_flux_at_wall](name:ion_particle_flux_at_wall), by resolving the charge-state dependence critical for understanding impurity transport and plasma-facing component lifetime.

NAMES.name: neon_fraction
NAMES.short: Ratio of the volume-averaged neon impurity density to the electron density, evaluated at the time of peak electron density in the plasma discharge.
NAMES.long: The neon fraction quantifies the relative concentration of neon impurity ions, defined as $f_{\text{Ne}} = n_\text{Ne} / n_e$, where $n_\text{Ne}$ is the volume-averaged neon density and $n_e$ is the electron density. This fraction is typically inferred from spectroscopic measurements of neon emission lines combined with plasma modeling, or from baseline-impurity gas-puffing rates. Values range from $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-1}$ in fusion plasmas, depending on impurity seeding and transport. The quantity is sign-invariant (positive definite), as both densities are inherently non-negative. See also [oxygen_fraction](name:oxygen_fraction) and [xenon_fraction_at_separatrix](name:xenon_fraction_at_separatrix) for other impurity species.

NAMES.name: neutral_gas_source_rate_at_wall
NAMES.short: Total instantaneous rate at which neutral gas particles are emitted from the entire plasma-facing wall surface due to plasma-wall interactions, integrated over the wall area and summed over all neutral species.
NAMES.long:
The neutral gas source rate at the wall quantifies the total number of neutral gas particles released per second from the plasma-facing wall surface, encompassing contributions from processes such as desorption, sputtering, and recycling. This quantity is integrated over the entire wall (units of s$^{-1}$), distinct from a volumetric source density (e.g., m$^{-3}$s$^{-1}$).

Typical values in fusion devices range from 10$^{18}$ to 10$^{22}$ s$^{-1}$, depending on the plasma confinement mode, wall material, and fueling conditions. The rate is often inferred from pressure measurements in the vacuum vessel or from modeling of neutral particle transport. It is a key input for predicting the neutral density distribution and fueling efficiency in the scrape-off layer and core plasma.

This quantity aggregates contributions from all neutral species (e.g., hydrogen isotopes, helium, impurities) incident upon the wall.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutral particles are emitted outward from the wall into the plasma-facing volume.

NAMES.name: oxygen_fraction
NAMES.short: Composition fraction of oxygen in the plasma, defined as the ratio of the oxygen impurity density to the electron density.
NAMES.long: The oxygen fraction quantifies the abundance of oxygen impurities relative to the electron population, typically expressed as $f_{\mathrm{O}} = n_{\mathrm{O}} / n_e$, where $n_{\mathrm{O}}$ is the oxygen density and $n_e$ is the electron density. Oxygen is a common low-Z impurity introduced through wall outgassing or plasma-facing component erosion; its fraction influences radiative power loss and plasma dilution. Typical core oxygen fractions in tokamaks range from $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-2}$, with higher values in the scrape-off layer. This quantity is measurable via visible or VUV spectroscopy of oxygen emission lines. The related [iron\_fraction](name:iron_fraction) and [total\_plasma\_fraction](name:total_plasma_fraction) describe other impurity species and total composition.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $n_{\mathrm{O}} > 0$, i.e., when oxygen is present in the plasma. The oxygen fraction is non-negative by definition.

NAMES.name: radial_electric_field_at_wall
NAMES.short: Projection of the electric field vector onto the major-radius direction at the plasma-facing wall surface.
NAMES.long: The radial electric field at the wall $E_{R|\text{wall}} = \mathbf{E} \cdot \hat{R}$ represents the component of the electrostatic field along the outward major-radius axis evaluated on the wall boundary. This field component influences the radial transport of charged particles to plasma-facing components and governs the sheath potential that forms at the wall surface. Typically derived from equilibrium reconstructions or Langmuir probe measurements, $E_R$ at the wall can range from 10 V/m to several kV/m depending on plasma conditions and wall-bias configurations. The sign of $E_R$ determines whether the radial force on ions accelerates them toward or away from the wall, affecting impurity transport and material erosion rates. For the corresponding vertical component, see [vertical_electric_field_at_wall](name:vertical_electric_field_at_wall).

NAMES.name: temperature_at_wall
NAMES.short: Temperature of the plasma-facing wall surface, defining the thermal boundary condition for plasma-wall interaction physics models.
NAMES.long: The wall temperature $T_w$ characterizes the kinetic energy of the material surface and the adjacent plasma boundary layer. It governs thermal loads on plasma-facing components by balancing incident power flux from ions, electrons, and neutrals against active cooling. Typical steady-state values range from 400 to 1000 K for beryllium or tungsten tiles in present-day devices, rising to 1500 K during transient events. The heat flux density $q$ from the plasma to the wall is related to $T_w$ by the surface energy balance: $q = \sigma \epsilon (T_w^4 - T_{\text{amb}}^4)$, where $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, $\epsilon$ is the surface emissivity, and $T_{\text{amb}}$ is the ambient temperature. This quantity is routinely measured using infrared thermography or thermocouple arrays embedded in tile surfaces.

NAMES.name: total_power_at_cooling_circuit_inlet
NAMES.short: Total thermal power extracted from the plasma-facing wall structures by the active coolant systems.
NAMES.long: The total power at the cooling circuit inlet represents the heat flux removed from the first wall and other plasma-facing components by the coolant, integrated over all active channels. This quantity is key to thermal management and balance-of-plant calculations, directly related to the heat load from the plasma and the efficiency of the cooling system. Measured in the coolant manifolds at the interface between the wall structures and the primary heat transport system, typical values for a fusion power plant can range from tens to hundreds of megawatts. The power is positive when heat flows from the wall into the coolant. Compare with [thermal_power_of_port](name:thermal_power_of_port) which describes power through a specific balance-of-plant component port, and [temperature_at_cooling_circuit_inlet](name:temperature_at_cooling_circuit_inlet) which provides the coolant temperature at the same location.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_nitrogen_fraction
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged ratio of the nitrogen impurity density to the electron density, evaluated over the plasma volume.
NAMES.long: The nitrogen fraction is defined as $\langle n_{\mathrm{N}} / n_e \rangle$, where $n_{\mathrm{N}}$ is the nitrogen impurity density and $n_e$ is the electron density. The angle brackets denote a volume average over the plasma. This quantity is dimensionless and ranges from near zero in a pure plasma to values up to about 0.1 in highly seeded discharges. It is typically evaluated at the time of peak electron density in the discharge to characterize the level of nitrogen seeding used for divertor detachment or radiative cooling.

NAMES.name: bremsstrahlung_power
NAMES.short: Total power radiated via bremsstrahlung emission from the plasma due to free electron scattering off ions.
NAMES.long: Bremsstrahlung power is the total radiated power from free-free electron-ion collisions in the plasma. It scales as $P_{br} \propto Z_{\text{eff}} n_e^2 T_e^{1/2}$, where $Z_{\text{eff}}$ is the effective ion charge, $n_e$ is the electron density, and $T_e$ is the electron temperature. This represents a significant volumetric power loss channel in high-temperature plasmas, particularly in the core. Typical values range from kilowatts to tens of megawatts in fusion-grade tokamaks, depending on density, temperature, and impurity content. The quantity is related to the total radiated power from impurity radiation, [radiated_power_due_to_impurity_radiation](name:radiated_power_due_to_impurity_radiation), and to the volumetric [power_density_due_to_radiation_emission](name:power_density_due_to_radiation_emission). Bremsstrahlung is measured indirectly via soft X-ray diagnostics and bolometry, and is a key input for power balance calculations.

NAMES.name: cold_neutral_initial_temperature
NAMES.short: Initial temperature of the cold neutral population for a specific hydrogen isotope, used as a model input parameter for edge plasma and neutral transport simulations.
NAMES.long:
The initial temperature of the cold neutral population characterizes the thermal energy of neutral atoms or molecules (e.g., H, D, T) entering the plasma edge from the wall or gas puff, before they undergo charge-exchange or ionization. This parameter sets the low-energy boundary condition for neutral transport models and directly influences the calculated penetration depth and the cold neutral density profile. The cold neutral temperature is typically on the order of 0.1–1 eV, corresponding to Franck–Condon dissociation energies or thermal energies of recycled molecules at the wall. It is measured via analysis of Balmer line emission spectra, where Doppler broadening of the narrow central peak yields the cold neutral temperature, while the broader pedestal is associated with the hot neutral population. In simulations, the initial value is often set to 0.5 eV for deuterium and 0.3 eV for helium, reflecting typical Franck–Condon energies. For a physically derived quasi-steady-state value, see [cold_neutral_temperature](name:cold_neutral_temperature); for the hot neutral counterpart see [hot_neutral_initial_temperature](name:hot_neutral_initial_temperature).

This parameter is a model initial condition, not a directly time-resolved measurement, and its value may be adjusted in interpretive or predictive simulations to match observed neutral fractions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when temperature is greater than absolute zero.

NAMES.name: curvature_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Geometric radius of curvature of a diagnostic optical element's surface in the X2 transverse direction, characterizing the surface shape for ray tracing.
NAMES.long: This quantity specifies the radius of curvature of an optical element (lens, mirror, or window) in the X2 transverse direction, as used in diagnostic ray-tracing and optical design. The radius of curvature $R_{X2}$ (in m) describes the spherical or cylindrical curvature of the surface, where $R > 0$ corresponds to a convex surface as seen from the incoming beam direction. The associated focal power scales as $1/R$, with tighter curvature giving stronger focusing. Pair with [major_radius_of_optical_element](name:major_radius_of_optical_element) for the element's spatial position and [area_of_optical_element](name:area_of_optical_element) for surface throughput calculations. Typical optical-component radii range from a few centimeters (high-curvature lenses in collimators) to several meters (weakly curved focusing mirrors) depending on the diagnostic geometry. Measurement relies on interferometric profilometry or coordinate measuring machine (CMM) data acquired during component fabrication.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the center of curvature lies in the direction of the inward surface normal on the X2 axis (convex surface as seen from the incident beam).

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_beam_source_rate
NAMES.short: Rate of 2.45 MeV neutron production from deuterium-deuterium fusion reactions where both reactants are fast ions from neutral beam injection, measured in hertz.
NAMES.long:
This quantity represents the total rate of neutron production from deuterium-deuterium (D-D) fusion reactions between fast deuterium ions originating from neutral beam injectors. The reaction channel is D + D → ³He (0.82 MeV) + n (2.45 MeV). The rate is obtained by integrating the beam-beam fusion reactivity over the overlapping fast ion distribution functions, taking into account the beam energy, density, and geometry of the injection system.

The typical value range for an ITER-like device with 1–1.5 MW of beam power is 10¹⁴–10¹⁶ neutrons per second. The rate is sensitive to beam energy (typically 50–500 keV), the overlap between different beam sources, and the residual thermal deuterium background.

\[
R_{\text{DD,beam-beam}} = \iint n_1(\mathbf{r}) n_2(\mathbf{r}) \langle \sigma v \rangle_{\text{DD}} \, d^3\mathbf{r}
\]

where \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) are the densities of fast deuterium ions from two beam sources (or the same beam population if self-reactive), and \(\langle \sigma v \rangle_{\text{DD}}\) is the D-D fusion reactivity averaged over the fast ion velocity distributions.

Measurement is performed with neutron flux monitors and activation samples calibrated for 2.45 MeV neutrons. Time resolution is typically 1–10 ms.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the computed neutron emission rate from the beam-beam reaction is directed outward from the plasma.

NAMES.name: diagnostic_aperture_radius
NAMES.short: Geometric radius of the circular entrance pupil that limits the photon collection solid angle for an X-ray crystal spectrometer channel.
NAMES.long:
The diagnostic aperture radius $r_a$ defines the circular entrance pupil of an X-ray crystal spectrometer channel. For a geometry type indicating a circular aperture, this radius determines the geometric acceptance area $A = \pi r_a^2$, which together with the solid angle of the viewed plasma volume sets the photon collection efficiency. Typical values range from 1 to 50 mm, chosen to balance signal throughput against desired spatial localization. The companion quantity [area_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:area_of_diagnostic_aperture) is derived directly from this radius. When rectangular collimation is used instead, the equivalent parameter is captured by [width](name:width).

Cr K-alpha He-li-like spectroscopy routinely uses apertures of 5–20 mm radius to achieve count rates above 100 kHz while maintaining 1–2 cm spatial resolution along the line of sight.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured outward from the aperture center, making it an inherently non-negative geometric length.

NAMES.name: etendue_of_spectrometer
NAMES.short: Geometric extent of the spectrometer optical system, defined as the product of the limiting aperture area and the solid angle of the accepted radiation.
NAMES.long: The etendue (geometric throughput, $G = A \Omega$) of a UV spectrometer characterizes the light-collection efficiency by combining the effective aperture area $A$ (in m$^2$) with the solid angle $\Omega$ (in sr) subtended by the optical system. It is an invariant quantity in an ideal lossless optical chain and determines the maximum signal flux incident on the detector. Typical values range from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-4}$ m$^2\cdot$sr for UV spectrometers on fusion diagnostics, depending on the f-number and entrance slit geometry. The etendue is related to the [area_of_optical_element](name:area_of_optical_element) and the [radius_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture) of individual components, which together define the overall throughput of the imaging system.

NAMES.name: hot_neutral_initial_temperature
NAMES.short: Temperature of the hot neutral population for a specific hydrogen isotope at the start of the observation or simulation.
NAMES.long:
The initial temperature of the hot neutral population characterizes the kinetic energy of neutral atoms that have undergone charge-exchange reactions with energetic ions. This quantity is derived from the Doppler broadening of neutral emission lines measured by visible spectroscopy, providing a boundary condition for neutral particle transport models. For typical tokamak edge conditions, hot neutral temperatures range from 100 to 1000 eV, depending on the local ion temperature and the energy distribution of the parent ions. The initial temperature is distinct from the steady-state hot neutral temperature; together with [cold_neutral_initial_temperature](name:cold_neutral_initial_temperature) it provides a complete initial condition for the neutral energy distribution in multispecies simulations.

See also [hot_neutral_temperature](name:hot_neutral_temperature) for the instantaneous temperature during the observation period.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the population temperature is above absolute zero.

NAMES.name: hot_neutral_temperature
NAMES.short: Maxwellian temperature of the hot neutral atom population, typically arising from charge-exchange reactions, as inferred from Doppler broadening in polarization spectroscopy.
NAMES.long: The hot neutral temperature $T_n$ quantifies the thermal energy of the suprathermal neutral population produced primarily via charge-exchange reactions between plasma ions and cold neutrals. These hot neutrals have energies comparable to the background ion temperature and are measurable through the Doppler broadening of spectral lines in polarization spectroscopy, often using a visible spectrometer. Typical values range from tens of eV in the edge to several keV in the core plasma. The temperature is extracted from a fit to the broadened line shape, assuming a Maxwellian velocity distribution for the hot neutral component. See also [cold_neutral_temperature](name:cold_neutral_temperature) for the thermal population and [hot_neutral_initial_temperature](name:hot_neutral_initial_temperature) for isotope-specific measurements.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the spectral line width increases, corresponding to higher neutral kinetic energy.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Major radius (R) coordinate of the center point of a diagnostic optical element, such as a lens or mirror, in the IMAS cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The major radius $R$ coordinates the spatial position of the optical element's geometric center in the machine's toroidal plane. This coordinate is essential for ray-tracing models that compute the diagnostic line of sight and for mapping the detector field of view onto the plasma volume. Typical values range from 0.5–5.0 m depending on the tokamak size, with in-vessel elements located closer to the plasma (e.g., $R=1.5$ m for a first-wall mirror on a medium-size device) and ex-vessel elements further out (e.g., $R=2.5$ m for a focusing lens). The position is routinely measured during diagnostic alignment and may be refined by in-situ calibration using backlit targets. This quantity is related to the major radius of the diagnostic aperture via [major_radius_of_diagnostic_antenna](name:major_radius_of_diagnostic_antenna), which defines the line-of-sight endpoint for the same optical chain.

For multi-element optics, the element properties are further described by [length_of_optical_element](name:length_of_optical_element) (thickness along the optical axis) and [area_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:area_of_diagnostic_aperture) (cross-sectional area defining the etendue).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the center point lies at a major radius value greater than that of the machine symmetry axis ($R>0$).

NAMES.name: radius_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: Geometric radius of the circular filter window aperture used in a hard X-ray diagnostic channel.
NAMES.long:
The filter window radius defines the physical size of the circular aperture through which hard X-ray radiation passes before reaching the detector. For a circular window geometry, the radius $r_w$ determines the window area $A_w = \pi r_w^2$, which directly affects the photon throughput and the field of view of the diagnostic channel. Typical values range from 1–50 mm depending on the diagnostic design and the energy range of the hard X-ray measurement.

The radius is a purely geometric parameter used together with the window thickness and material properties to model the transmission and attenuation of hard X-ray photons. This quantity is related to [area_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:area_of_diagnostic_aperture) for the corresponding aperture component.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radius is measured outward from the center of the circular aperture.

NAMES.name: temperature_of_camera
NAMES.short: Apparent temperature of a surface observed by a camera, derived from calibrated digital counts via Planck's law inversion under an assumed emissivity.
NAMES.long:
The apparent temperature $T_{\mathrm{app}}$ is obtained by inverting the integrated Planck law:

$$
L(\lambda_1,\lambda_2; T_{\mathrm{app}}) = \int_{\lambda_1}^{\lambda_2} \frac{2hc^2}{\lambda^5}\,\frac{1}{\exp\left(\frac{hc}{\lambda k_B T_{\mathrm{app}}}\right)-1}\,d\lambda
$$

where $L$ is the measured radiance integrated over the camera's spectral bandpass $[\lambda_1,\lambda_2]$, $h$ is Planck's constant, $c$ the speed of light, and $k_B$ Boltzmann's constant. The inversion assumes a uniform surface emissivity $\varepsilon$ (usually set to 1.0 for blackbody or a user-provided value). The resulting $T_{\mathrm{app}}$ equals the true thermodynamic temperature only when $\varepsilon = 1$ and the radiation originates from a single surface; in practice, corrections for varying emissivity, reflected background, and transmission losses are required. Typical values in fusion devices range from 200 K (cool vessel walls) to over 1500 K (divertor strike points during heat loads).

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_camera
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle coordinate of the camera center in the cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long: The toroidal angle $\phi_{\text{cam}}$ of the camera center defines the camera position and is measured from a reference direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ coordinate system. This angle locates the camera in the toroidal direction and is essential for accurate tomographic reconstruction and line-of-sight geometry registration. Typical values range from 0 to $2\pi$ radians. This quantity is analogous to [toroidal_angle_of_reflectometer_antenna](name:toroidal_angle_of_reflectometer_antenna) and complements the vertical coordinate [vertical_coordinate_of_camera](name:vertical_coordinate_of_camera).
NAMES.sign: Positive when increasing in the counter-clockwise direction viewed from above (along $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: tritium_tritium_beam_source_rate
NAMES.short: Instantaneous rate of neutron production from fusion reactions where both reactants are fast tritium ions from neutral beam injection. This rate is always non-negative, including zero when no neutrons are produced.
NAMES.long: The tritium–tritium (TT) beam–beam source rate quantifies the instantaneous number of neutrons produced per second in reactions where two fast tritium ions, both originating from neutral beam injection, undergo fusion. The amplitude is determined by the reaction cross-section, the fast tritium density, and the relative velocity distribution of the interacting beam populations. Typical values in high-power beam-heated plasmas range from zero up to several $10^{16}$ Hz, depending on the beam power, plasma density, and tritium fraction. The rate is measured directly via neutron detectors or inferred from beam parameters and is essential for characterizing fusion performance and fast-ion confinement.
NAMES.sign: Positive when neutrons are produced.

NAMES.name: upper_wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short: Upper bound of the wavelength transmission band of an optical filter in a visible bremsstrahlung diagnostic channel. This defines the longest wavelength that the filter transmits, determining the spectral range for the channel.
NAMES.long:
For an optical filter in a visible bremsstrahlung diagnostic channel, this quantity specifies the upper boundary of the wavelength passband. Together with the lower wavelength bound, it defines the spectral interval over which the channel measures bremsstrahlung emission from the plasma. The transmitted power through the filter is proportional to the integral of the plasma emissivity over this wavelength range.

Typical values for visible bremsstrahlung filters range from 400 nm to 700 nm, depending on diagnostic design and the need to avoid intense line emission.

Related quantities include the lower bound of the filter wavelength range and the visible bremsstrahlung channel gain.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the filter passband extends to longer wavelengths, with the upper bound always being greater than the lower bound.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) coordinate of the geometric center of an optical element (lens, mirror, or filter) within a spectrometer diagnostic channel.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $z_{\rm el}$ defines the height of the optical element center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame of the tokamak. This geometric parameter is essential for ray-tracing models that compute the line of sight and the collection efficiency of the spectrometer system. Typical values range from $-2$ m to $+2$ m depending on the port location. This quantity is paired with the major radius coordinate $[R_{\rm el}](name:major_radius_of_optical_element)$ to fully locate the element in the poloidal plane.

The optical element may be a lens, mirror, grating, or filter window. The coordinate is referenced to the machine symmetry axis and the tokamak midplane, consistent with the geometry conventions used for other diagnostic components such as $[vertical\_coordinate\_of\_camera](name:vertical_coordinate_of_camera)$ and $[vertical\_coordinate\_of\_diagnostic\_aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture)$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the element center is above the midplane ($Z=0$).

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Spectral wavelength values at which the material optical properties (refractive index, extinction coefficient, transmission coefficient) of an optical element are tabulated.
NAMES.long:
The wavelength array provides the spectral abscissa for material properties of an optical element, such as the refractive index, extinction coefficient, or transmission coefficient, used in modeling the optical response of diagnostic components. These properties are wavelength-dependent and are typically measured or tabulated from material databases, covering the relevant spectral range of the diagnostic (e.g., 0.2–20 µm for IR cameras). The array defines the discrete sampling points at which these properties are known, enabling interpolation for accurate ray-tracing or radiometric calculations. For a given optical element, the values of [refractive_index_of_optical_element](name:refractive_index_of_optical_element) are provided at each corresponding wavelength. This quantity must be strictly increasing in value.

Typical wavelength ranges span the ultraviolet to infrared (0.1–50 µm) depending on the diagnostic system. The number of sampling points is determined by the required spectral resolution for the material model. The associated geometric scale can be compared to the [length_of_optical_element](name:length_of_optical_element) and [area_of_optical_element](name:area_of_optical_element) for full system characterization.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wavelength values are ordered from shortest to longest.

NAMES.name: nuclear_power_of_breeder_blanket
NAMES.short: Total nuclear heating power deposited in the entire breeding blanket assembly by neutron and gamma radiation from the fusion plasma.
NAMES.long: This quantity represents the integral power deposited by neutron and gamma interactions across all components of the breeding blanket, including breeder zones, structural materials, and coolant channels. The nuclear heating arises primarily from neutron elastic and inelastic scattering, neutron capture reactions, and gamma-ray energy deposition, contributing directly to the blanket thermal power budget. Typical values for a DEMO-class reactor range from several hundred megawatts to over a gigawatt, depending on fusion power, blanket material composition, and neutron multiplication. This power load is a key input to thermal-hydraulic design and tritium breeding ratio calculations. For layer-specific partitioning, see [nuclear_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer](name:nuclear_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer); for the shield component, see [nuclear_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield](name:nuclear_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield). The total is distinct from the [neutron_flux_at_wall](name:neutron_flux_at_wall), which describes the incident neutron current rather than the deposited power.

NAMES.name: nuclear_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer
NAMES.short: Total nuclear heating power deposited in a breeding blanket layer from neutron and gamma interactions.
NAMES.long: The nuclear power $P_{\text{nuc}}$ represents the total thermal power deposited within a specific layer of a breeding blanket module through neutron and gamma-ray energy deposition. This heating arises from nuclear reactions, including neutron scattering and capture, as well as gamma-ray absorption, and is a critical parameter for assessing the thermal load on the blanket layer. The power is typically computed from coupled neutronics and thermal-hydraulic simulations using Monte Carlo transport codes with nuclear cross-section libraries; deposited energy tallies provide the volumetric heating rate, which is integrated over the layer volume to obtain $P_{\text{nuc}}$. For DEMO-class breeder blanket designs, layer power loads range from 10 to 200 MW, depending on the layer's proximity to the plasma and neutron flux attenuation through the blanket structure. The layer nuclear power is closely related to [nuclear_power_of_breeder_blanket](name:nuclear_power_of_breeder_blanket), which sums the heating across all layers and the blanket shield, and [nuclear_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield](name:nuclear_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield), which captures the heating in the shield region. Local heating intensity is described by [nuclear_power_density_at_midplane](name:nuclear_power_density_at_midplane).

NAMES.name: nuclear_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield
NAMES.short: Total nuclear heating power deposited by neutrons and gamma rays in the neutron shield structures of the breeding blanket.
NAMES.long: This quantity represents the integrated power from nuclear reactions — primarily neutron and gamma interactions — that is deposited as heat within the shield components surrounding the breeder blanket. The shield structures absorb high-energy neutrons escaping the breeder zone, converting their kinetic energy into thermal energy via elastic and inelastic scattering, capture reactions, and subsequent gamma-ray absorption. This heating load must be managed by the shield cooling system to maintain structural integrity and is a key input for thermal-hydraulic design of the blanket shield. Typical values for a fusion power plant range from tens to hundreds of megawatts depending on the neutron wall loading and shield material composition. The total shield power complements the nuclear heating in the breeder modules, which is tracked by [nuclear_power_density_at_midplane](name:nuclear_power_density_at_midplane) and is coupled to the incident neutron flux quantified by [neutron_flux_at_wall](name:neutron_flux_at_wall).

NAMES.name: pressure_at_cooling_circuit_inlet
NAMES.short: Static pressure of the coolant at the inlet of a breeding blanket module cooling circuit. This pressure determines the hydraulic driving force for coolant flow through the blanket and affects the pumping power requirements.
NAMES.long:
The coolant static pressure at the blanket module cooling circuit inlet sets the hydraulic boundary condition for the primary heat transport system. In fusion breeding blankets, the coolant (typically pressurized water, helium, or liquid metal) is pumped through the module to extract nuclear heating and surface heat flux, with the inlet pressure designed to maintain single-phase flow or suppress bulk boiling under nominal operating conditions. Typical inlet pressures range from 15–25 MPa for pressurized-water-cooled lithium–lead (WCLL) blankets and 2–10 MPa for helium-cooled ceramic breeder (HCPB) concepts. This quantity is closely tied to `temperature_at_cooling_circuit_inlet` to define the coolant thermodynamic state, and together with `total_power_at_cooling_circuit_inlet` it characterizes the module energy balance and pumping requirements.

The inlet pressure is also related to `pressure_of_port` in the balance-of-plant context, where it interfaces with the primary coolant loop piping and pump discharge conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the coolant static pressure is greater than the local saturation pressure, ensuring subcooled liquid conditions at the module entrance.

NAMES.name: resistance_of_vacuum_vessel
NAMES.short: Ohmic electrical resistance of a block element in the discretized vacuum vessel wall, governing eddy current dissipation during transient events.
NAMES.long: The electrical resistance $R$ of a discrete vacuum vessel wall element determines the resistive voltage drop $V = IR$ and ohmic power dissipation $P = I^2R$ when eddy currents are induced during plasma disruptions or fast coil current changes. In the 2D wall description, the vessel wall is discretized into toroidally axisymmetric conducting elements, each characterized by its resistance to toroidal current flow. Typical values for ITER-grade vacuum vessel segments are in the micro-ohm to milliohm range, depending on element geometry and the resistivity of the structural material (e.g., stainless steel at operating temperature). Accurate resistance values are essential for electromagnetic transient simulations that predict induced currents, electromagnetic forces, and structural heating. See also [resistivity_of_vacuum_vessel](name:resistivity_of_vacuum_vessel) for the material property that, combined with element geometry, yields this resistance, and [resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil) for a related coil-system quantity.

NAMES.name: volume_of_breeder_blanket
NAMES.short: Total volume occupied by the liquid lead-lithium (PbLi) breeder material within the breeding blanket modules.
NAMES.long: The volume of the breeder blanket containing liquid lead-lithium (PbLi) determines the tritium breeding inventory and the total mass of the liquid breeder material. For a given neutron fluence, the tritium breeding rate scales with this volume, assuming the lithium enrichment and neutron multiplication are set. The PbLi volume is a key engineering parameter that couples with the [neutron_flux_at_wall](name:neutron_flux_at_wall) and the material's lithium density to define the tritium production capacity of the blanket. In fusion reactor designs, typical PbLi volumes per module range from $0.1$ to $10\,\text{m}^3$, depending on the blanket radial build and the coverage of the first wall. This volume is derived from the CAD geometry of the breeder zone, excluding structural steel, cooling channels, and other internal components.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the breeder blanket physical geometry occupies non-zero volume in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: coulomb_logarithm
NAMES.short: Dimensionless factor quantifying the effectiveness of Coulomb collisions in a plasma, defined as the natural logarithm of the ratio of the Debye length to the impact parameter for 90-degree deflection. It characterizes the relative importance of small-angle versus large-angle scattering events.
NAMES.long: The Coulomb logarithm $\ln \Lambda$ is a fundamental parameter in plasma physics that determines the effectiveness of small-angle Coulomb collisions relative to large-angle scattering. It is defined as $\ln \Lambda = \ln\left(\frac{b_{\max}}{b_{\min}}\right)$, where $b_{\max} \approx \lambda_D$ is the Debye length (maximum impact parameter for collective shielding, in meters) and $b_{\min}$ is the characteristic impact parameter for 90-degree deflection (in meters). For thermal electrons and ions, $b_{\min} \approx \frac{Z e^2}{k_B T}$, where $Z$ is the charge number, $e$ is the elementary charge, $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant, and $T$ is the temperature (in keV). In fusion plasmas, $\ln \Lambda$ typically ranges from 10 to 20, decreasing with higher density and temperature. The Coulomb logarithm appears in expressions for the Spitzer resistivity, electron-ion energy equilibration rate, and collision frequencies Boosting the resistive current ramp-up rate and the electron-ion temperature equilibration timescale during plasma initiation. The value is always positive for classical plasmas where $\lambda_D \gg b_{\min}$.

NAMES.name: effective_charge
NAMES.short: Density-weighted mean ionic charge state of the plasma, quantifying the impurity content relative to the electron density.
NAMES.long:
The effective ionic charge $Z_{\text{eff}}$ is defined as $Z_{\text{eff}} = \sum_i n_i Z_i^2 / n_e$, where $n_i$ is the density of ion species $i$ with charge $Z_i$ and $n_e$ is the electron density. It is a key metric for plasma purity, as higher $Z_{\text{eff}}$ indicates increased impurity content, which enhances radiative power losses and dilutes the fuel. A value of $Z_{\text{eff}} = 1$ corresponds to a pure hydrogenic plasma. In tokamak scrape-off layers and divertor regions, $Z_{\text{eff}}$ is typically elevated due to erosion of plasma-facing components. This quantity is routinely inferred from visible bremsstrahlung measurements and from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy. It is related to the [ion_charge](name:ion_charge) of each species and to the [electron_density](name:electron_density) via the quasi-neutrality condition.

Typical values in fusion plasmas range from 1.0 to 3.0 in the core, and can exceed 5.0 in the divertor region during detached conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when plasma impurity content produces a net positive charge balance.

NAMES.name: electron_collisionality
NAMES.short: Collision frequency of electrons normalized to the bounce frequency, characterizing the neoclassical transport regime.
NAMES.long:
Electron collisionality, denoted $
u^*_e$, is defined as the ratio of the effective electron collision frequency $
u_e$ to the bounce frequency $\omega_b$ of trapped particles on a given flux surface: $
u^*_e = 
u_e / \omega_b$. This dimensionless parameter distinguishes the three neoclassical transport regimes: the banana regime ($
u^*_e \ll 1$), the plateau regime ($
u^*_e \sim 1$), and the Pfirsch-Schlüter regime ($
u^*_e \gg 1$). It is computed from the electron density and temperature profiles, and is essential for predicting confinement and bootstrap current fractions in tokamak and stellarator plasmas. Typical core values range from $10^{-2}$ to $10$, depending on density and temperature. See also [normalized_electron_collisionality](name:normalized_electron_collisionality) for an alternative normalization convention.

In the banana regime, the collisionless trapped-particle orbits dominate heat and particle transport, while in the plateau and Pfirsch-Schlüter regimes, the transport is increasingly collisional and local. The quantity is closely related to [coulomb_logarithm](name:coulomb_logarithm), which sets the magnitude of the collision frequency, and to [effective_charge](name:effective_charge), which influences the collision frequency through impurity content.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the collision frequency exceeds the bounce frequency.

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Local number density of free electrons at the internal transport barrier location in the confined plasma.
NAMES.long:
The electron number density $n_e$ at the internal transport barrier (ITB) location defines the local electron particle density $n_e(\rho_{\mathrm{ITB}})$ in particles per cubic meter. This quantity is a key input for transport analysis, since the ITB is a region of strongly reduced anomalous transport that modifies the density and temperature profiles. Typical core ITB densities range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in diverted tokamak plasmas, depending on the fueling and heating conditions. The density is routinely measured by Thomson scattering, microwave reflectometry, or interferometry, and is used together with the electron temperature to evaluate the local pressure gradient, a driver for ITB formation. The related quantity [electron_density](name:electron_density) gives the full radial profile, while [iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:iron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [helium_3_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:helium_3_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) provide comparative impurity densities at the same location.

This single-value summary provides a direct measure of the ITB plasma conditions for global confinement analysis.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electron particle number increases, corresponding to higher local charge carrier concentration.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Number density of singly ionized helium-3 (³He⁺) particles at the location of the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long: The helium-3 ion density $n_{^3\text{He}^+}$ at the internal transport barrier (ITB) quantifies the concentration of this minority fusion-born or externally injected species at the radial position where sheared plasma rotation or reversed magnetic shear suppresses turbulent transport, forming a transport barrier. ITBs are characterized by steep density and temperature gradients, so the local helium-3 density is both a tracer of barrier confinement quality and a source for fusion reactions in advanced scenarios. Measured by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) or inferred from equilibrium reconstruction, with typical values ranging from $10^{16}$ to $10^{19}\,\text{m}^{-3}$ in the barrier region of medium- to large-size tokamaks. Related quantities include the helium-3 density profiles at other internal locations such as [helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis) and [helium_3_density_at_separatrix](name:helium_3_density_at_separatrix), as well as the local barrier properties captured by [magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the helium-3 density at the ITB location is non-zero. Density is a non-negative scalar; negative values are unphysical and would indicate a measurement error or inversion artifact.

NAMES.name: helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Number density of helium-3 ions at the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long: The number density of singly-ionized helium-3 ions at the magnetic axis.  Helium-3 is a minority ion species commonly introduced through neutral beam injection or ion cyclotron resonance heating; its density at the axis is a key input for fusion power calculations and fast-ion confinement studies.  Density values are always non-negative and are typically in the range $10^{16}$ to $10^{20}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, depending on fueling and transport conditions.  In tokamaks, the on-axis density of helium-3 is often inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or from neutral particle analyzer measurements, and may be compared with the line-averaged or volume-averaged density to assess profile peaking.

NAMES.name: ion_atomic_number
NAMES.short: Nuclear charge number (proton number) identifying a specific ion element in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The ion atomic number $Z$ identifies the element of an ion species by its nuclear charge (number of protons). In magnetically confined fusion plasmas, $Z$ distinguishes fuel species (deuterium $Z=1$, helium $Z=2$) from impurity species (carbon $Z=6$, tungsten $Z=74$). This quantity is an input parameter for transport modeling and atomic physics calculations, used together with the ion density to compute radiative losses and effective charge. For a given ion species, $Z$ is independent of the ionization state and remains fixed across the plasma domain. Related quantities include `[ion_density](name:ion_density)` for the species density and `[ion_state_average_charge](name:ion_state_average_charge)` for the mean charge state.

In simulations, $Z$ is typically specified at the domain boundary as part of the species composition and is constant in time. The range of $Z$ values encountered spans $Z=1$ (hydrogen isotopes) to $Z=74$ (tungsten) in present-day tokamaks, and up to $Z=92$ (uranium) in inertial confinement experiments.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion species has a positive nuclear charge, which always holds for physical plasma elements.

NAMES.name: ion_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.short: Particle diffusion coefficient for thermal ions, governing radial transport due to collisional and turbulent processes in the confined plasma.
NAMES.long:
The ion diffusion coefficient $D_i$ parameterizes the radial particle flux of thermal ions in the neoclassical and anomalous transport equations, relating the flux density to the ion density gradient via $
Gamma_i = -D_i \nabla n_i$. This coefficient captures both collisional (neoclassical) transport and turbulent (anomalous) contributions, with typical values ranging from $10^{-2}\,\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ in the core to $10^{-1}\,\text{m}^2/\text{s}$ near the edge of H-mode tokamak plasmas. The diffusion coefficient is inferred from transport analysis codes that solve the continuity equation for each ion species, using measured density profiles and sources. This scalar quantity differs from the [ion momentum diffusion coefficient](name:poloidal_ion_momentum_diffusion_coefficient) which governs toroidal rotation damping, and from the [neutral state energy diffusion coefficient](name:neutral_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient) for neutral species. The sign convention ensures that particle transport is directed down the density gradient (outward) for a positive ion density gradient minus an inward pinch term.

The diffusion coefficient is independent of the specific ion charge state and applies to the bulk ion population, distinct from the enhanced diffusivity at a neoclassical tearing mode [center](name:diffusion_coefficient_at_neoclassical_tearing_mode_center).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the particle flux is directed radially outward (down the density gradient for a monotonically decreasing density profile).

NAMES.name: ion_mass
NAMES.short: Mass of an ion species, including molecular ions, expressed in unified atomic mass units (u) for use in transport and atomic physics calculations.
NAMES.long: The mass of an ion species quantifies the inertial and collisional properties of charged particles in the plasma, directly affecting gyroradius, cyclotron frequency, and energy exchange rates. In fusion plasmas, this mass can range from 1 u for protons to over 200 u for high-Z impurities like tungsten, and it is a key input for calculating the Coulomb logarithm and ion thermal velocity. For molecular ions, the mass is the sum of the constituent atomic masses, distinguished from the per-nucleon value given by [ion_atomic_mass](name:ion_atomic_mass). The mass also determines the isotope-dependent drift velocities and is essential for modeling impurity transport and neutral beam injection. See also [neutral_mass](name:neutral_mass) for neutral species and [ion_count](name:ion_count) for the number of atoms per molecular ion.

NAMES.name: iron_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Number density of iron impurity ions located at the magnetic axis, the innermost flux surface of the confined plasma.
NAMES.long:
The iron density at the magnetic axis $n_\text{Fe}(R_\text{axis})$ quantifies the concentration of iron ions sourced from plasma-facing component erosion that have accumulated at the center of the plasma. Iron is a high-Z impurity that can radiatively cool the core, so this density is a critical input to transport modeling and impurity-seeding studies. The quantity is routinely inferred by combining spectroscopic measurements (e.g., X-ray line emission from highly ionized charge states) with collisional-radiative modeling to recover the total iron density from individual charge-state densities. Core values in present-day tokamaks range from $10^{14}\,\text{m}^{-3}$ for low-erosion conditions up to $10^{18}\,\text{m}^{-3}$ during deliberate seeding or transient events. This quantity is the central-position specialization of the general iron density field; see [iron_density_at_separatrix](name:iron_density_at_separatrix) for the edge value and [volume_averaged_iron_density](name:volume_averaged_iron_density) for the global core average.

Typical inboard-outboard impurity accumulation patterns make the magnetic axis value a key benchmark for neoclassical transport codes and for validating impurity-peaking models against [ion_temperature_at_magnetic_axis](name:ion_temperature_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the number of iron ions per unit volume is defined.

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Dimensionless measure of the radial variation of the safety factor, defined as the fractional change of q per unit normalized toroidal flux radius, evaluated at the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The magnetic shear $s$ is a measure of the radial variation of the safety factor $q$, defined as

$$ s = \frac{\rho_\mathrm{tor}}{q} \frac{dq}{d\rho_\mathrm{tor}} $$

where $\rho_\mathrm{tor}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius. At the internal transport barrier (ITB), $s$ characterizes the steepness of the radial gradient of the magnetic field line pitch and is closely linked to the formation and stability of the barrier.

Typical values at an ITB are in the range $s \approx 0$ to $2$, often near zero at the barrier center in reversed-shear scenarios. Values far from zero indicate strong shear and are associated with reduced turbulent transport.

In practice, $s$ is derived from equilibrium reconstructions, for example using magnetics and MSE data. The sign of $s$ follows the sign of $dq/d\rho_\mathrm{tor}$: positive $s$ indicates that $q$ increases with radius (normal magnetic shear), while negative $s$ indicates reversed shear (decreasing $q$ with radius).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $dq/d\rho_\mathrm{tor} > 0$ (normal shear).

NAMES.name: minimum_charge_of_ion_state
NAMES.short: Minimum ionization charge state (Z_min) of a bundled ion charge-state group used in GGD plasma transport models, with zero indicating a neutral species.
NAMES.long:
The minimum charge state $Z_{\min}$ defines the lower bound of the charge-state bundle for a given ion species in multi-fluid transport simulations. The bundle groups multiple ionization states (e.g., $Z_{\min}$ to $Z_{\max}$) into a single fluid species to reduce computational cost while preserving charge balance in reaction rates and transport coefficients. For a neutral species, $Z_{\min} = 0$; for a single charge-state representation, $Z_{\min} = Z_{\max}$.

The charge-state bundle $[Z_{\min}, Z_{\max}]$ is paired with the average charge to compute effective atomic data from the Atomic and Molecular Numerical Database (AMNS).

Typical values range from $Z_{\min} = 0$ (e.g., neutral deuterium) to $Z_{\min} = 6$ (e.g., fully stripped carbon). See also [ion_state_average_charge](name:ion_state_average_charge) for the mean charge within the bundle and [ion_state_maximum_charge](name:ion_state_maximum_charge) for the upper bound.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the charge state is positive; zero for neutral species.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the radial location of the internal transport barrier (ITB).
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the internal transport barrier is defined as
$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor, norm}}^{(\text{ITB})} \equiv \frac{\Phi(R_{\text{ITB}}, Z_{\text{ITB}})}{\Phi_{\text{sep}}},
$$
where $\Phi$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by a flux surface, $\Phi_{\text{sep}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary (separatrix or last closed flux surface), and $(R_{\text{ITB}}, Z_{\text{ITB}})$ denotes the radial location of the ITB. The coordinate $\rho_{\mathrm{tor, norm}}$ is dimensionless and ranges from $0$ at the magnetic axis to $1$ at the plasma boundary. Typical values for an ITB are in the range $0.0$ to $0.6$ (core region).

The ITB is a region of steep gradient in the radial electric field and ion temperature, often associated with improved confinement. The position is determined from experimental profiles (e.g., $T_i$, $E_r$) or from transport models.

Related quantities: The absolute toroidal magnetic flux at the ITB location is obtained by multiplying $\rho_{\mathrm{tor, norm}}^{(\text{ITB})}$ by the toroidal magnetic flux at the separatrix.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flux surface is inside the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: parallel_electron_velocity
NAMES.short: Projection of the bulk electron fluid velocity vector onto the direction parallel to the local magnetic field line.
NAMES.long: The parallel electron velocity $v_{\parallel e} = \mathbf{v}_e \cdot \hat{b}$ is the field-aligned component of the electron fluid flow, where $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/B$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field. This component dominates the toroidal current drive in Ohm's law ($E_\parallel = \eta j_\parallel + \text{non-inductive sources}$) and is critical for calculating the parallel electric field. Typical core values in H-mode tokamaks range from $\sim 10^3$ to $10^5$ m/s, depending on rotation and current drive; the poloidal component $\mathbf{v}_e \cdot \hat{\theta}$ governs cross-field transport and is tracked by [poloidal_electron_velocity](name:poloidal_electron_velocity). Diagnostics include charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy (for impurity ion proxies) and inference from equilibrium reconstruction of the radial electric field via force balance. The associated energy flow is described by [parallel_electron_energy_flux](name:parallel_electron_energy_flux).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron fluid velocity points in the direction of increasing distance along the magnetic field line (toward the positive toroidal direction for a field line with positive $q$).

NAMES.name: parallel_fast_electron_pressure
NAMES.short: Component of the anisotropic fast electron pressure tensor oriented parallel to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long: The parallel fast electron pressure $p_{\parallel,f} = m_e \int v_{\parallel}^2 f_f(v)\,d^3v$ quantifies the kinetic stress from suprathermal electrons with velocities aligned with the magnetic field, where $m_e$ is the electron mass, $v_{\parallel}$ is the velocity component along the field, and $f_f(v)$ is the fast electron distribution function. This component is part of the anisotropic pressure tensor described by $[\text{fast\_electron\_pressure}](name:fast_electron_pressure)$ and complements the [perpendicular fast electron pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_electron_pressure). It is essential for modeling fast electron confinement, current drive efficiency, and magnetohydrodynamic stability, with typical values ranging from 0.1 to 10 kPa in the core of high-power auxiliary-heated plasmas. The parallel pressure is inferred from measurements such as hard X-ray bremsstrahlung spectra or electron cyclotron emission, combined with Fokker-Planck modeling of the suprathermal distribution.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the kinetic stress from suprathermal electrons aligned with the local magnetic field is compressive.

NAMES.name: parallel_fast_neutral_pressure
NAMES.short: Scalar projection of the fast neutral pressure tensor onto the direction parallel to the local magnetic field line, representing the component of kinetic stress carried by non-thermal neutral particles along the magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The parallel fast neutral pressure is the component of the neutral pressure tensor in the direction parallel to the local magnetic field line. It is defined as $p_{\parallel,n} = \int m_n v_{\parallel}^2 f_n(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}) \, d^3v$, where $m_n$ is the neutral mass, $v_{\parallel}$ is the velocity component along the magnetic field, and $f_n$ is the fast neutral velocity distribution function. This quantity is typically on the order of 0.1–10 Pa in the edge and scrape-off layer of magnetically confined plasmas, depending on neutral density and temperature. It is a key input for parallel momentum balance equations involving neutral particles, often appearing alongside the parallel fast neutral velocity in transport models. The perpendicular counterpart is given by `perpendicular_fast_neutral_pressure`.

Typical values are positive and range from sub-Pa levels in the plasma core to a few Pa near the first wall. The pressure is always non-negative for any physically realizable distribution of fast neutrals.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_state_velocity
NAMES.short: Projection of the ExB drift velocity of ions in a given charge state onto the direction parallel to the local magnetic field line.
NAMES.long: The parallel ion state velocity $v_{\parallel,Z}$ is the component of the fluid velocity $\boldsymbol{v}_Z$ of ions in charge state $Z$ resolved along the equilibrium magnetic field direction. It determines the convective transport of ions and their associated momentum, energy, and particle flux along field lines in the plasma core and edge. Measured via charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) by analyzing the Doppler shift of impurity line emission resolved by charge state; typical values range from $10^3$ to $10^5$ m/s depending on plasma rotation and radial location. The full velocity vector is given by the parent quantity [ion_state_velocity](name:ion_state_velocity), which includes the poloidal component [poloidal_ion_state_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_state_velocity). For charge-state-averaged parallel flow, see [parallel_ion_velocity](name:parallel_ion_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flow is in the direction of the equilibrium magnetic field $\boldsymbol{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_velocity
NAMES.short: Projection of the bulk ion fluid velocity vector along the local magnetic field direction.
NAMES.long: The parallel ion velocity $v_{\parallel,i} = \mathbf{v}_i \cdot \hat{b}$ quantifies the field-aligned flow of the bulk main ion species, averaged over all charge states. In tokamaks, the parallel ion flow is driven by the Pfirsch–Schlüter current, neoclassical viscosity, and momentum injection from neutral beams; it reaches values of 10–200 km/s in the core and can reverse sign near the separatrix. The parallel velocity is measured by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) or directly from the Doppler shift of impurity emission lines. The full velocity vector is given by [ion_velocity](name:ion_velocity), with the poloidal component described by [poloidal_ion_velocity](name:poloidal_ion_velocity). A charge-state-resolved counterpart is [parallel_ion_state_velocity](name:parallel_ion_state_velocity), while the electron parallel flow is captured by [parallel_electron_velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the velocity aligns with the direction of the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ in the toroidal direction (increasing toroidal angle $\phi$).

NAMES.name: parallel_neutral_state_velocity
NAMES.short: Projection of the E×B drift velocity of neutral particles in a given charge state onto the direction parallel to the local magnetic field line.
NAMES.long: The parallel component of the E×B drift velocity for neutrals in a specific charge state is defined as $v_{\parallel, \mathrm{E}\times\mathrm{B}} = (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{b} / B^2$, where $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/B$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field. This quantity captures the field-aligned flow of charge-state-resolved neutral populations driven by the cross-field electric field, and is essential for modeling neutral particle transport and momentum exchange with the background plasma. Typical values in the edge region of tokamaks range from hundreds of m/s to a few km/s, depending on the radial electric field and magnetic configuration. The quantity is distinguished from the charge-state-averaged counterpart by resolving the velocity for a specific quantum state of the neutral population. See also the parent quantity [neutral_state_velocity](name:neutral_state_velocity), the charge-state-averaged [parallel_neutral_velocity](name:parallel_neutral_velocity), and the poloidal counterpart [poloidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift](name:poloidal_neutral_state_velocity_due_to_e_cross_b_drift).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the projection of the E×B drift velocity onto the local magnetic field direction points in the same direction as the magnetic field vector $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_neutral_velocity
NAMES.short: Projection of the charge-state-averaged neutral particle fluid velocity vector onto the direction parallel to the local magnetic field line.
NAMES.long:
The parallel neutral velocity $v_{\parallel,n} = \mathbf{v}_n \cdot \hat{b}$ quantifies the field-aligned component of the bulk neutral fluid motion, where $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the total magnetic field. This component governs the parallel transport of neutral particles and momentum, particularly in the edge and divertor regions where charge-exchange and ionization processes couple neutral and plasma flows. Typical magnitudes range from $10^3$ to $10^5$ m/s depending on the neutral source (gas puffing, recycling, or beam injection) and the local plasma collisionality. Measured indirectly through spectroscopic Doppler shifts of neutral emission lines (e.g., D$\alpha$ or H$\alpha$) or inferred from kinetic neutral transport codes.

The parallel neutral velocity is a key observable for the plasma edge flow balance and is related to the bulk [neutral_velocity](name:neutral_velocity) vector field, and to the [parallel_electron_velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity) and [parallel_neutral_momentum](name:parallel_neutral_momentum) quantities for the electron and momentum channels, respectively.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutral velocity component points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle along the field line (the field-line direction of $\hat{b}$).

NAMES.name: parallel_non_inductive_current_density
NAMES.short: Flux-surface-averaged non-inductive current density parallel to the magnetic field, including bootstrap and auxiliary drive contributions.
NAMES.long: The parallel non-inductive current density $j_{\parallel}^{\rm ni}$ is defined as the flux-surface average of the component of the non-inductive current density vector parallel to the local magnetic field, $j_{\parallel}^{\rm ni} = \langle \mathbf{j}^{\rm ni} \cdot \mathbf{B} \rangle / \langle B \rangle$, where $\langle B \rangle$ is the flux-surface-averaged magnetic field strength. This definition ensures that $j_{\parallel}^{\rm ni}$ represents the parallel component exactly on all flux surfaces, not only on-axis. It bundles all current not sustained by the inductive electric field: the bootstrap current arising from neoclassical effects in a pressure pedestal, plus auxiliary currents driven by neutral-beam injection (NBI) and electron-cyclotron (ECCD) or lower-hybrid (LHCD) wave heating. Typical core values range from 0.1–1 MA/m² in H-mode tokamaks, peaking in the steep-gradient region of the pedestal. In practice, this quantity is derived from transport simulations or reconstructed via equilibrium codes that solve the current diffusion equation using measured plasma profiles. It is distinguished from the scalar non-inductive current density by averaging over both angle and radial surfaces, and from the total parallel current density by excluding the inductive (Ohmic) component.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above).

NAMES.name: perpendicular_fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.short: Perpendicular component of the anisotropic pressure tensor carried by the fast (suprathermal) particle population.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular fast particle pressure $p_{\perp,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the pressure component orthogonal to the local magnetic field direction, arising from the gyromotion of energetic particles. In an anisotropic plasma, the full pressure tensor is expressed as $\mathbf{P} = p_\parallel \mathbf{b}\mathbf{b} + p_\perp (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{b}\mathbf{b})$, where $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{B}/B$ is the unit vector along the field. This quantity sums contributions from all suprathermal species, including fast ions and fast electrons, and is obtained from the second moment of the fast-particle distribution function integrated over energy-pitch space. Typical fast-particle perpendicular pressures in the core of ITER baseline scenarios reach tens of kilopascals, strongly coupled to the heating and current drive sources. The flux-surface-averaged quantity enters the Grad–Shafranov equilibrium force balance via the total perpendicular pressure, linking it to the Shafranov shift and local magnetic shear. Standard diagnostics for inferring this quantity include fast-ion $D_\alpha$ (FIDA) measurements, neutron emission spectrometry, and equilibrium reconstruction constrained by external magnetic measurements. For the total anisotropic pressure, refer to the parent quantity [fast_particle_pressure](name:fast_particle_pressure). See also [perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure) and [perpendicular_fast_electron_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_electron_pressure) for individual species contributions, and [parallel_fast_electron_pressure](name:parallel_fast_electron_pressure) for the parallel counterpart.

Typical experimental values in present-day tokamaks (e.g., JET, DIII-D) range from 0.1–10 kPa during neutral beam injection, increasing to tens of kilopascals in burning plasma regimes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pressure tensor component normal to the local magnetic field carries compressive energy density.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux evaluated at the radial location of the internal transport barrier (ITB), which defines the flux surface at the foot of the barrier.
NAMES.long: The poloidal magnetic flux $\psi_{\rm ITB}$ is the value of $\psi$ on the flux surface that marks the onset of the internal transport barrier, a region of reduced turbulent transport in the plasma core. It is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction and serves as a radial coordinate reference for profiling transport coefficients and gradients across the barrier. Typical values in a tokamak with an ITB range from 0.2 to 0.8 of the poloidal flux at the separatrix, depending on barrier strength and heating power. This quantity is the natural companion to [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_separatrix](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_separatrix) and [normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_internal_transport_barrier) for barrier characterisation, and relates to the magnetic shear via [magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal flux $\psi$ increases radially outward from the magnetic axis across the barrier.

NAMES.name: radial_current_density_due_to_inertial
NAMES.short: Radial component of the plasma current density arising from the ion polarization drift, representing the inertial response of the plasma to time-varying electric fields. Defined in the cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, it is a key term in radial force balance and toroidal angular momentum transport.
NAMES.long: This quantity is the radial ($R$) component of the inertial current density $\mathbf{j}_{\text{inertial}}$. In the MHD framework it is the leading-order term from the momentum equation, neglecting displacement current, and is expressed as $j_{\text{inertial}}^r \simeq (n_i m_i / B^2) \partial E_\perp / \partial t$, where $n_i$ is ion density, $m_i$ ion mass, $B$ magnetic field magnitude, and $E_\perp$ the perpendicular electric field. This current arises from the ion polarization drift in time-varying electric fields and is distinct from the diamagnetic drift current, which originates from pressure gradients. Typical magnitudes range from $10^3$ to $10^5$ A/m$^2$ in the core and $10$ to $100$ kA/m$^2$ in the edge of H-mode tokamak plasmas. It constrains the radial electric field via quasi-neutrality and is routinely derived from experimental profiles or gyrokinetic simulations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radial component points outward from the magnetic axis in the $(R, \phi, Z)$ cylindrical system.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_momentum_flux
NAMES.short: Radial component of the momentum flux carried collectively by all ion charge states across a flux surface, governing radial transport of toroidal and poloidal momentum.
NAMES.long: The radial ion momentum flux is a scalar component of the ion momentum flux tensor, quantifying the rate at which ion momentum is transported per unit area radially outward across a flux surface. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, this flux mediates the radial redistribution of plasma rotation, arising from turbulent eddies (Reynolds stress), neoclassical processes, and external torque injection. The quantity is defined as $\Pi_{\mathrm{radial}} = \langle m_i n_i v_r v_\parallel \rangle$ summed over all ion charge states, where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $n_i$ is the ion density, $v_r$ is the radial drift velocity, and $v_\parallel$ is the parallel flow velocity; the angle brackets denote flux-surface averaging. Typical values in the edge region of a tokamak range from $10^3$ to $10^5$ kg·m$^{-1}$·s$^{-2}$, depending on plasma rotation and turbulence levels. This flux is routinely inferred from experimental measurements of the radial force balance and from gyrokinetic simulations, and it connects directly to the evolution of the poloidal and toroidal rotation profiles. See also the parent quantity [ion_momentum_flux](name:ion_momentum_flux) which represents the scalar total, and the charge-state-resolved sibling [radial_ion_state_momentum_flux](name:radial_ion_state_momentum_flux).

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_momentum_flux
NAMES.short: Radial component of the momentum flux tensor carried by neutral particles across a flux surface in the edge plasma.
NAMES.long: This quantity represents the radial transport of momentum per unit area per unit time by neutral particles. It is a component of the full momentum flux tensor $\Pi_{\rm neut}$, which in the edge plasma is dominated by charge-exchange and elastic collisions with the bulk ions. The radial neutral momentum flux plays a key role in the toroidal rotation balance of the edge plasma, as neutrals can act as a momentum sink via ion–neutral friction. Typical radial momentum flux values in the scrape-off layer of a medium-size tokamak range from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-1}\,\text{kg}\,\text{m}^{-1}\,\text{s}^{-2}$, depending on the neutral density and parallel flow velocity. This quantity is related to [neutral_momentum_flux](name:neutral_momentum_flux) as its radial projectionais measured by edge neutral particle analyzers or inferred from spectroscopic measurements of neutral line emission combined with collisional-radiative models.

NAMES.name: radial_neutral_velocity
NAMES.short: Radial component of the charge-state-averaged bulk fluid velocity of neutral particles, describing net radial transport due to pressure gradients and collisional processes.
NAMES.long:
This quantity represents the mass-weighted mean flow velocity of neutral particles projected onto the radial ($R$) direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.  It captures the net radial motion of the neutral ensemble, arising from charge-exchange momentum exchange with the ion population, pressure gradients, and thermal diffusion, averaged over all charge states.  The radial neutral velocity is a key input for edge and scrape-off layer transport modeling, where neutrals from recycling and fueling sources penetrate the confined plasma and carry momentum.  It is typically inferred from fluid or kinetic neutral transport codes (e.g., EIRENE, UEDGE) or from spectroscopic measurements of neutral line emission.  Typical values range from $10^2$–$10^4$ m/s in the edge and SOL, increasing toward the separatrix as neutrals are accelerated by charge-exchange collisions with the ion population.

This scalar component is derived from the full velocity vector [neutral_velocity](name:neutral_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the neutral velocity points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Safety factor q at the radial location of an internal transport barrier, where steep gradients in rotation and pressure reduce turbulent transport.
NAMES.long:
The safety factor $q$ is defined as $q = \frac{d\Phi}{d\Psi} / (2\pi)$, where $\Phi$ is the toroidal magnetic flux and $\Psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux. This ratio measures the helicity of magnetic field lines in a toroidal plasma confinement device.

At the internal transport barrier (ITB) location, the safety factor often exhibits a local plateau or reversed shear profile that contributes to the formation of the barrier. Typical values at an ITB depend on the plasma scenario: for a monotonic $q$-profile, the ITB may occur at $q \sim 1.5$–$3$; for a reversed-shear scenario, the ITB radius can coincide with the minimum $q$ value $q_\mathrm{min}$ which may be in the range $2$–$4$.

This quantity is the value of $q$ evaluated at the radial position where the ITB is identified, typically from profiles of ion temperature, electron temperature, toroidal rotation, or density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $q$ is defined in the right-handed $(R, \phi, Z)$ cylindrical basis, corresponding to the usual toroidal-poloidal sense.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_density
NAMES.short: Number density of the bulk thermal electron population, following a Maxwellian velocity distribution.
NAMES.long:
The thermal electron density $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ represents the number of free electrons per unit volume in the thermal (Maxwellian) population of the plasma, excluding suprathermal or runaway electrons. It is a fundamental parameter in plasma transport, setting the plasma frequency $\omega_{pe} = \sqrt{n_{e,\mathrm{th}} e^2 / (m_e \epsilon_0)}$, the electron pressure $p_e = n_{e,\mathrm{th}} k_B T_e$, and the collision rates. Typical core values in tokamaks range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{20}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, while the scrape-off layer density is typically $10^{18} \,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ or lower. This quantity is routinely measured by interferometry, reflectometry, and Langmuir probes, and is distinguished from the total electron density by excluding the fast electron component. It is closely related to [thermal_electron_pressure](name:thermal_electron_pressure) and [electron_density](name:electron_density).

For transport modeling, the thermal electron density profile is a key input to the electron density gradient drive for turbulence and the bootstrap current calculation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the number of thermal electrons per unit volume is positive.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_pressure
NAMES.short: Isotropic thermal pressure of the bulk Maxwellian electron population, arising from random thermal motion and excluding suprathermal contributions.
NAMES.long:
The thermal electron pressure $p_{e,\mathrm{th}} = n_e k_B T_e$ is the isotropic scalar pressure of the bulk Maxwellian electron population, where $n_e$ is the electron density and $T_e$ is the electron temperature. This quantity excludes the pressure contribution from fast (suprathermal) electrons; the total electron pressure is the sum $p_{e,\mathrm{total}} = p_{e,\mathrm{th}} + p_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$. The thermal electron pressure is routinely inferred from Thomson scattering or electron cyclotron emission measurements of $n_e$ and $T_e$; typical core values in tokamak plasmas range from 10 to 500 kPa. The thermal electron density [thermal_electron_density](name:thermal_electron_density) is a closely related quantity, while the isotropic thermal pressure summed over all species is captured by [thermal_pressure](name:thermal_pressure).

The thermal electron pressure provides the dominant contribution to the total plasma pressure in most fusion-relevant regimes and enters directly into the radial force balance via the pressure-gradient drive for the diamagnetic current and the Pfirsch–Schlüter current.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plasma exerts an outward isotropic force per unit area.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_electron_density
NAMES.short: Temporal rate of change of the electron number density.
NAMES.long: The time derivative of the electron density, $\partial n_e / \partial t$, represents the net rate of change of the free electron population per unit volume, including contributions from ionization, recombination, and transport processes. This quantity is the continuity-equation source term for the electron density evolution, where positive values indicate increasing electron inventory and negative values indicate net loss.
