In fusion plasmas, it is inferred from diagnostic time traces of line-averaged density (interferometry) or volume-averaged density, with typical core magnitudes of $10^{19}$--$10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$ during density ramps, transients, or pellet injection events. The time derivative is linked to the particle sources and sinks in the electron continuity equation and provides a global measure of density evolution that complements the local profiles of `[electron_density](name:electron_density)` and its radial gradient.

NAMES.name: toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the bulk plasma center-of-mass fluid velocity, weighted by species mass.
NAMES.long: The toroidal center-of-mass velocity quantifies the net rotation of the bulk plasma in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, averaged over all species present. In tokamaks this rotation is the dominant component, typically reaching $10\!-\!100$ km/s in the core, and is driven by neutral beam injection, the intrinsic plasma torque, and turbulent momentum transport. It is routinely measured via charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) on impurity ions, or inferred from motional Stark effect diagnostics, and enters the radial force balance $E_r = v_\phi B_\theta - v_\theta B_\phi + (1/Z_i e n_i) \nabla p_i$. This component is distinguished from the total rotation vector `[center_of_mass_velocity](name:center_of_mass_velocity)` by isolating only the toroidal projection; the poloidal counterpart is `[poloidal_center_of_mass_velocity](name:poloidal_center_of_mass_velocity)`.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the bulk plasma rotates in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above).

NAMES.name: toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Toroidal flow velocity of helium-3 ions at the radius of the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal velocity $v_{\phi,\mathrm{^3He}}$ of the helium-3 ion population at the internal transport barrier (ITB) characterizes the toroidal rotation of this minority species at the narrow radial layer where turbulent transport is sharply reduced. The ITB position is identified by a steep gradient region in the ion temperature or toroidal rotation profiles. This velocity is typically measured from the Doppler shift of charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) lines on the 529 nm $\mathrm{^3He^{2+}}$ transition, or inferred from the main-ion toroidal velocity via neoclassical theory. Typical values in ITB plasmas range from 20 to 150 km/s, with direction determined by the balance of neutral beam torque and intrinsic rotation. The sign convention follows the IMAS cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

See also [toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_pedestal) for the same species at other radial positions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $v_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above).

NAMES.name: toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Toroidal flow velocity of the helium-3 ion population at the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long: The toroidal velocity $v_{\phi, \text{He}^3}$ of the helium-3 ion species at the magnetic axis captures the bulk rotation of the minority helium-3 population in the direction of the toroidal angle $\phi$. This rotation results from the combined effects of momentum transport, neutral beam injection, and intrinsic rotation sources, and is a key input for modeling fast-particle confinement and Alfvén eigenmode stability. The velocity is typically measured via charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) on the helium-3 emission line, providing line-of-sight integrated signals that are inverted to local values. Core toroidal rotation velocities in tokamaks range from a few km/s in ohmic plasmas to over 300 km/s in strongly beam-heated H-modes. The helium-3 rotation often differs from the bulk deuterium rotation due to differences in collisional coupling and diamagnetic contributions, making this a valuable constraint for multi-species transport analysis. Related quantities include [toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_pedestal) and [helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the helium-3 ions rotate in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above).

NAMES.name: toroidal_neon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the neon ion fluid rotation velocity at the radial location of the internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long: The toroidal rotation velocity $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ne}}$ of the neon ion population at the internal transport barrier (ITB) quantifies the toroidal flow of this impurity species. The ITB is a plasma region characterized by a steep gradient in the toroidal rotation profile, often correlated with reduced turbulent transport and improved confinement. This quantity is routinely measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) using the Doppler shift of neon emission lines, with typical values in the range 10–100 km/s for the core ITB in H-mode tokamak plasmas. The toroidal velocity of neon is closely related to the bulk ion rotation and can differ from the main ion velocity due to impurity poloidal asymmetries and neoclassical effects — see [toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_pedestal) for comparisons at other radial locations and ion species.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal velocity points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above the machine).

NAMES.name: toroidal_neon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Toroidal rotation velocity of neon impurity ions at the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long: The toroidal component $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Ne}}$ of the neon ion fluid velocity at the magnetic axis, defined as the $\hat{\phi}$ projection of the local flow vector. This quantity is a key measure of the central rotation of intrinsic or injected neon impurities, typically measured by charge exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) via Doppler shifts of visible transitions from the Ne$^{10+}$ or He-like charge states. Core neon rotation velocities in conventional tokamaks range from $10^5$ to over $10^6$ m/s depending on the neutral beam torque input and the collisional coupling between neon and the bulk deuterium. The value at the magnetic axis is often the peak rotation velocity, linking to studies of neoclassical impurity transport and radial electric field estimates via the force balance equation. See also the radial profile provided by [toroidal_neon_velocity_at_pedestal](name:toroidal_neon_velocity_at_pedestal) and the analogous quantity for another impurity species, [toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_magnetic_axis](name:toroidal_helium_3_velocity_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal flow is directed in the increasing $\phi$ direction (counter-clockwise viewed from above).

NAMES.name: toroidal_neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.short: The toroidal component of the momentum diffusion coefficient for neutral particles, characterizing the rate of diffusive transport of toroidal angular momentum by neutral atoms and molecules across the plasma edge.
NAMES.long: The toroidal neutral momentum diffusion coefficient $D^{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{neut}}$ enters the momentum balance equation for neutral particles, $\partial_t (m_n n_n v^{\mathrm{tor}}_n) + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{tor}}_{\mathrm{neut}} = S^{\mathrm{tor}}_{\mathrm{neut}}$, where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{tor}}_{\mathrm{neut}} = -D^{\mathrm{tor},\mathrm{neut}} \nabla (m_n n_n v^{\mathrm{tor}}_n)$, with $m_n$ the neutral mass, $n_n$ the neutral density, and $v^{\mathrm{tor}}_n$ the toroidal neutral fluid velocity. This quantity reflects the impact of charge-exchange and elastic scattering collisions on neutrals that carry momentum from the core toward the wall. It is analogous to the toroidal ion momentum diffusion coefficient $D_{\mathrm{ion}}^{\mathrm{tor}}$, but accounts for the longer mean free path and weaker magnetic coupling of neutrals. While the radial component (`[radial_neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:radial_neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient)`) governs the loss of angular momentum across flux surfaces, the toroidal component captures the diffusive redistribution of toroidal momentum within a flux surface by neutrals. Typical values in the scrape-off layer range from $1\, \mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}$ to $100\, \mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}$, depending on neutral density and collisionality. This quantity is related to the full vector coefficient `[neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:neutral_momentum_diffusion_coefficient)` and to its radial counterpart `[toroidal_momentum_diffusion_coefficient](name:toroidal_momentum_diffusion_coefficient)`.

NAMES.name: toroidal_neutral_state_velocity
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the flow velocity for neutral particles in a specific quantum state, resolved relative to the geometric toroidal direction.
NAMES.long: The toroidal component $v_{\phi}^{\mathrm{neutral,state}}$ represents the velocity of neutral particles (e.g., ground-state or excited-state hydrogen, deuterium) along the toroidal direction $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This quantity is used in neutral particle transport models to assess momentum exchange through charge-exchange and ionization processes. Typical magnitudes range from $10^3$ to $10^5$ m/s in tokamak edge and divertor regions, depending on the neutral density and plasma flow.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the velocity points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: toroidal_total_current_density
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the total electric current density vector, representing the net current density flowing in the geometric toroidal direction on the generalized grid.
NAMES.long: The toroidal total current density $j_{\phi,\text{total}}$ is the projection of the total current density vector $\mathbf{j}_{\text{total}}$ onto the toroidal unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame: $j_{\phi,\text{total}} = \mathbf{j}_{\text{total}} \cdot \hat{\phi}$. It sums all current contributions in the toroidal direction, including the plasma current, eddy currents induced by time-varying magnetic fields, and any externally driven currents. This quantity is typically computed from equilibrium reconstruction or from generalized grid (GGD) field values in the plasma edge and scrape-off layer, with magnitudes reaching $10^5$–$10^7$ A/m$^2$ in the core and decreasing toward the plasma boundary. The toroidal component is the dominant contribution to the total current density in tokamaks, directly related to the confining poloidal magnetic field via Ampère's law. See the vector parent [total_current_density](name:total_current_density) and the plasma-only variant [toroidal_current_density](name:toroidal_current_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $j_{\phi,\text{total}}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise when viewed from above).

NAMES.name: total_ion_density
NAMES.short: Number density of all ion species combined, summing thermal and suprathermal populations and all charge states, at each location in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The total ion density $n_{i,\text{total}}$ is the sum over all ion species, charge states, and thermal plus suprathermal populations at a given spatial location. It is a fundamental transport quantity that determines the ion contribution to quasineutrality alongside the electron density $n_e$, and enters the calculation of the plasma effective charge $Z_{\text{eff}}$ and ion pressure. Typical values range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{20}\,\text{m}^{-3}$ in the core of magnetically confined plasmas, dropping by orders of magnitude at the edge. The total ion density is routinely inferred from Thomson scattering (via $n_e$ and $Z_{\text{eff}}$) or measured directly by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy combined with neutral beam injection. It is closely related to the flux-surface-averaged total ion density at the separatrix `[flux_surface_averaged_total_ion_density_at_separatrix](name:flux_surface_averaged_total_ion_density_at_separatrix)` and to the total ion density at the magnetic axis `[total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis)`.

Cross-references to `[ion_density](name:ion_density)`, `[electron_density](name:electron_density)`, and `[thermal_density](name:thermal_density)` provide related density quantifications.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $n_{i,\text{total}}$ is a positive scalar number density.

NAMES.name: total_ion_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Total number density of all ion species at the magnetic axis, characterizing the core ion population available for fusion reactions.
NAMES.long:
The total ion density at the magnetic axis is the sum over all thermal ion species (including main fuel, impurity, and fast ions) of their number densities, evaluated at the innermost flux surface where $\nabla \psi = 0$. This density is a critical input for calculating core fusion power, as the reaction rate scales as $n_i^2 \langle \sigma v \rangle$, with $\langle \sigma v \rangle$ the Maxwellian-averaged cross section. It is typically measured via charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or inferred from equilibrium reconstruction combined with Thomson scattering data; values in the core of present tokamaks range from $10^{19}\,\text{m}^{-3}$ to $10^{20}\,\text{m}^{-3}$. The density complements the energy content described by [ion_temperature_at_magnetic_axis](name:ion_temperature_at_magnetic_axis) and provides a boundary condition for impurity transport models anchored at the magnetic axis.

Related quantities include [total_ion_density_at_separatrix](name:total_ion_density_at_separatrix) and [total_ion_density_at_divertor_target](name:total_ion_density_at_divertor_target), which describe the same sum at outer locations, enabling density gradient analysis.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the particle number count increases, always positive for physical plasmas.

NAMES.name: total_ion_pressure
NAMES.short: Total pressure of the thermal ion population, summed over all ion species and charge states.
NAMES.long:
The total ion pressure $p_i$ is defined as the sum of partial pressures of all thermal ion species in the plasma, $p_i = \sum_s n_s k_B T_s$, where $n_s$ and $T_s$ are the density and temperature of species $s$, and $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant. This quantity excludes non-thermal (e.g., fast ion) contributions and magnetic pressure, and it enters the total plasma pressure balance $p_\text{tot} = p_e + p_i + p_\text{fast} + p_\text{mag}$ for equilibrium reconstruction and transport modeling. Typical values range from 10–100 kPa in the core of a tokamak plasma to 0.1–1 kPa in the scrape-off layer. It is routinely inferred from ion temperature and density profiles measured by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or Thomson scattering combined with Langmuir probe data. See [thermal_pressure](name:thermal_pressure) for the electron counterpart and [ion_temperature](name:ion_temperature) for the underlying kinetic parameter.

This pressure contributes to the plasma diamagnetic current and energy confinement, and is a key input to stability analyzes as part of the plasma beta $\beta = 2\mu_0 p / B^2$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pressure acts outward from the magnetic axis, by convention the total pressure is positive-definite.

NAMES.name: vertical_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) component of the current density driven by the traceless (anisotropic) part of the ion stress tensor, arising from heat-viscous momentum transport in the edge and scrape-off layer plasma.
NAMES.long: The vertical current density $j_{z}^{\text{HV}} = \hat{Z} \cdot \mathbf{j}_{\text{HV}}$ is the projection of the heat-viscosity-driven current density vector onto the geometric vertical axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ coordinate system. This current arises from the collisional momentum exchange due to the traceless part of the ion stress tensor, which is generated by ion temperature gradients and the ion diamagnetic drift. The heat-viscosity current density is related to the total current density set by the ion momentum balance: $\mathbf{j}_{\text{HV}} = - (c/B) \, \hat{b} \times \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_{\text{HV}}$, where $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{\text{HV}}$ is the heat-viscous stress tensor and $\hat{b}$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field. Typical vertical components are of order 0.1–10 kA·m$^{-2}$ in the pedestal region of H-mode tokamak plasmas, where large temperature gradients drive strong heat-viscous forces. This quantity is the vertical component of [current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) and forms a family with [vertical_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) and [toroidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current density vector points in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$ (upward in the machine frame).

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Free electron number density averaged over the confined plasma volume bounded by the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged electron density $\langle n_e \rangle \equiv V^{-1} \int_V n_e \, dV$ characterizes the global particle inventory of the confined plasma, where $V$ is the volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface. Together with the volume-averaged electron temperature $[\text{volume\_averaged\_electron\_temperature}](name:volume_averaged_electron_temperature)$ and the plasma volume, it sets the global particle and energy confinement times. This quantity is a key input for the Greenwald density limit $n_G = I_p / (\pi a^2)$ and is routinely derived from interferometry or Thomson scattering profiles integrated over the equilibrium flux-surface geometry. Typical values range from $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in low-density L-mode to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in high-density H-mode and $10^{21}$ m$^{-3}$ in ITER baseline scenarios.

This global parameter is directly comparable to the volume-averaged runaway electron density $[\text{volume\_averaged\_runaway\_electron\_density}](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_density)$ for disruption studies and complements the electron density profile $[\text{electron\_density}](name:electron_density).$
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron density integrated over the confined volume is positive.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_electron_temperature
NAMES.short: Thermal energy of the electron population averaged over the confined plasma volume inside the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged electron temperature $\langle T_e \rangle$ is a global confinement metric obtained by integrating the local electron temperature profile over the plasma volume $V$ enclosed by the last closed flux surface (LCFS): $\langle T_e \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V T_e \, dV$. It characterizes the overall electron thermal energy content of the plasma and is routinely derived from Thomson scattering or electron cyclotron emission measurements in combination with equilibrium reconstruction. Typical core values in diverted tokamak H-mode plasmas range from 0.5 to 5 keV, depending on heating power and size. This quantity is directly related to the volume-averaged electron density $[\text{name:flux_surface_averaged_electron_density}]$ and the total stored thermal energy through the relation $W_\text{th} = \frac{3}{2} \langle n_e T_e + n_i T_i \rangle V$. See also the volume-averaged ion temperature $[\text{name:volume_averaged_ion_temperature}]$ and the line-averaged electron temperature $[\text{name:line_averaged_electron_temperature}]$.

$\langle T_e \rangle$ is always positive for a physical electron population, as it represents the mean kinetic energy per electron. It serves as a key scalar metric in confinement scaling laws such as the ITER H-mode power threshold and energy confinement time databases.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron thermal energy exceeds the background noise floor.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_helium_3_density
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged number density of helium-3 ions over the entire confined plasma region.
NAMES.long: The volume-averaged helium-3 ion density $\langle n_{^3\text{He}} \rangle_V = V^{-1} \int_V n_{^3\text{He}}(\mathbf{r})\,dV$ quantifies the mean concentration of singly-ionized helium-3 (³He⁺) particles across the confined plasma volume. This quantity is a global measure of ³He fueling, commonly from neutral beam injection or RF minority heating, and is used to assess fusion reactivity in D-³He scenarios or as a minority ICRH absorber. Typical values range from $10^{17}$ to $10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on the ³He gas puff rate and plasma transport conditions. The volume-averaged density is derived from the 3-D density field $n_{^3\text{He}}(\mathbf{r})$, which may be measured by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy (CXRS) or inferred from neutral particle analysis. See also [line_averaged_helium_3_density](name:line_averaged_helium_3_density) for the line-of-sight chord average, and [helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:helium_3_density_at_magnetic_axis) for the on-axis value.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the total number of ³He ions in the confined volume is non-negative (intrinsically positive-definite density).

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_ion_density
NAMES.short: Ion number density averaged over the confined plasma volume inside the last closed flux surface. This global quantity serves as a core fuel density metric for confinement analysis.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged ion density $\langle n_i \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V n_i(\mathbf{r}) \, dV$ integrates the local ion density $n_i(\mathbf{r})$ over the plasma volume $V$ contained within the last closed flux surface (LCFS). It provides a single-figure measure of the ion species density for confinement scaling and fueling studies. In conventional tokamak operation, $\langle n_i \rangle$ typically ranges from $10^{19}\,\text{m}^{-3}$ in low-density L-mode plasmas to $10^{20}\,\text{m}^{-3}$ in high-density H-mode scenarios; for a pure deuterium plasma it is approximately half the volume-averaged electron density. This quantity is extracted from kinetic profile measurements (e.g., charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or Thomson scattering with a representative ion species assumption) and used as input to global particle and energy confinement databases. It is complementary to [volume averaged electron temperature](name:volume_averaged_electron_temperature) for assessing thermal pressure and to [flux surface averaged total ion density at separatrix](name:flux_surface_averaged_total_ion_density_at_separatrix) for boundary condition analysis.

The term 'ion' here refers to a specific ion species (e.g., deuterium or carbon) as indicated by the subject qualifier in the standard name.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the volume integral yields a positive number density.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_iron_density
NAMES.short: Number density of iron impurity ions averaged over the entire confined plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged iron density $ ar{n}_{\mathrm{Fe}} = (1/V) \int n_{\mathrm{Fe}}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV$ quantifies the total iron impurity content in the plasma normalized by the plasma volume $V$. It is a key metric for assessing radiative power losses, fuel dilution, and core plasma contamination from wall-sputtered impurities. Typical values in diverted tokamak plasmas range from $10^{13}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ in low-impurity H-modes up to $10^{17}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ in high-density or disrupted discharges where wall erosion is significant. The volume average smooths profile peaking and is complemented by local measurements such as [iron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:iron_density_at_magnetic_axis) and [flux_surface_averaged_iron_density](name:flux_surface_averaged_iron_density), which capture spatial variation.

Volume-averaged iron density is routinely inferred from bolometric and spectroscopic measurements combined with impurity transport modeling using codes such as STRAHL or AURORA. The quantity respects the sum rule: $\bar{n}_{\mathrm{Fe}} = \bar{n}_\mathrm{e} \cdot \langle c_{\mathrm{Fe}} \rangle$, where $\langle c_{\mathrm{Fe}} \rangle$ is the iron concentration and $\bar{n}_\mathrm{e}$ is the volume-averaged electron density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the iron ion density is radially integrable over the plasma volume (non-negative physical density).

NAMES.name: gyrokinetic_magnetic_shear
NAMES.short: Dimensionless magnetic shear at the outboard midplane normalized radius, used to parameterize the parallel variation of the safety factor in local gyrokinetic flux-tube simulations.
NAMES.long:
The gyrokinetic magnetic shear quantifies the radial gradient of the safety factor $q$ relative to a local flux-surface minor radius $r$, defined as $\hat{s} = (r/q)\,dq/dr$ for a given reference flux surface. It controls the ballooning-mode structure and is a key stability parameter for drift-wave microinstabilities, with typical values ranging from $\hat{s} \approx 0.5$ (weak shear) to $\hat{s} \approx 3$ (strong shear) in tokamak core plasmas. This quantity is extracted from the equilibrium reconstruction at the outboard midplane position where the local minor radius $r$ is measured, and it is used as an input to gyrokinetic codes to set the flux-surface geometry. The definition follows the standard local-shear convention, which differs from the equilibrium IDS magnetic shear (defined with the normalized toroidal flux coordinate).

Related quantities include [magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis](name:magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis) and [magnetic_shear_at_separatrix](name:magnetic_shear_at_separatrix), which evaluate the local magnetic shear at specific radial positions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the safety factor increases with minor radius.

NAMES.name: lower_triangularity_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless shaping parameter quantifying the D-shaped asymmetry of the lower half of a tokamak flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The lower triangularity $\delta_{\text{lower}} = (R_{\text{lower}} - R_{\text{geo}}) / a$ measures the radial shift of the flux surface midpoint at the lower midplane relative to the geometric center, normalized by the minor radius $a$. This parameter characterizes the bean-shaped distortion of the plasma cross-section and influences magnetohydrodynamic stability and confinement. In local gyrokinetic simulations using Miller parametrization, $\delta_{\text{lower}}$ together with the flux surface elongation and the radial shape derivatives defines the magnetic geometry at a given flux surface. Typical values for conventional tokamaks range from $\delta_{\text{lower}} \approx 0.1$ to $0.5$ for strongly shaped plasmas, with the separatrix value usually larger than interior surfaces.

The lower triangularity complements the upper triangularity; together they describe the vertical asymmetry of the flux surface shape, linked to [upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface](name:upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface) and [elongation_of_flux_surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flux surface midpoint is shifted radially inward at the lower midplane, corresponding to a D-shaped cross-section.

NAMES.name: normalized_debye_length
NAMES.short: Debye length normalized to a reference value, setting the spatial scale for gyrokinetic simulations and indicating the strength of electrostatic screening.
NAMES.long: The normalized Debye length is defined as $\lambda_D / \lambda_{D,ref}$, where $\lambda_D = \sqrt{\epsilon_0 T_e / n_e e^2}$ is the electron Debye length and $\lambda_{D,ref}$ is a reference Debye length from the gyrokinetic normalization scheme. A value much less than 1 indicates strong electrostatic screening relative to the reference scale, justifying the quasi-neutrality approximation in the simulation. Typical values in the turbulent core of tokamak plasmas range from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: normalized_temperature
NAMES.short: Temperature of a gyrokinetic particle species normalized to a reference temperature for the simulation.
NAMES.long:
The normalized temperature $T/T_{\mathrm{ref}}$ scales the species temperature by the reference temperature $T_{\mathrm{ref}}$ that defines the simulation's thermal energy scale. In local gyrokinetic flux-tube simulations this dimensionless ratio, together with [normalized_density](name:normalized_density) and [normalized_mass](name:normalized_mass), defines the species input parameters for the linearized collision operator and the background Maxwellian. The reference temperature is typically the on-axis or volume-averaged electron temperature; typical values for a deuterium main-ion species are $T/T_{\mathrm{ref}} = 1$ when the species temperature is set equal to the reference.

The combination of normalized temperature with [normalized_density](name:normalized_density) and [normalized_mass](name:normalized_mass) determines the species pressure ratio and the diamagnetic drift frequencies that drive microinstabilities.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the species temperature exceeds the reference temperature.

NAMES.name: parallel_gyrocenter_energy
NAMES.short: Normalized velocity-space moment of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function, integrating the product of the parallel kinetic energy and the perpendicular kinetic energy.
NAMES.long:
The parallel gyrocenter energy moment $\langle  rac{1}{2} m v_	ext{par}^2 angle_	ext{gc}$ is the gyrocenter energy component along the magnetic field direction, defined as the velocity-space integral of $ rac{1}{2} m v_	ext{par}^2 f_	ext{gc}$ normalized to the reference density and temperature scale. Together with the perpendicular gyrocenter energy, which is the integral of $ rac{1}{2} m v_	ext{perp}^2 f_	ext{gc}$, it composes the total gyrocenter energy vector $[\text{gyrocenter\_energy}](name:gyrocenter_energy)$. This moment quantifies the parallel kinetic energy stored in the perturbed distribution for a linear eigenmode, and its ratio to the perpendicular moment informs the anisotropy of the fluctuation energy in gyrokinetic turbulence simulations. Typical values for core microturbulence are order unity when normalized, reflecting near-equipartition between parallel and perpendicular energy in electrostatic instabilities. The sign convention is set by the gyrocenter distribution moment definition: $\langle \frac{1}{2} m v_\text{par}^2 \rangle_\text{gc} = \int \frac{1}{2} m v_\text{par}^2 \, f_\text{gc} \, d^3 v$, where the moment is positive for any positive $f_\text{gc}$.

See also the perpendicular counterpart $[\text{perpendicular\_gyrocenter\_energy}](name:perpendicular_gyrocenter_energy)$ for the complementary component, and note that the sum of these two moments gives the total $[\text{gyrocenter\_energy}](name:gyrocenter_energy)$ per mode.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function is non-negative over the velocity-space volume.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_gyrocenter_energy
NAMES.short: Normalized perpendicular kinetic energy moment of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution for a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the normalized perpendicular gyrocenter energy, computed as the velocity-space moment $\int \frac{1}{2} m v_\perp^2 \, \delta f_g \, J_1(k_\perp \rho_g) \, d^3\mathbf{v}$, where $\delta f_g$ is the perturbed gyrocenter distribution, $J_1$ is the first-order Bessel function with argument $k_\perp \rho_g$, $m$ is the species mass, and $v_\perp$ is the speed perpendicular to the magnetic field. It represents the second component of the two-component vector `[gyrocenter_energy](name:gyrocenter_energy)`. This moment quantifies how the perturbed distribution transfers energy into perpendicular gyromotion, and is typically evaluated for each complex eigenmode in local gyrokinetic simulations at a single wavevector. The perpendicular gyrocenter energy is related to the perpendicular pressure through the second moment of the distribution; see `[perpendicular_gyrocenter_pressure](name:perpendicular_gyrocenter_pressure)`. Typical values in normalized gyrokinetic units range from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-1}$ for low-amplitude linear modes.

Cross-reference: This scalar is the perpendicular component of `[gyrocenter_energy](name:gyrocenter_energy)` and complements `[parallel_gyrocenter_energy](name:parallel_gyrocenter_energy)`. It is distinct from the particle-frame quantity `[perpendicular_particle_energy](name:perpendicular_particle_energy)`, which does not include the gyroaveraging Bessel factor.
NAMES.sign: Positive for any perturbed gyrocenter distribution with non-zero perpendicular kinetic energy.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_gyrocenter_pressure
NAMES.short: Normalized perpendicular pressure moment of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution, weighted by the first-order Bessel function J1, for a linear gyrokinetic eigenmode.
NAMES.long: The perpendicular pressure moment of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function, normalized to a reference value, is defined as the velocity-space integral of the product of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution, the perpendicular energy (proportional to the square of the perpendicular velocity), and the first-order Bessel function J1. This weighting arises from the gyroaverage operation in gyrokinetic theory, accounting for finite Larmor radius effects. The moment characterizes the perpendicular temperature perturbation associated with a linear eigenmode, typically derived from gyrokinetic simulations using a local flux-tube model. Typical values in the plasma core range from 1e-5 to 1 (normalized), with the sign determined by the eigenmode structure. Normalization is to a reference pressure, often the equilibrium thermal pressure at a reference radius.

NAMES.name: perturbed_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Normalized perturbed parallel magnetic field eigenmode component in local linear gyrokinetic simulations, representing the electromagnetic fluctuation along the guide field.
NAMES.long: The normalized perturbed parallel magnetic field $\delta B_{\|}/B_0$ is a dimensionless quantity characterizing the electromagnetic fluctuation of the magnetic field along the equilibrium guide field direction in local linear gyrokinetic simulations. It is defined as the parallel component of the perturbed magnetic vector potential normalized to the equilibrium magnetic field strength $B_0$ and the perpendicular wavenumber $k_\perp$, satisfying $\delta B_{\|} = - i k_\perp \delta A_{\|}$. Typical values range from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-1}$, depending on plasma beta and the mode being considered (e.g., kinetic ballooning modes yield larger values than ion temperature gradient modes). The quantity is resolved in the perpendicular wavenumber plane spanned by $k_x$ (radial binormal wavenumber, m$^{-1}$) and $k_y$ (poloidal binormal wavenumber, m$^{-1}$).

NAMES.name: radial_particle_flux
NAMES.short: Normalized radial particle flux driven by the perturbed parallel magnetic field component, resolved in the radial dimension of the IMAS cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long: The radial particle flux Γ<sub>r</sub> quantifies the net outward (or inward) transport of particles across flux surfaces due to electromagnetic fluctuations at the gyrokinetic scale. It is normalized to a reference gyrokinetic flux unit (e.g., n<sub>ref</sub> c<sub>s</sub> ρ<sub>s</sub><sup>2</sup>/a), making it dimensionless. The flux is driven by the perturbed magnetic-field component parallel to the equilibrium field ($\delta B_\parallel$) via the $\tilde{\mathbf{E}} \times \mathbf{B}$ drift nonlinearity, where $\tilde{\mathbf{E}}$ is the fluctuating electric field and $\mathbf{B}$ is the equilibrium magnetic field. This radial component isolates the transport perpendicular to flux surfaces, as opposed to the poloidal or toroidal projections. Typical values in gyrokinetic simulations of core tokamak turbulence range from $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-2}$ (normalized units) for ion-scale modes, with sign indicating net inward (negative) or outward (positive) transport. The flux is computed from a velocity-space integral of the perturbed gyrocenter distribution function and the radial component of the magnetic drift. This quantity is a specialization of the more generic [particle_flux](name:particle_flux) and relates to the [turbulent_energy_flux](name:turbulent_energy_flux) via the convective heat transport channel. It is distinct from the [toroidal_momentum_flux](name:toroidal_momentum_flux), which involves the parallel momentum density. The [beta](name:beta) measures the electromagnetic strength that modifies the fluctuation amplitude and thus the flux magnitude.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net particle flux is directed outward (from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary).

NAMES.name: upper_triangularity_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: A dimensionless shaping parameter quantifying the asymmetry of the upper half of a tokamak flux surface, defined as (R_upper - R_geo)/a, where R_upper is the radial distance at the upper midplane and R_geo is the geometric center radius.
NAMES.long:
Upper triangularity $\delta_{\text{upper}}$ is a dimensionless shaping parameter that measures the D-shaped elongation of the upper half of a magnetic flux surface in a tokamak. It is defined as:

$$
\delta_{\text{upper}} = \frac{R_{\text{upper}} - R_{\text{geo}}}{a},
$$

where $R_{\text{upper}}$ is the major radius coordinate in the IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame at the upper midplane (the intersection of the flux surface with the horizontal plane at $Z = Z_{\text{axis}} + \kappa a$, with $\kappa$ the elongation), $R_{\text{geo}}$ is the geometric center radius of the flux surface (the midpoint between the innermost and outermost radial extents of the surface at the outboard midplane), and $a$ is the minor radius.

A positive $\delta_{\text{upper}}$ corresponds to a D-shaped cross-section with the inward-pointing apex toward the machine symmetry axis. Typical values range from 0 (elliptical shape) to approximately 0.5 (highly triangular), with values between 0.2 and 0.4 common in H-mode plasmas.

This quantity is of primary interest in gyrokinetic turbulence simulation codes, where it affects the magnetic drift frequency and geometry of flux surfaces, thereby influencing microinstability growth rates and turbulent transport levels.
